abstract: We present a general and systematic method for neural network design based on the genetic algorithm. The technique works in conjunction with network learning rules, addressing aspects of the network's gross architecture, connectivity, and learning rule parameters. Networks can be optimiled for various application(cid:173) specific criteria, such as learning speed, generalilation, robustness and connectivity. The approach is model-independent. We describe a prototype system, NeuroGENESYS, that employs the backpropagation learning rule. Experiments on several small problems have been conducted. In each case, NeuroGENESYS has produced networks that perform significantly better than the randomly generated networks of its initial population. The com(cid:173) putational feasibility of our approach is discussed.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a systematic method for designing neural networks with a genetic algorithm. The search addresses broad architectural choices, connectivity, and parameters of the learning rule. It operates alongside network learning, making the design of the learning system itself part of the optimization problem.

The method can target criteria that depend on the application, including learning speed, generalization, robustness, and connectivity. This matters because a suitable architecture depends on what the network must accomplish and which properties are valuable. The general approach is described as independent of a particular network model, while the prototype, NeuroGENESYS, uses backpropagation.

Experiments on several small problems show that NeuroGENESYS produces networks that perform significantly better than the randomly generated networks in its starting population. That comparison demonstrates improvement through the design search on the problems considered. The paper also discusses computational feasibility, treating the cost of finding an architecture as part of the practical question of whether automated network design is useful.
summary.tldr: NeuroGENESYS uses genetic search to improve network architectures and learning parameters for application-specific goals.

title: Designing Application-Specific Neural Networks Using the Genetic Algorithm

abstract: The Hopfield network (Hopfield, 1982,1984) provides a simple model of an associative memory in a neuronal structure. This model, however, is based on highly artificial assumptions, especially the use of formal-two state neu(cid:173) rons (Hopfield, 1982) or graded-response neurons (Hopfield, 1984). \Vhat happens if we replace the formal neurons by 'real' biological neurons? \Ve address this question in two steps. First, we show that a simple model of a neuron can capture all relevant features of neuron spiking, i. e., a wide range of spiking frequencies and a realistic distribution of interspike inter(cid:173) vals. Second, we construct an associative memory by linking these neurons together. The analytical solution for a large and fully connected network shows that the Hopfield solution is valid only for neurons with a short re(cid:173) fractory period. If the refractory period is longer than a crit.ical duration ie, the solutions are qualitatively different. The associative character of the solutions, however, is preserved.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether associative memory survives when a Hopfield network's simplified neurons are replaced with models that capture biological spiking. The issue is whether the memory behavior depends on the artificial two-state or graded-response units used in the original formulation, or can persist under a different description of individual neurons.

The authors proceed in two stages. They first introduce a simple neuron model that reproduces a broad range of firing frequencies and a realistic distribution of times between spikes. They then connect these neurons into an associative memory and derive an analytical solution for a large, fully connected network.

The result identifies the refractory period, the recovery interval following a spike, as a decisive parameter. The Hopfield solution remains valid only when this interval is short. Beyond a critical duration, the solutions change qualitatively, yet retain their associative character. Thus, introducing spiking dynamics changes the form of the network's behavior without eliminating the memory property under the conditions analyzed.
summary.tldr: Associative memory persists in a spiking-neuron network even when longer refractory periods produce behavior different from the Hopfield solution.

title: Associative Memory in a Network of `Biological' Neurons

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational account of rodent navigation that brings together representations of location, heading, and movement-based position updating. Its place-cell analogue represents where the animal is, while its head-direction analogue represents which way it faces independently of location. Navigation requires these representations to remain consistently aligned.

The authors examine this coordination through simulations of interactions between the place and head-direction systems. The simulations address observations of hippocampal place-cell responses when visual cue cards in a cylindrical arena are duplicated or rotated. Such manipulations change the environmental information available for aligning the animal's internal spatial representations.

The supplied experimental description concerns rats repeatedly entering a familiar arena at the same location without prior disorientation. Within this setting, the authors report that interactions between the modeled systems can account for observed responses to cue changes. The significance is an explanation based on coordination between internal representations: place-cell behavior is interpreted in relation to the heading system and the broader navigational model.
summary.tldr: Simulated interactions between place and head-direction systems account for rat place-cell responses to altered visual cues.

title: Modeling Interactions of the Rat's Place and Head Direction Systems

abstract: We propose a neuromorphic architecture for real-time processing of acoustic transients in analog VLSI. We show how judicious normalization of a time-frequency signal allows an elegant and robust implementation of a correlation algorithm. The algorithm uses binary multiplexing instead of analog-analog multiplication. This removes the need for analog storage and analog-multiplication. Simulations show that the resulting algorithm has the same out-of-sample classification performance (-93% correct) as a baseline template-matching algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a neuromorphic architecture for processing brief acoustic events in real time using analog VLSI. Its central problem is how to implement a correlation algorithm in hardware without requiring analog operations that complicate the circuit. The input is represented as a signal organized across time and frequency.

The authors normalize this representation so that correlation can use binary multiplexing in place of multiplication between analog signals. That change also removes the need for analog storage. The important design step is therefore a transformation of the signal representation that changes which hardware operations are needed to perform the comparison.

Simulations report approximately 93 percent correct classification on examples outside the sample used to develop the classifier, matching a baseline template-matching algorithm. The result supports preserving classification performance while simplifying the proposed implementation. The evidence described is simulation evidence: it establishes the behavior of the resulting algorithm while the architecture targets real-time analog processing.
summary.tldr: Signal normalization enables acoustic-transient classification with simpler analog hardware operations while matching template-matching performance in simulations.

title: Bangs, Clicks, Snaps, Thuds and Whacks: An Architecture for Acoustic Transient Processing

abstract: Recent works in parameter estimation and neural coding have demonstrated that optimal performance are related to the mutual information between parameters and data. We consider the mutual information in the case where the dependency in the parameter (a vector 8) of the conditional p.d.f. of each observation (a vector 0, is through the scalar product 8.~ only. We derive bounds and asymptotic behaviour for the mutual information and compare with results obtained on the same model with the" replica technique" .

We consider the mutual information in the case where the dependency in the parameter (a vector 8) of the conditional p.d.f. of each observation (a vector 0, is through the scalar product 8.~ only. paragraphs: The paper investigates mutual information between model parameters and observations. This quantity concerns how much the data reveal about the parameters. The motivation comes from work in parameter estimation and neural coding that relates optimal performance to this information, making it a useful object for theoretical analysis.

The authors focus on a particular model structure: the conditional probability density of an observation depends on the parameter vector only through its scalar product with that observation. This restriction specifies exactly how the parameters enter the observation model. The resulting analysis therefore concerns this structured dependence rather than arbitrary relationships between parameters and data.

Within that setting, the authors derive bounds and asymptotic behavior for mutual information. They also compare their results with those obtained using the replica technique on the same model. The contribution is a mathematical characterization of parameter-observation information and a comparison between analytical approaches, providing results tied to the stated scalar-product assumption.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds parameter-observation mutual information for a scalar-product-dependent model and compares its asymptotic results with replica calculations.

title: Unsupervised and Supervised Clustering: The Mutual Information between Parameters and Observations

abstract: We propose a general Bayesian framework for performing independent component analysis (leA) which relies on ensemble learning and lin(cid:173) ear response theory known from statistical physics. We apply it to both discrete and continuous sources. For the continuous source the underde(cid:173) termined (overcomplete) case is studied. The naive mean-field approach fails in this case whereas linear response theory-which gives an improved estimate of covariances-is very efficient. The examples given are for sources without temporal correlations. However, this derivation can eas(cid:173) ily be extended to treat temporal correlations. Finally, the framework offers a simple way of generating new leA algorithms without needing to define the prior distribution of the sources explicitly.
authors: Pedro A. d. F. R. Højen-Sørensen

paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks underlying independent sources in observed data. This paper proposes a Bayesian framework for that task using ensemble learning and linear response theory from statistical physics. The framework is applied to both discrete and continuous sources, giving the authors a common approach across different kinds of hidden signals.

For continuous sources, the paper examines the underdetermined case, where there are more sources than observed mixtures. The authors report that a naive mean-field approximation fails in this setting. Linear response theory improves the covariance estimates and is described as very efficient, making the treatment of relationships among uncertain quantities a central part of the method.

The examples use sources without temporal correlations. The authors state that the derivation can readily be extended to include such correlations, distinguishing that proposed extension from the examples actually presented. They also explain that the framework offers a straightforward route to new ICA algorithms without explicitly specifying the source prior distribution.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian ICA framework uses linear response theory to improve covariance estimates where naive mean-field inference fails.

title: Ensemble Learning and Linear Response Theory for ICA

abstract: We propose a generative model for text and other collections of dis(cid:173) crete data that generalizes or improves on several previous models including naive Bayes/unigram, mixture of unigrams [6], and Hof(cid:173) mann's aspect model, also known as probabilistic latent semantic indexing (pLSI) [3]. In the context of text modeling, our model posits that each document is generated as a mixture of topics, where the continuous-valued mixture proportions are distributed as a latent Dirichlet random variable. Inference and learning are carried out efficiently via variational algorithms. We present em(cid:173) pirical results on applications of this model to problems in text modeling, collaborative filtering, and text classification.

In the context of text modeling, our model posits that each document is generated as a mixture of topics, where the continuous-valued mixture proportions are distributed as a latent Dirichlet random variable. Inference and learning are carried out efficiently via variational algorithms. We present em(cid:173) pirical results on applications of this model to problems in text modeling, collaborative filtering, and text classification.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a generative model for text and other collections of discrete data. In the text setting, a document is represented as a mixture of topics. The mixture proportions are continuous-valued latent variables, so a document’s representation can express varying amounts of several topics.

The distinguishing probabilistic ingredient is a Dirichlet distribution over those topic proportions. The model therefore includes uncertainty and variation in the mixtures from which documents are generated. The authors position it as generalizing or improving on earlier approaches, including naive Bayes or unigram models, mixtures of unigrams, and probabilistic latent semantic indexing.

Inference and learning use efficient variational algorithms. These provide the computational means to work with the model’s unobserved quantities and fit it to data. The authors present empirical applications in text modeling, collaborative filtering, and text classification. Together, the model and inference approach establish a way to describe discrete collections through latent mixtures, with the reported applications demonstrating its use across several tasks rather than text modeling alone.
summary.tldr: Latent Dirichlet allocation models documents as topic mixtures with Dirichlet-distributed proportions and uses variational algorithms for learning and inference.

title: Latent Dirichlet Allocation

abstract: We have implemented a real time front end for detecting voiced speech and estimating its fundamental frequency. The front end performs the signal processing for voice-driven agents that attend to the pitch contours of human speech and provide continuous audiovisual feedback. The al- gorithm we use for pitch tracking has several distinguishing features: it makes no use of FFTs or autocorrelation at the pitch period; it updates the pitch incrementally on a sample-by-sample basis; it avoids peak picking and does not require interpolation in time or frequency to obtain high res- olution estimates; and it works reliably over a four octave range, in real time, without the need for postprocessing to produce smooth contours. The algorithm is based on two simple ideas in neural computation: the introduction of a purposeful nonlinearity, and the error signal of a least squares ﬁt. The pitch tracker is used in two real time multimedia applica- tions: a voice-to-MIDI player that synthesizes electronic music from vo- calized melodies, and an audiovisual Karaoke machine with multimodal feedback. Both applications run on a laptop and display the user’s pitch scrolling across the screen as he or she sings into the computer.

paragraphs: The paper presents a real-time front end that detects voiced speech and estimates its fundamental frequency. It is intended for voice-driven agents that follow speech pitch contours and provide continuous audiovisual feedback. The tracker updates its estimate with every sample, enabling the system to follow vocal pitch as the sound arrives.

The algorithm combines a purposeful nonlinearity with the error signal from a least-squares fit. It avoids FFTs, autocorrelation at the pitch period, and peak picking. It also produces high-resolution estimates without time or frequency interpolation. The authors report reliable real-time operation across four octaves, with smooth contours that do not require post-processing.

Two laptop applications demonstrate its use. A voice-to-MIDI player turns vocalized melodies into synthesized electronic music, while an audiovisual karaoke system supplies multimodal feedback. Both display the singer's pitch as a scrolling trace. These implementations connect the signal-processing method to interactive experiences in which the user can continuously see and hear feedback related to their voice.
summary.tldr: A sample-by-sample pitch tracker supports real-time voice-to-MIDI and karaoke feedback, with reported reliable operation across four octaves.

title: Real Time Voice Processing with Audiovisual Feedback: Toward Autonomous Agents with Perfect Pitch

abstract: We present a probabilistic model applied to the fMRI video rating prediction task of the Pittsburgh Brain Activity Interpretation Competition (PBAIC) [2]. Our goal is to predict a time series of subjective, semantic ratings of a movie given functional MRI data acquired during viewing by three subjects. Our method uses conditionally trained Gaussian Markov random fields, which model both the relationships between the subjects' fMRI voxel measurements and the ratings, as well as the dependencies of the ratings across time steps and between subjects. We also employed non-traditional methods for feature selection and regularization that exploit the spatial structure of voxel activity in the brain. The model displayed good performance in predicting the scored ratings for the three subjects in test data sets, and a variant of this model was the third place entrant to the 2006 PBAIC.

paragraphs: This paper predicts a time series of subjective semantic ratings of a movie from fMRI measurements collected while three people watch it. The task comes from the Pittsburgh Brain Activity Interpretation Competition. Predicting the ratings involves relating brain measurements to the reported judgments while accounting for structure across both time and subjects.

The authors use conditionally trained Gaussian Markov random fields. These model the relationship between voxel measurements and ratings, as well as dependencies between ratings at different time steps and across people. Feature selection and regularization also exploit the spatial organization of brain activity, bringing spatial information into the process of building the predictor.

The model performs well on the scored ratings for the three subjects in the test datasets. A variant placed third in the 2006 competition. These findings support the usefulness of the combined probabilistic approach for the reported task, where temporal and cross-subject dependencies are modeled alongside the relationship between brain activity and ratings.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian graphical model predicts movie ratings from fMRI while modeling temporal and cross-subject dependencies, with a variant placing third in PBAIC.

title: Temporal and Cross-Subject Probabilistic Models for fMRI Prediction Tasks

abstract: We show how to use unlabeled data and a deep belief net (DBN) to learn a good covariance kernel for a Gaussian process. We first learn a deep generative model of the unlabeled data using the fast, greedy algorithm introduced by Hinton et.al. If the data is high-dimensional and highly-structured, a Gaussian kernel applied to the top layer of features in the DBN works much better than a similar kernel applied to the raw input. Performance at both regression and classification can then be further improved by using backpropagation through the DBN to discriminatively fine-tune the covariance kernel.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process uses a covariance kernel to express relationships between inputs. This paper learns that kernel using features from a deep belief network trained on unlabeled data. The approach connects representation learning with Gaussian-process prediction, making the learned description of the input part of the covariance model.

The first stage learns a deep generative model through a fast greedy training procedure. A Gaussian kernel is then applied to features in the network’s top layer. For high-dimensional, highly structured data, the authors report that this works much better than applying a similar kernel directly to raw inputs. The advantage is stated for that kind of data.

A further stage uses backpropagation through the deep belief network to fine-tune the covariance kernel discriminatively. The authors report additional improvements for both regression and classification. The overall method thus uses unlabeled data to learn structure and then adjusts the representation for prediction. Its key finding is that the feature space in which a kernel operates can substantially affect Gaussian-process performance.
summary.tldr: Deep belief network features improve Gaussian-process kernels for highly structured, high-dimensional data, with further gains from discriminative fine-tuning.

title: Using Deep Belief Nets to Learn Covariance Kernels for Gaussian Processes

abstract: Learning distance functions with side information plays a key role in many machine learning and data mining applications. Conventional approaches often assume a Mahalanobis distance function. These approaches are limited in two aspects: (i) they are computationally expensive (even infeasible) for high dimensional data because the size of the metric is in the square of dimensionality; (ii) they assume a fixed metric for the entire input space and therefore are unable to handle heterogeneous data. In this paper, we propose a novel scheme that learns nonlinear Bregman distance functions from side information using a non-parametric approach that is similar to support vector machines. The proposed scheme avoids the assumption of fixed metric because its local distance metric is implicitly derived from the Hessian matrix of a convex function that is used to generate the Bregman distance function. We present an efficient learning algorithm for the proposed scheme for distance function learning. The extensive experiments with semi-supervised clustering show the proposed technique (i) outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches for distance function learning, and (ii) is computationally efficient for high dimensional data.

paragraphs: Learning a distance function lets side information shape what a system treats as similar. Conventional Mahalanobis approaches use a fixed metric across the input space and require a matrix whose size grows quadratically with dimensionality. This paper targets both the computational burden and the difficulty of representing heterogeneous data with one fixed metric.

The proposed method learns nonlinear Bregman distances through a nonparametric scheme resembling support vector machines. A convex function generates the distance, and its Hessian implicitly determines the local metric. Because that local metric comes from the function's curvature, the method avoids assuming the same metric everywhere in the input space.

The authors provide an efficient learning algorithm and evaluate it through semi-supervised clustering experiments. They report better performance than leading distance-learning approaches and computational efficiency on high-dimensional data. These empirical results support the proposed combination of local flexibility and efficient learning. The central contribution is a learned distance representation that can vary across the space while incorporating side information.
summary.tldr: Learning nonlinear Bregman distances provides locally varying metrics and improves reported semi-supervised clustering performance on high-dimensional data.

title: Learning Bregman Distance Functions and Its Application for Semi-Supervised Clustering

abstract: Dimensionality reduction is often needed in many applications due to the high dimensionality of the data involved. In this paper, we first analyze the scatter measures used in the conventional linear discriminant analysis~(LDA) model and note that the formulation is based on the average-case view. Based on this analysis, we then propose a new dimensionality reduction method called worst-case linear discriminant analysis~(WLDA) by defining new between-class and within-class scatter measures. This new model adopts the worst-case view which arguably is more suitable for applications such as classification. When the number of training data points or the number of features is not very large, we relax the optimization problem involved and formulate it as a metric learning problem. Otherwise, we take a greedy approach by finding one direction of the transformation at a time. Moreover, we also analyze a special case of WLDA to show its relationship with conventional LDA. Experiments conducted on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of WLDA when compared with some related dimensionality reduction methods.

paragraphs: Linear discriminant analysis reduces dimensionality using measures of variation within classes and separation between classes. This paper analyzes those scatter measures and characterizes the conventional formulation as taking an average-case view. It proposes worst-case linear discriminant analysis, or WLDA, using newly defined within-class and between-class measures.

The authors argue that this worst-case perspective can be more suitable for classification. They offer two optimization approaches depending on problem size. When the number of examples or features is not very large, they relax the problem into a metric-learning formulation. For larger settings, a greedy method constructs the transformation one direction at a time.

The paper also analyzes a special case to clarify the relationship between WLDA and conventional LDA. Experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness against related dimensionality reduction methods. These findings support the proposed perspective in the evaluated settings, while the claim that worst-case scatter is more suitable for classification remains a motivation rather than a universal conclusion.
summary.tldr: WLDA replaces average-case scatter measures with a worst-case formulation and shows effective dimensionality reduction in benchmark comparisons.

title: Worst-Case Linear Discriminant Analysis

abstract: For many of the state-of-the-art computer vision algorithms, image segmentation is an important preprocessing step. As such, several image segmentation algorithms have been proposed, however, with certain reservation due to high computational load and many hand-tuning parameters. Correlation clustering, a graph-partitioning algorithm often used in natural language processing and document clustering, has the potential to perform better than previously proposed image segmentation algorithms. We improve the basic correlation clustering formulation by taking into account higher-order cluster relationships. This improves clustering in the presence of local boundary ambiguities. We first apply the pairwise correlation clustering to image segmentation over a pairwise superpixel graph and then develop higher-order correlation clustering over a hypergraph that considers higher-order relations among superpixels. Fast inference is possible by linear programming relaxation, and also effective parameter learning framework by structured support vector machine is possible. Experimental results on various datasets show that the proposed higher-order correlation clustering outperforms other state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms.

Correlation clustering, a graph-partitioning algorithm often used in natural language processing and document clustering, has the potential to perform better than previously proposed image segmentation algorithms. We improve the basic correlation clustering formulation by taking into account higher-order cluster relationships. This improves clustering in the presence of local boundary ambiguities. We first apply the pairwise correlation clustering to image segmentation over a pairwise superpixel graph and then develop higher-order correlation clustering over a hypergraph that considers higher-order relations among superpixels. Fast inference is possible by linear programming relaxation, and also effective parameter learning framework by structured support vector machine is possible. Experimental results on various datasets show that the proposed higher-order correlation clustering outperforms other state-of-the-art image segmentation algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies image segmentation through correlation clustering, a method for partitioning a graph into groups. It begins with a graph whose nodes are superpixels and whose pairwise relationships inform which regions belong together. The motivation includes the computational burden and manual parameter tuning associated with existing segmentation approaches.

The authors extend this pairwise formulation to a hypergraph that can express relationships involving groups of superpixels. These higher-order relationships improve clustering when local boundaries are ambiguous. The approach allows a segmentation decision to account for a larger grouping, instead of relying exclusively on separate relationships between pairs of regions.

The formulation supports fast inference through a linear-programming relaxation and parameter learning through a structured support vector machine. These components address both how to compute a segmentation and how to learn the parameters governing it. Experiments on multiple datasets show the higher-order method outperforming other state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. The reported contribution combines richer relationships between image regions with an inference and learning framework that makes those relationships usable.
summary.tldr: Higher-order correlation clustering uses group relationships among superpixels to improve segmentation around ambiguous boundaries.

title: Higher-Order Correlation Clustering for Image Segmentation

abstract: We propose an approach to multivariate nonparametric regression that generalizes reduced rank regression for linear models. An additive model is estimated for each dimension of a $q$-dimensional response, with a shared $p$-dimensional predictor variable. To control the complexity of the model, we employ a functional form of the Ky-Fan or nuclear norm, resulting in a set of function estimates that have low rank. Backfitting algorithms are derived and justified using a nonparametric form of the nuclear norm subdifferential. Oracle inequalities on excess risk are derived that exhibit the scaling behavior of the procedure in the high dimensional setting. The methods are illustrated on gene expression data.

It extends reduced-rank regression beyond linear models by estimating an additive model for each response dimension. The goal is to retain flexibility in the individual prediction functions while controlling the complexity of the collection as a whole.

To impose that control, the authors introduce a functional version of the Ky-Fan, or nuclear, norm. This produces a collection of estimated functions with low rank. The rank restriction applies across the function estimates, bringing the organizing idea of reduced-rank linear regression into a nonparametric setting.

The paper derives backfitting algorithms and justifies them using a nonparametric nuclear-norm subdifferential. It also establishes oracle inequalities for excess risk that describe how the procedure scales in high dimensions. These results address both how to compute the estimates and how their predictive risk behaves in the analysis. An application to gene expression data illustrates the methods, connecting the multivariate formulation to a setting with multiple quantities to predict.
summary.tldr: A functional nuclear-norm penalty extends reduced-rank regression to multivariate additive models, with algorithms and high-dimensional risk guarantees.

title: Nonparametric Reduced Rank Regression

abstract: We introduce a novel variational method that allows to approximately integrate out kernel hyperparameters, such as length-scales, in Gaussian process regression. This approach consists of a novel variant of the variational framework that has been recently developed for the Gaussian process latent variable model which additionally makes use of a standardised representation of the Gaussian process. We consider this technique for learning Mahalanobis distance metrics in a Gaussian process regression setting and provide experimental evaluations and comparisons with existing methods by considering datasets with high-dimensional inputs.
originalAbstract: We introduce a novel variational method that allows to approximately integrate out kernel hyperparameters, such as length-scales, in Gaussian process regression. This approach consists of a novel variant of the variational framework that has been recently developed for the Gaussian process latent variable model which additionally makes use of a standardised representation of the Gaussian process. We consider this technique for learning Mahalanobis distance metrics in a Gaussian process regression setting and provide experimental evaluations and comparisons with existing methods by considering datasets with high-dimensional inputs.

paragraphs: Gaussian process regression depends on a kernel that determines which inputs should count as similar. Parameters such as length scales control that judgment, and the paper asks how to account for uncertainty in these parameters instead of treating a single fitted setting as settled.

The authors introduce a variational approximation that approximately integrates out kernel hyperparameters. Their construction adapts a variational framework developed for Gaussian process latent variable models and combines it with a standardized representation of the Gaussian process. They apply the method specifically to learning Mahalanobis distance metrics for regression.

Experiments compare the approach with existing methods on datasets with high-dimensional inputs. The abstract does not provide numerical results or identify a consistent winner, so its supported contribution is the inference method and its evaluation in this setting. The central idea is to make uncertainty about input geometry part of the regression calculation.
summary.tldr: Variational inference accounts for uncertainty in Gaussian-process distance metrics.

title: Variational Inference for Mahalanobis Distance Metrics in Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: We study matrix completion problem with side information. Side information has been considered in several matrix completion applications, and is generally shown to be useful empirically. Recently, Xu et al. studied the effect of side information for matrix completion under a theoretical viewpoint, showing that sample complexity can be significantly reduced given completely clean features. However, since in reality most given features are noisy or even weakly informative, how to develop a general model to handle general feature set, and how much the noisy features can help matrix recovery in theory, is still an important issue to investigate. In this paper, we propose a novel model that balances between features and observations simultaneously, enabling us to leverage feature information yet to be robust to feature noise. Moreover, we study the effectof general features in theory, and show that by using our model, the sample complexity can still be lower than matrix completion as long as features are sufficiently informative. This result provides a theoretical insight of usefulness for general side information. Finally, we consider synthetic data and two real applications - relationship prediction and semi-supervised clustering, showing that our model outperforms other methods for matrix completion with features both in theory and practice.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs missing matrix entries from the entries that are observed. Extra features can help, and earlier theory had established substantial reductions in required observations when those features were completely clean. This paper asks what remains possible when the additional information contains noise or provides only weak guidance.

The proposed model balances information from features with information from observed entries. That balance is intended to retain the benefit of useful features while remaining robust to feature noise. The authors analyze general feature sets and show that the required number of observations can still be lower than for matrix completion without features, provided the features are sufficiently informative.

The empirical study uses synthetic data together with relationship prediction and semi-supervised clustering applications. The authors report improvements over other methods for matrix completion with features, alongside their theoretical comparison. The central implication is conditional but useful: side information need not be perfectly clean to reduce data requirements. Its contribution depends on how informative it remains, and the model explicitly accommodates the competing evidence from features and observations.
summary.tldr: Balancing noisy features with observed entries can reduce matrix completion's sample requirements when the features remain sufficiently informative.

title: Matrix Completion with Noisy Side Information

abstract: Accurately differentiating between what are truly unpredictably random and systematic changes that occur at random can have profound effect on affect and cognition. To examine the underlying computational principles that guide different learning behavior in an uncertain environment, we compared an R-W model and a Bayesian approach in a visual search task with different volatility levels. Both R-W model and the Bayesian approach reflected an individual's estimation of the environmental volatility, and there is a strong correlation between the learning rate in R-W model and the belief of stationarity in the Bayesian approach in different volatility conditions. In a low volatility condition, R-W model indicates that learning rate positively correlates with lose-shift rate, but not choice optimality (inverted U shape). The Bayesian approach indicates that the belief of environmental stationarity positively correlates with choice optimality, but not lose-shift rate (inverted U shape). In addition, we showed that comparing to Expert learners, individuals with high lose-shift rate (sub-optimal learners) had significantly higher learning rate estimated from R-W model and lower belief of stationarity from the Bayesian model.

paragraphs: The paper compares an R-W learning model with a Bayesian approach in a visual-search task whose environmental volatility varies. The motivating distinction is between unpredictable randomness and changes in an underlying regularity. How a learner interprets that uncertainty can influence whether recent outcomes should cause substantial changes in behavior.

Both models reflected individuals' estimates of volatility, and the R-W learning rate strongly correlated with the Bayesian belief in stationarity across volatility conditions. In the low-volatility condition, the R-W learning rate correlated positively with lose-shift behavior, meaning switching after a loss, while its relationship with choice optimality had an inverted-U shape. These results show how the two modeling approaches connect different aspects of uncertainty estimation to behavior, with distinct relationships to switching and successful choices.
summary.tldr: R-W and Bayesian models both track perceived volatility but reveal different relationships between uncertainty estimates, switching after losses, and choice quality.

title: Learning under uncertainty: a comparison between R-W and Bayesian approach

abstract: Given a task of predicting Y from X, a loss function L, and a set of probability distributions Gamma on (X,Y), what is the optimal decision rule minimizing the worst-case expected loss over Gamma? In this paper, we address this question by introducing a generalization of the maximum entropy principle. Applying this principle to sets of distributions with marginal on X constrained to be the empirical marginal, we provide a minimax interpretation of the maximum likelihood problem over generalized linear models as well as some popular regularization schemes. For quadratic and logarithmic loss functions we revisit well-known linear and logistic regression models. Moreover, for the 0-1 loss we derive a classifier which we call the minimax SVM. The minimax SVM minimizes the worst-case expected 0-1 loss over the proposed Gamma by solving a tractable optimization problem. We perform several numerical experiments to show the power of the minimax SVM in outperforming the SVM.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction when several probability distributions could describe the relationship between inputs and outputs. It asks which prediction rule has the smallest expected loss under the most unfavorable distribution in a specified set. This makes the choice of that set central: the guarantee concerns the uncertainty represented there.

The authors develop a generalization of the maximum entropy principle to address this question. When the input distribution is constrained to match the empirical distribution, their framework gives a minimax interpretation of maximum likelihood learning for generalized linear models and some familiar regularization schemes. Quadratic and logarithmic losses connect the framework to linear and logistic regression.

For the loss that counts classification mistakes, the framework produces a classifier called the minimax SVM. Its tractable optimization problem minimizes worst-case expected error over the proposed distribution set. Numerical experiments report improvements over the SVM, supporting the practical value of this particular formulation alongside its theoretical interpretation.
summary.tldr: A generalized maximum entropy principle connects supervised learning to minimax prediction and yields a tractable classifier that improves on SVMs in reported experiments.

title: A Minimax Approach to Supervised Learning

abstract: We exhibit a strong link between frequentist PAC-Bayesian bounds and the Bayesian marginal likelihood. That is, for the negative log-likelihood loss function, we show that the minimization of PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds maximizes the Bayesian marginal likelihood. This provides an alternative explanation to the Bayesian Occam's razor criteria, under the assumption that the data is generated by an i.i.d. distribution. Moreover, as the negative log-likelihood is an unbounded loss function, we motivate and propose a PAC-Bayesian theorem tailored for the sub-gamma loss family, and we show that our approach is sound on classical Bayesian linear regression tasks.

This provides an alternative explanation to the Bayesian Occam's razor criteria, under the assumption that the data is generated by an i.i.d. distribution. Moreover, as the negative log-likelihood is an unbounded loss function, we motivate and propose a PAC-Bayesian theorem tailored for the sub-gamma loss family, and we show that our approach is sound on classical Bayesian linear regression tasks.

paragraphs: PAC-Bayesian theory studies generalization guarantees, while Bayesian marginal likelihood is used to assess models through the probability they assign to observed data. This paper establishes a strong connection between these two perspectives. For negative log-likelihood loss, minimizing the PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds considered by the authors maximizes Bayesian marginal likelihood.

The connection provides an alternative explanation for Bayesian Occam's razor, the principle underlying a preference for models that balance fit and complexity. The explanation is developed under the assumption that observations are independently drawn from the same distribution. It relates a Bayesian model-assessment criterion to a frequentist statement about generalization.

Negative log-likelihood is unbounded, so a theory designed only around bounded losses would not directly address the setting. The authors therefore propose a PAC-Bayesian theorem tailored to the sub-gamma loss family. They demonstrate the soundness of their approach on classical Bayesian linear-regression tasks, connecting the theoretical equivalence to a familiar inference problem where the loss behavior matters.
summary.tldr: For negative log-likelihood loss, minimizing the studied PAC-Bayesian bounds maximizes Bayesian marginal likelihood under an i.i.d. data assumption.

title: PAC-Bayesian Theory Meets Bayesian Inference

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the underlying graph of an unknown Ising model on p spins from a collection of i.i.d. samples generated from the model. We suggest a new estimator that is computationally efficient and requires a number of samples that is near-optimal with respect to previously established information theoretic lower-bound. Our statistical estimator has a physical interpretation in terms of "interaction screening". The estimator is consistent and is efficiently implemented using convex optimization. We prove that with appropriate regularization, the estimator recovers the underlying graph using a number of samples that is logarithmic in the system size p and exponential in the maximum coupling-intensity and maximum node-degree.

paragraphs: The paper considers reconstructing the interaction graph of an unknown Ising model from independent samples generated by that model. The graph identifies which spins interact directly. The challenge is to recover this structure with both manageable computation and a number of observations close to what is fundamentally required.

The authors introduce a statistically consistent estimator with a physical interpretation called interaction screening. It can be implemented efficiently through convex optimization. This combines a statistically justified estimation procedure with a computational formulation that can be solved efficiently, rather than treating sample requirements and algorithmic cost as separate concerns.

With appropriate regularization, the authors prove graph recovery using a sample count logarithmic in the number of spins. The same bound grows exponentially with maximum coupling intensity and maximum node degree, so system size alone does not determine the data requirement. Relative to an established information-theoretic lower bound, the sample requirement is near-optimal. The result clarifies both the estimator's efficiency and the structural factors that make recovery harder.
summary.tldr: Interaction screening efficiently recovers Ising-model graphs with near-optimal sample requirements under appropriate regularization.

title: Interaction Screening: Efficient and Sample-Optimal Learning of Ising Models

abstract: The coordinate descent (CD) method is a classical optimization algorithm that has seen a revival of interest because of its competitive performance in machine learning applications. A number of recent papers provided convergence rate estimates for their deterministic (cyclic) and randomized variants that differ in the selection of update coordinates. These estimates suggest randomized coordinate descent (RCD) performs better than cyclic coordinate descent (CCD), although numerical experiments do not provide clear justification for this comparison. In this paper, we provide examples and more generally problem classes for which CCD (or CD with any deterministic order) is faster than RCD in terms of asymptotic worst-case convergence. Furthermore, we provide lower and upper bounds on the amount of improvement on the rate of CCD relative to RCD, which depends on the deterministic order used. We also provide a characterization of the best deterministic order (that leads to the maximum improvement in convergence rate) in terms of the combinatorial properties of the Hessian matrix of the objective function.

A number of recent papers provided convergence rate estimates for their deterministic (cyclic) and randomized variants that differ in the selection of update coordinates. These estimates suggest randomized coordinate descent (RCD) performs better than cyclic coordinate descent (CCD), although numerical experiments do not provide clear justification for this comparison. In this paper, we provide examples and more generally problem classes for which CCD (or CD with any deterministic order) is faster than RCD in terms of asymptotic worst-case convergence. Furthermore, we provide lower and upper bounds on the amount of improvement on the rate of CCD relative to RCD, which depends on the deterministic order used. We also provide a characterization of the best deterministic order (that leads to the maximum improvement in convergence rate) in terms of the combinatorial properties of the Hessian matrix of the objective function.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent optimizes an objective by updating individual coordinates. Cyclic methods follow a fixed order, while randomized methods choose coordinates randomly. Earlier convergence estimates suggested an advantage for randomization, but numerical experiments did not clearly establish that comparison. This paper investigates situations in which a deterministic update order has a theoretical advantage.

The authors provide examples and broader problem classes where cyclic coordinate descent, or descent with any deterministic order, converges faster than its randomized counterpart in an asymptotic worst-case sense. This establishes that the apparent ranking from earlier estimates does not describe all problem classes.

They also bound the size of the improvement and show that it depends on the chosen deterministic order. A further result characterizes the best order through combinatorial properties of the objective's Hessian matrix, linking scheduling decisions to the objective's structure. The contribution therefore goes beyond demonstrating that fixed orders can win: it analyzes how much they can help and what determines the most favorable ordering.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies problem classes where deterministic coordinate descent is asymptotically faster than randomization and characterizes how update order affects the gain.

title: When Cyclic Coordinate Descent Outperforms Randomized Coordinate Descent

abstract: Reinforcement learning is a powerful paradigm for learning optimal policies from experimental data. However, to find optimal policies, most reinforcement learning algorithms explore all possible actions, which may be harmful for real-world systems. As a consequence, learning algorithms are rarely applied on safety-critical systems in the real world. In this paper, we present a learning algorithm that explicitly considers safety, defined in terms of stability guarantees. Specifically, we extend control-theoretic results on Lyapunov stability verification and show how to use statistical models of the dynamics to obtain high-performance control policies with provable stability certificates. Moreover, under additional regularity assumptions in terms of a Gaussian process prior, we prove that one can effectively and safely collect data in order to learn about the dynamics and thus both improve control performance and expand the safe region of the state space. In our experiments, we show how the resulting algorithm can safely optimize a neural network policy on a simulated inverted pendulum, without the pendulum ever falling down.

paragraphs: Learning a control policy through experimentation can expose a physical system to harmful actions. This paper incorporates safety directly into model-based reinforcement learning, defining safety through stability guarantees. It extends Lyapunov stability verification to use statistical models of system dynamics and obtain control policies accompanied by provable stability certificates.

The method also addresses how to gather more information safely. Under additional regularity assumptions expressed through a Gaussian process prior, the authors prove that data can be collected safely and effectively to improve the dynamics model. Better knowledge can then improve control performance and expand the region of states certified as safe.

The experiments optimize a neural network policy for a simulated inverted pendulum without the pendulum falling during learning. This demonstrates the approach in a concrete control task. The theoretical guarantees retain their stated assumptions, and the paper's safety concept is stability: the contribution connects policy improvement and exploration to an explicit control-theoretic certificate.
summary.tldr: A model-based reinforcement learning method uses stability certificates to improve control and, under stated assumptions, safely expand the certified region.

title: Safe Model-based Reinforcement Learning with Stability Guarantees

abstract: Despite remarkable advances in image synthesis research, existing works often fail in manipulating images under the context of large geometric transformations. Synthesizing person images conditioned on arbitrary poses is one of the most representative examples where the generation quality largely relies on the capability of identifying and modeling arbitrary transformations on different body parts. Current generative models are often built on local convolutions and overlook the key challenges (e.g. heavy occlusions, different views or dramatic appearance changes) when distinct geometric changes happen for each part, caused by arbitrary pose manipulations. This paper aims to resolve these challenges induced by geometric variability and spatial displacements via a new Soft-Gated Warping Generative Adversarial Network (Warping-GAN), which is composed of two stages: 1) it first synthesizes a target part segmentation map given a target pose, which depicts the region-level spatial layouts for guiding image synthesis with higher-level structure constraints; 2) the Warping-GAN equipped with a soft-gated warping-block learns feature-level mapping to render textures from the original image into the generated segmentation map. Warping-GAN is capable of controlling different transformation degrees given distinct target poses. Moreover, the proposed warping-block is light-weight and flexible enough to be injected into any networks. Human perceptual studies and quantitative evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our Warping-GAN that significantly outperforms all existing methods on two large datasets.

paragraphs: Generating a person in a new pose requires moving and transforming different body parts by different amounts. Large changes can introduce occlusions, new views, and substantial appearance changes. This paper argues that local convolutional processing alone often fails to address those geometric demands and introduces a two-stage Warping-GAN to handle them.

The first stage predicts a body-part segmentation map from the target pose. This map supplies a region-level layout that guides image generation. The second stage uses a soft-gated warping block to learn feature-level mappings, transferring texture information from the original image into that layout. The design separates establishing target structure from rendering appearance within it.

The model can control different transformation degrees for different target poses, and the proposed warping block is described as lightweight and flexible enough for integration into other networks. Human perceptual studies and quantitative evaluations report significant improvements over existing methods on two large datasets. These results support explicit geometric handling as a useful component of pose-guided person synthesis.
summary.tldr: Warping-GAN combines target body-part layouts with soft-gated feature warping to improve person-image generation under large pose changes.

title: Soft-Gated Warping-GAN for Pose-Guided Person Image Synthesis

abstract: Neural networks are a powerful class of nonlinear functions that can be trained end-to-end on various applications. While the over-parametrization nature in many neural networks renders the ability to fit complex functions and the strong representation power to handle challenging tasks, it also leads to highly correlated neurons that can hurt the generalization ability and incur unnecessary computation cost. As a result, how to regularize the network to avoid undesired representation redundancy becomes an important issue. To this end, we draw inspiration from a well-known problem in physics -- Thomson problem, where one seeks to find a state that distributes N electrons on a unit sphere as evenly as possible with minimum potential energy. In light of this intuition, we reduce the redundancy regularization problem to generic energy minimization, and propose a minimum hyperspherical energy (MHE) objective as generic regularization for neural networks. We also propose a few novel variants of MHE, and provide some insights from a theoretical point of view. Finally, we apply neural networks with MHE regularization to several challenging tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our intuition, by showing the superior performance with MHE regularization.

While the over-parametrization nature in many neural networks renders the ability to fit complex functions and the strong representation power to handle challenging tasks, it also leads to highly correlated neurons that can hurt the generalization ability and incur unnecessary computation cost. As a result, how to regularize the network to avoid undesired representation redundancy becomes an important issue. To this end, we draw inspiration from a well-known problem in physics -- Thomson problem, where one seeks to find a state that distributes N electrons on a unit sphere as evenly as possible with minimum potential energy. In light of this intuition, we reduce the redundancy regularization problem to generic energy minimization, and propose a minimum hyperspherical energy (MHE) objective as generic regularization for neural networks. We also propose a few novel variants of MHE, and provide some insights from a theoretical point of view. Finally, we apply neural networks with MHE regularization to several challenging tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our intuition, by showing the superior performance with MHE regularization.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can learn rich functions, but their neurons may also become highly correlated. The paper identifies this redundancy as a possible source of poorer generalization and unnecessary computation. It proposes minimum hyperspherical energy, or MHE, as a regularization objective intended to discourage redundant representations during training.

The guiding analogy comes from the Thomson problem in physics: arranging electrons on a unit sphere so that their potential energy is minimized and they spread out. The authors translate that intuition into an energy-minimization approach to neural network regularization. The objective uses a geometric notion of spreading to encourage diversity among learned representations.

The paper develops several variants of MHE, provides theoretical insights, and evaluates regularized networks on multiple challenging tasks. The experiments report superior performance with MHE, supporting the intuition that reducing representation redundancy can be useful. The stated findings concern the effectiveness of the regularizer; the motivation about unnecessary computation does not itself establish a measured reduction in runtime or model size.
summary.tldr: Minimum hyperspherical energy regularization uses a physics-inspired spreading objective to reduce neural representation redundancy and improve empirical performance.

title: Learning towards Minimum Hyperspherical Energy

abstract: We propose a general, theoretically justified mechanism for processing missing data by neural networks. Our idea is to replace typical neuron's response in the first hidden layer by its expected value. This approach can be applied for various types of networks at minimal cost in their modification. Moreover, in contrast to recent approaches, it does not require complete data for training. Experimental results performed on different types of architectures show that our method gives better results than typical imputation strategies and other methods dedicated for incomplete data.
originalAbstract: We propose a general, theoretically justified mechanism for processing missing data by neural networks. Our idea is to replace typical neuron's response in the first hidden layer by its expected value. This approach can be applied for various types of networks at minimal cost in their modification. Moreover, in contrast to recent approaches, it does not require complete data for training. Experimental results performed on different types of architectures show that our method gives better results than typical imputation strategies and other methods dedicated for incomplete data.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how neural networks can process examples whose input values are incomplete. Its central idea is to change the response of neurons in the first hidden layer: each ordinary response is replaced by its expected value. This places the handling of missing information at the point where the network begins turning inputs into internal features.

The authors present the mechanism as theoretically justified and broadly applicable across network types. It requires only small modifications to the network and does not require complete examples for training. That property matters when missingness affects the training data itself, because the procedure can be used without first obtaining a fully observed training collection.

Experiments across different architectures show better results than typical imputation strategies and other methods intended for incomplete data. These findings support expected first-layer responses as a useful alternative for the evaluated settings. The contribution combines a specific change to neural computation with flexibility across architectures and the ability to train directly when data is incomplete.
summary.tldr: Replacing first-layer neuron responses with expected values enables training on incomplete data and outperforms compared missing-data methods in experiments.

title: Processing of missing data by neural networks

abstract: Our goal is to predict future video frames given a sequence of input frames. Despite large amounts of video data, this remains a challenging task because of the high-dimensionality of video frames. We address this challenge by proposing the Decompositional Disentangled Predictive Auto-Encoder (DDPAE), a framework that combines structured probabilistic models and deep networks to automatically (i) decompose the high-dimensional video that we aim to predict into components, and (ii) disentangle each component to have low-dimensional temporal dynamics that are easier to predict. Crucially, with an appropriately specified generative model of video frames, our DDPAE is able to learn both the latent decomposition and disentanglement without explicit supervision. For the Moving MNIST dataset, we show that DDPAE is able to recover the underlying components (individual digits) and disentanglement (appearance and location) as we would intuitively do. We further demonstrate that DDPAE can be applied to the Bouncing Balls dataset involving complex interactions between multiple objects to predict the video frame directly from the pixels and recover physical states without explicit supervision.

paragraphs: Predicting future video frames is difficult because each frame contains many pixel values that change together. This paper proposes the Decompositional Disentangled Predictive Auto-Encoder, or DDPAE, to organize that complexity. It breaks video into components and gives each component a representation with low-dimensional dynamics that are easier to predict.

DDPAE combines deep networks with structured probabilistic modeling. Decomposition separates components of the scene, while disentanglement separates aspects of each component, such as appearance and position. With an appropriately specified generative model of the frames, both kinds of structure can be learned without explicit supervision describing those components or factors.

On Moving MNIST, the model recovers individual digits and separates their appearance from their locations. On Bouncing Balls, it predicts frames directly from pixels and recovers physical states despite interactions among multiple objects. These demonstrations show how a structured internal representation can emerge during video prediction. The unsupervised-learning claim depends on the suitability of the generative model used to describe the frames.
summary.tldr: DDPAE learns component-based video representations with simpler dynamics, enabling unsupervised structure recovery under an appropriate generative model.

title: Learning to Decompose and Disentangle Representations for Video Prediction

abstract: We present a representation learning algorithm that learns a low-dimensional latent dynamical system from high-dimensional sequential raw data, e.g., video. The framework builds upon recent advances in amortized inference methods that use both an inference network and a refinement procedure to output samples from a variational distribution given an observation sequence, and takes advantage of the duality between control and inference to approximately solve the intractable inference problem using the path integral control approach. The learned dynamical model can be used to predict and plan the future states; we also present the efficient planning method that exploits the learned low-dimensional latent dynamics. Numerical experiments show that the proposed path-integral control based variational inference method leads to tighter lower bounds in statistical model learning of sequential data. Supplementary video: https://youtu.be/xCp35crUoLQ

paragraphs: The paper learns a compact dynamical system from high-dimensional sequences such as video. The aim is to represent how a sequence evolves using a low-dimensional latent state. This learned state and its dynamics provide a basis for predicting future states and planning, linking representation learning with decisions about future evolution.

The inference procedure combines a neural inference network with a refinement process. Together, they produce samples from a variational distribution conditioned on an observed sequence. The authors exploit a connection between control and inference, using path-integral control to approximately solve an inference problem that is otherwise intractable. The refinement therefore forms part of the method for obtaining the latent representation.

The paper also introduces an efficient planning method that uses the learned latent dynamics. Numerical experiments show tighter lower bounds for statistical learning of sequential data when using the proposed inference procedure. This supports the approach as a way to improve the variational learning objective while producing a dynamical model that can also support prediction and planning.
summary.tldr: Path-integral control refines variational inference to learn compact dynamics from sequences and support prediction and planning.

title: Adaptive Path-Integral Autoencoders: Representation Learning and Planning for Dynamical Systems

abstract: Generating novel graph structures that optimize given objectives while obeying some given underlying rules is fundamental for chemistry, biology and social science research. This is especially important in the task of molecular graph generation, whose goal is to discover novel molecules with desired properties such as drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility, while obeying physical laws such as chemical valency. However, designing models that finds molecules that optimize desired properties while incorporating highly complex and non-differentiable rules remains to be a challenging task. Here we propose Graph Convolutional Policy Network (GCPN), a general graph convolutional network based model for goal-directed graph generation through reinforcement learning. The model is trained to optimize domain-specific rewards and adversarial loss through policy gradient, and acts in an environment that incorporates domain-specific rules. Experimental results show that GCPN can achieve 61% improvement on chemical property optimization over state-of-the-art baselines while resembling known molecules, and achieve 184% improvement on the constrained property optimization task.

paragraphs: Generating useful molecules requires more than producing plausible graphs. A system must pursue desired properties while respecting chemical rules such as valency. Some objectives and rules are complex or non-differentiable, making them difficult to incorporate directly into ordinary gradient-based generation. This paper frames the task as goal-directed graph generation through reinforcement learning.

The Graph Convolutional Policy Network uses a graph convolutional model to guide generation. Policy-gradient training combines domain-specific rewards with an adversarial loss, while the environment incorporates domain-specific rules. This arrangement gives property optimization and rule compliance explicit roles in the generation process. In the molecular application, it also allows the system to pursue improvements while producing structures resembling known molecules.

The experiments report a 61% improvement in chemical-property optimization over state-of-the-art baselines and a 184% improvement on constrained property optimization. These are results for the evaluated tasks, rather than guarantees about every generated molecule. They support the broader proposal that reinforcement learning can coordinate graph-based generation, complex objectives, and structural requirements within one model.
summary.tldr: GCPN uses reinforcement learning to generate molecular graphs that optimize target properties while operating under domain-specific rules.

title: Graph Convolutional Policy Network for Goal-Directed Molecular Graph Generation

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of learning an unknown graph via queries on groups of nodes, with the result indicating whether or not at least one edge is present among those nodes. While learning arbitrary graphs with $n$ nodes and $k$ edges is known to be hard in the sense of requiring $\Omega( \min\{ k^2 \log n, n^2\})$ tests (even when a small probability of error is allowed), we show that learning an Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graph with an average of $\kbar$ edges is much easier; namely, one can attain asymptotically vanishing error probability with only $O(\kbar \log n)$ tests. We establish such bounds for a variety of algorithms inspired by the group testing problem, with explicit constant factors indicating a near-optimal number of tests, and in some cases asymptotic optimality including constant factors. In addition, we present an alternative design that permits a near-optimal sublinear decoding time of $O(\kbar \log^2 \kbar + \kbar \log n)$.

In addition, we present an alternative design that permits a near-optimal sublinear decoding time of $O(\kbar \log^2 \kbar + \kbar \log n)$.

paragraphs: The paper studies reconstructing an unknown graph using queries about groups of nodes. Each query returns only whether at least one edge connects nodes within the chosen group. A positive answer therefore reveals that an edge exists somewhere in the group without identifying its endpoints.

For arbitrary graphs, this limited feedback can require many tests. The authors show that reconstruction becomes substantially easier when the graph follows an Erdős-Rényi random model. With n nodes and an expected edge count of k-bar, their methods use order k-bar times log n tests while achieving an error probability that vanishes asymptotically.

The algorithms draw on group testing, where pooled queries locate hidden items efficiently. The authors establish explicit constant factors, obtaining near-optimal test counts and, in some cases, asymptotic optimality including constants. They also give an alternative design with near-optimal sublinear decoding time of order k-bar log squared k-bar plus k-bar log n. The random-graph assumption is central to the improvement over the difficulty of reconstructing arbitrary graphs.
summary.tldr: Group-testing-inspired algorithms reconstruct Erdős-Rényi graphs with near-optimal numbers of edge-detection queries and efficient decoding.

title: Learning Erdos-Renyi Random Graphs via Edge Detecting Queries

abstract: In interactive machine learning (IML), we iteratively make decisions and obtain noisy observations of an unknown function. While IML methods, e.g., Bayesian optimization and active learning, have been successful in applications, on real-world systems they must provably avoid unsafe decisions. To this end, safe IML algorithms must carefully learn about a priori unknown constraints without making unsafe decisions. Existing algorithms for this problem learn about the safety of all decisions to ensure convergence. This is sample-inefficient, as it explores decisions that are not relevant for the original IML objective. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework that renders any existing unsafe IML algorithm safe. Our method works as an add-on that takes suggested decisions as input and exploits regularity assumptions in terms of a Gaussian process prior in order to efficiently learn about their safety. As a result, we only explore the safe set when necessary for the IML problem. We apply our framework to safe Bayesian optimization and to safe exploration in deterministic Markov Decision Processes (MDP), which have been analyzed separately before. Our method outperforms other algorithms empirically.

paragraphs: Interactive learning repeatedly chooses actions and receives noisy observations about an unknown function. When actions can be unsafe, the learner must discover unknown constraints while avoiding violations. The paper argues that existing safe methods waste observations by investigating the safety of decisions that do not matter to the original learning objective.

The proposed framework acts as an add-on to an existing interactive learning algorithm. It takes that algorithm's suggested decisions and learns about their safety using regularity assumptions expressed through a Gaussian process prior. Safety exploration is therefore directed by the underlying task: the method explores the safe set only when that exploration is needed for the learning problem.

The authors apply the framework to safe Bayesian optimization and safe exploration in deterministic Markov decision processes, bringing together settings previously analyzed separately. They report empirical improvements over other algorithms. The safety framework depends on its stated regularity assumptions, while its practical contribution is a way to focus safety-related observations on decisions relevant to the task.
summary.tldr: A safety add-on uses Gaussian-process regularity assumptions to focus exploration on decisions relevant to an interactive learner's objective.

title: Safe Exploration for Interactive Machine Learning

abstract: We show that the basic classification framework alone can be used to tackle some of the most challenging tasks in image synthesis. In contrast to other state-of-the-art approaches, the toolkit we develop is rather minimal: it uses a single, off-the-shelf classifier for all these tasks. The crux of our approach is that we train this classifier to be adversarially robust. It turns out that adversarial robustness is precisely what we need to directly manipulate salient features of the input. Overall, our findings demonstrate the utility of robustness in the broader machine learning context.

paragraphs: The paper explores how far a basic image-classification framework can go in image synthesis. Its toolkit uses a single off-the-shelf classifier across the synthesis tasks considered. The central question is whether a model trained to classify images can also provide a useful means of changing their visually important content.

The crucial ingredient is training the classifier to be adversarially robust. The authors find that this robustness enables direct manipulation of salient input features. In the proposed approach, the classifier therefore does more than assign a category: its learned behavior supports operations on the image content that matters for the synthesis task.

The findings show that this minimal classification-based toolkit can tackle challenging image-synthesis tasks. Their significance is that robustness has a constructive role beyond the classifier's original prediction setting. A single robust model supplies the basis for the toolkit across the tasks studied, connecting a property of classification training to the ability to manipulate images. The paper presents this as evidence for the broader usefulness of adversarial robustness in machine learning.
summary.tldr: A single adversarially robust classifier can support challenging image-synthesis tasks by enabling direct manipulation of salient image features.

title: Image Synthesis with a Single (Robust) Classifier

abstract: Representation learning over graph structured data has been mostly studied in static graph settings while efforts for modeling dynamic graphs are still scant. In this paper, we develop a novel hierarchical variational model that introduces additional latent random variables to jointly model the hidden states of a graph recurrent neural network (GRNN) to capture both topology and node attribute changes in dynamic graphs. We argue that the use of high-level latent random variables in this variational GRNN (VGRNN) can better capture potential variability observed in dynamic graphs as well as the uncertainty of node latent representation. With semi-implicit variational inference developed for this new VGRNN architecture (SI-VGRNN), we show that flexible non-Gaussian latent representations can further help dynamic graph analytic tasks. Our experiments with multiple real-world dynamic graph datasets demonstrate that SI-VGRNN and VGRNN consistently outperform the existing baseline and state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin in dynamic link prediction.

We argue that the use of high-level latent random variables in this variational GRNN (VGRNN) can better capture potential variability observed in dynamic graphs as well as the uncertainty of node latent representation.
