paragraphs: Graphs can change over time through both their connections and their node attributes. This paper develops a hierarchical variational model for learning representations of those changes. Its Variational Graph Recurrent Neural Network introduces additional latent random variables that jointly model the hidden states of a graph recurrent network.

The authors argue that these higher-level random variables can better express variation in dynamic graphs and uncertainty about node representations. They also develop a version using semi-implicit variational inference, called SI-VGRNN. This extension permits flexible, non-Gaussian latent representations, expanding the forms of uncertainty and variability the model can represent.

Experiments on multiple real-world dynamic graph datasets evaluate the models through dynamic link prediction. Both VGRNN and SI-VGRNN consistently outperform the existing baselines and state-of-the-art methods considered, with significant margins reported. The results support the usefulness of probabilistic latent representations for the evaluated task, and indicate that allowing more flexible latent distributions can further help dynamic graph analysis. The empirical finding concerns those tested datasets and comparisons.
summary.tldr: Variational graph recurrent networks model changing connections, node attributes, and representation uncertainty, improving dynamic link prediction on multiple real-world datasets.

title: Variational Graph Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Statistical Relational Learning (SRL) methods are the most widely used techniques to generate distributional representations of the symbolic Knowledge Bases (KBs). These methods embed any given KB into a vector space by exploiting statistical similarities among its entities and predicates but without any guarantee of preserving the underlying logical structure of the KB. This, in turn, results in poor performance of logical reasoning tasks that are solved using such distributional representations. We present a novel approach called Embed2Reason (E2R) that embeds a symbolic KB into a vector space in a logical structure preserving manner. This approach is inspired by the theory of Quantum Logic. Such an embedding allows answering membership based complex logical reasoning queries with impressive accuracy improvements over popular SRL baselines.

paragraphs: Knowledge-base embeddings turn symbolic entities and predicates into vector representations. The paper argues that common Statistical Relational Learning methods build these representations from statistical similarities without guaranteeing preservation of the knowledge base’s logical structure. That mismatch can undermine logical reasoning performed using the resulting vectors.

The authors introduce Embed2Reason, or E2R, an embedding approach inspired by Quantum Logic. Its stated purpose is to preserve logical structure while mapping a symbolic knowledge base into a vector space. The role of Quantum Logic here is to motivate the representation. Logical organization becomes a property the embedding is designed to retain.

The resulting representations support complex logical queries based on membership, and the abstract reports substantial accuracy improvements over popular Statistical Relational Learning baselines. This finding connects the embedding’s design objective with the reasoning task it serves. The contribution is a representation strategy that treats logical structure as central to answering queries, with reported empirical improvements for the membership-based reasoning considered in the paper.
summary.tldr: Embed2Reason uses ideas from Quantum Logic to preserve knowledge-base structure in vector embeddings and improve membership-based logical reasoning.

title: Quantum Embedding of Knowledge for Reasoning

abstract: We propose a recurrent neural-network for real-time reconstruction of acoustic camera spherical maps. The network, dubbed DeepWave, is both physically and algorithmically motivated: its recurrent architecture mimics iterative solvers from convex optimisation, and its parsimonious parametrisation is based on the natural structure of acoustic imaging problems. Each network layer applies successive filtering, biasing and activation steps to its input, which can be interpreted as generalised deblurring and sparsification steps. To comply with the irregular geometry of spherical maps, filtering operations are implemented efficiently by means of graph signal processing techniques. Unlike commonly-used imaging network architectures, DeepWave is moreover capable of directly processing the complex-valued raw microphone correlations, learning how to optimally back-project these into a spherical map. We propose moreover a smart physically-inspired initialisation scheme that attains much faster training and higher performance than random initialisation. Our real-data experiments show DeepWave has similar computational speed to the state-of-the-art delay-and-sum imager with vastly superior resolution. While developed primarily for acoustic cameras, DeepWave could easily be adapted to neighbouring signal processing fields, such as radio astronomy, radar and sonar.

paragraphs: DeepWave reconstructs spherical acoustic images from microphone measurements in real time. Its design combines the structure of acoustic imaging with the repeated-update pattern of convex optimization solvers. This gives the network a compact, physically motivated parameterization and ties its operations to the reconstruction problem it is intended to solve.

Each layer performs filtering, biasing, and activation, which can be interpreted as generalized deblurring and sparsification. Graph signal processing implements filtering on the irregular geometry of spherical maps. The network also accepts complex-valued microphone correlations directly and learns their back-projection into an image. A physically motivated initialization scheme gives faster training and higher performance than random initialization in the reported comparison.

Experiments on real data show computational speed similar to the delay-and-sum imager, with substantially higher resolution. The result suggests that an architecture shaped by both physical structure and iterative algorithms can improve reconstruction quality while retaining real-time speed. The authors also identify radio astronomy, radar, and sonar as possible adaptation targets, presenting those as prospective applications rather than demonstrated results.
summary.tldr: DeepWave combines acoustic physics and iterative-solver structure to produce higher-resolution spherical sound maps at competitive real-time speed.

title: DeepWave: A Recurrent Neural-Network for Real-Time Acoustic Imaging

abstract: In this paper, we provide an efficient approximation algorithm for finding the most likelihood configuration (MAP) of size $k$ for Determinantal Point Processes (DPP) in the online setting where the data points arrive in an arbitrary order and the algorithm cannot discard the selected elements from its local memory. Given a tolerance additive error $\eta$, our \online algorithm achieves a $k^{O(k)}$ multiplicative approximation guarantee with an additive error $\eta$, using a memory footprint independent of the size of the data stream. We note that the exponential dependence on $k$ in the approximation factor is unavoidable even in the offline setting. Our result readily implies a streaming algorithm with an improved memory bound compared to existing results.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we provide an efficient approximation algorithm for finding the most likelihood configuration (MAP) of size $k$ for Determinantal Point Processes (DPP) in the online setting where the data points arrive in an arbitrary order and the algorithm cannot discard the selected elements from its local memory. Given a tolerance additive error $\eta$, our \online algorithm achieves a $k^{O(k)}$ multiplicative approximation guarantee with an additive error $\eta$, using a memory footprint independent of the size of the data stream. We note that the exponential dependence on $k$ in the approximation factor is unavoidable even in the offline setting. Our result readily implies a streaming algorithm with an improved memory bound compared to existing results.

paragraphs: The paper considers finding a size-k configuration with high probability under a determinantal point process. Its target is the maximum-probability configuration, known as MAP inference. The online setting adds two important constraints: data can arrive in any order, and selected elements cannot later be discarded from the algorithm's local memory.

The authors give an efficient approximation algorithm whose memory footprint does not depend on the total length of the incoming stream. For a chosen additive tolerance η, its guarantee combines a multiplicative approximation factor of k raised to O(k) with additive error η. The guarantee therefore explicitly depends on the requested configuration size and allows the specified additive error.

The exponential dependence on k in the approximation factor is unavoidable even when all data are available offline, according to the paper. This situates the online result against a difficulty already present without streaming constraints. The result also directly yields a streaming algorithm with a better memory bound than existing results.
summary.tldr: An online algorithm approximates size-k DPP MAP inference using memory independent of stream length, with explicit multiplicative and additive guarantees.

title: Online MAP Inference of Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: This work studies the problem of object goal navigation which involves navigating to an instance of the given object category in unseen environments. End-to-end learning-based navigation methods struggle at this task as they are ineffective at exploration and long-term planning. We propose a modular system called, `Goal-Oriented Semantic Exploration' which builds an episodic semantic map and uses it to explore the environment efficiently based on the goal object category. Empirical results in visually realistic simulation environments show that the proposed model outperforms a wide range of baselines including end-to-end learning-based methods as well as modular map-based methods and led to the winning entry of the CVPR-2020 Habitat ObjectNav Challenge. Ablation analysis indicates that the proposed model learns semantic priors of the relative arrangement of objects in a scene, and uses them to explore efficiently. Domain-agnostic module design allows us to transfer our model to a mobile robot platform and achieve similar performance for object goal navigation in the real-world.

paragraphs: Object goal navigation requires an agent to find an instance of a requested object category in an unseen environment. The paper identifies exploration and long-term planning as difficulties for end-to-end learned navigation systems. It proposes Goal-Oriented Semantic Exploration, a modular system that organizes navigation around a semantic map built during an episode.

The system uses both that map and the target object category to guide exploration. Ablation analysis indicates that it learns regularities in the relative arrangement of objects and uses those regularities to search efficiently. The semantic information therefore contributes to deciding where to explore, connecting the requested category to the structure encountered in a scene.

In visually realistic simulations, the system outperforms a broad range of end-to-end and modular map-based baselines. It also led to the winning entry in the CVPR-2020 Habitat ObjectNav Challenge. The authors transfer the model to a mobile robot through its domain-agnostic module design and report similar real-world navigation performance, providing evidence that the modular approach can carry beyond simulation.
summary.tldr: A modular semantic mapping system uses learned object-layout regularities to improve goal-directed exploration in simulation and on a mobile robot.

title: Object Goal Navigation using Goal-Oriented Semantic Exploration

abstract: Autoregressive models use chain rule to define a joint probability distribution as a product of conditionals. These conditionals need to be normalized, imposing constraints on the functional families that can be used. To increase flexibility, we propose autoregressive conditional score models (AR-CSM) where we parameterize the joint distribution in terms of the derivatives of univariate log-conditionals (scores), which need not be normalized. To train AR-CSM, we introduce a new divergence between distributions named Composite Score Matching (CSM). For AR-CSM models, this divergence between data and model distributions can be computed and optimized efficiently, requiring no expensive sampling or adversarial training. Compared to previous score matching algorithms, our method is more scalable to high dimensional data and more stable to optimize. We show with extensive experimental results that it can be applied to density estimation on synthetic data, image generation, image denoising, and training latent variable models with implicit encoders.

paragraphs: Autoregressive models describe a joint distribution through a sequence of conditional distributions. Each conditional normally needs to be normalized, which constrains how it can be represented. This paper proposes representing the derivatives of the logarithms of those conditionals instead. These derivatives, called scores, do not themselves require normalization, giving the model greater flexibility.

The resulting autoregressive conditional score model is trained using a new distribution-comparison objective called Composite Score Matching. For this model family, the objective can be evaluated and optimized efficiently without expensive sampling or adversarial training. The approach therefore changes both what the network represents and how the mismatch between model and data is measured.

The authors report greater scalability to high-dimensional data and more stable optimization than previous score-matching algorithms. Their experiments cover synthetic density estimation, image generation, image denoising, and latent-variable models with implicit encoders. Together, these applications demonstrate that the conditional-score formulation can support several modeling tasks while avoiding the normalization constraints that motivated the work.
summary.tldr: Autoregressive conditional score models gain flexibility by learning conditional log-density derivatives with an efficient score-matching objective.

title: Autoregressive Score Matching

abstract: We consider a natural model of online preference aggregation, where sets of preferred items R_1, R_2, ..., R_t, ..., along with a demand for k_t items in each R_t, appear online. Without prior knowledge of (R_t, k_t), the learner maintains a ranking \pi_t aiming that at least k_t items from R_t appear high in \pi_t. This is a fundamental problem in preference aggregation with applications to e.g., ordering product or news items in web pages based on user scrolling and click patterns. The widely studied Generalized Min-Sum-Set-Cover (GMSSC) problem serves as a formal model for the setting above. GMSSC is NP-hard and the standard application of no-regret online learning algorithms is computationally inefficient, because they operate in the space of rankings. In this work, we show how to achieve low regret for GMSSC in polynomial-time. We employ dimensionality reduction from rankings to the space of doubly stochastic matrices, where we apply Online Gradient Descent. A key step is to show how subgradients can be computed efficiently, by solving the dual of a configuration LP. Using deterministic and randomized rounding schemes, we map doubly stochastic matrices back to rankings with a small loss in the GMSSC objective.

The learner must choose its ranking without knowing the next request. Generalized Min-Sum-Set-Cover formalizes this problem, with applications such as ordering products or news according to user preferences.

The authors instead optimize in the space of doubly stochastic matrices, a reduced representation that supports Online Gradient Descent. The paper establishes low regret with polynomial-time computation. Its contribution is to connect an efficiently optimized representation to usable rankings, making online learning tractable for this NP-hard underlying ranking problem.
summary.tldr: Optimizing matrix representations and rounding them into rankings enables polynomial-time, low-regret learning for online preference aggregation.

title: Efficient Online Learning of Optimal Rankings: Dimensionality Reduction via Gradient Descent

abstract: Extracting relevant features from data sets where the number of observations (n) is much smaller then the number of predictors (p) is a major challenge in modern statistics. Sorted L-One Penalized Estimation (SLOPE)—a generalization of the lasso—is a promising method within this setting. Current numerical procedures for SLOPE, however, lack the efficiency that respective tools for the lasso enjoy, particularly in the context of estimating a complete regularization path. A key component in the efficiency of the lasso is predictor screening rules: rules that allow predictors to be discarded before estimating the model. This is the first paper to establish such a rule for SLOPE. We develop a screening rule for SLOPE by examining its subdifferential and show that this rule is a generalization of the strong rule for the lasso. Our rule is heuristic, which means that it may discard predictors erroneously. In our paper, however, we show that such situations are rare and easily safeguarded against by a simple check of the optimality conditions. Our numerical experiments show that the rule performs well in practice, leading to improvements by orders of magnitude for data in the (p >> n) domain, as well as incurring no additional computational overhead when (n > p).

Its numerical procedures have lacked some of the efficiency available for the lasso, especially when fitting models across a regularization path. Screening rules offer one route to faster fitting by discarding predictors before solving each model.

The authors derive a screening rule from SLOPE's subdifferential, the mathematical object describing its generalized slopes. Their rule extends the lasso's strong screening rule to SLOPE. It is heuristic and can wrongly discard useful predictors, so the paper includes a safeguard based on checking optimality conditions. The authors report that such errors are rare.

Numerical experiments show improvements by orders of magnitude when predictors greatly outnumber observations, with no additional computational overhead when observations outnumber predictors. The safeguard is important to interpreting the method: the speedup comes from aggressive screening paired with a check, rather than an assertion that screening never makes mistakes. This makes a key computational strategy available for SLOPE fitting.
summary.tldr: A heuristic screening rule accelerates SLOPE fitting, with optimality checks guarding against incorrectly discarded predictors.

title: The Strong Screening Rule for SLOPE

abstract: Coresets are small data summaries that are sufficient for model training. They can be maintained online, enabling efficient handling of large data streams under resource constraints. However, existing constructions are limited to simple models such as k-means and logistic regression. In this work, we propose a novel coreset construction via cardinality-constrained bilevel optimization. We show how our framework can efficiently generate coresets for deep neural networks, and demonstrate its empirical benefits in continual learning and in streaming settings.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small summary of a dataset intended to retain the information needed for model training. Such summaries are useful when observations arrive continuously and resources prevent retaining or processing everything. The paper addresses a restriction of existing coreset constructions, which the abstract describes as being limited to relatively simple models such as k-means and logistic regression.

The proposed construction uses cardinality-constrained bilevel optimization. The cardinality constraint limits the size of the summary, while the two-level formulation connects summary construction with the model-training problem it is meant to support. This makes the choice of retained information part of an optimization framework directed toward training usefulness.

The authors show that their framework can efficiently construct coresets for deep neural networks and report empirical benefits in continual learning and streaming. The significance is extending compact training summaries to a more expressive class of models. The stated evidence supports their usefulness in these settings without asserting that every small summary exactly reproduces full-data training.
summary.tldr: A size-constrained bilevel optimization framework constructs deep-network coresets with empirical benefits for continual learning and streaming.

title: Coresets via Bilevel Optimization for Continual Learning and Streaming

abstract: Direct optimization (McAllester et al., 2010; Song et al., 2016) is an appealing framework that replaces integration with optimization of a random objective for approximating gradients in models with discrete random variables (Lorberbom et al., 2018). A* sampling (Maddison et al., 2014) is a framework for optimizing such random objectives over large spaces. We show how to combine these techniques to yield a reinforcement learning algorithm that approximates a policy gradient by finding trajectories that optimize a random objective. We call the resulting algorithms \emph{direct policy gradient} (DirPG) algorithms. A main benefit of DirPG algorithms is that they allow the insertion of domain knowledge in the form of upper bounds on return-to-go at training time, like is used in heuristic search, while still directly computing a policy gradient. We further analyze their properties, showing there are cases where DirPG has an exponentially larger probability of sampling informative gradients compared to REINFORCE. We also show that there is a built-in variance reduction technique and that a parameter that was previously viewed as a numerical approximation can be interpreted as controlling risk sensitivity. Empirically, we evaluate the effect of key degrees of freedom and show that the algorithm performs well in illustrative domains compared to baselines.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Direct Policy Gradient algorithms for reinforcement learning with discrete actions. The approach combines direct optimization, which approximates gradients by optimizing a random objective, with A* sampling, which supports that optimization over large spaces. The resulting method finds trajectories that optimize a random objective and uses them to approximate a policy gradient.

Experiments examine key design choices and show good performance against baselines in illustrative domains. The exponential advantage is therefore a result for particular cases, alongside supporting empirical examples.
summary.tldr: DirPG approximates policy gradients through randomized trajectory optimization, allowing search bounds and offering more informative gradients in some analyzed cases.

title: Direct Policy Gradients: Direct Optimization of Policies in Discrete Action Spaces

abstract: Loss functions are a cornerstone of machine learning and the starting point of most algorithms. Statistics and Bayesian decision theory have contributed, via properness, to elicit over the past decades a wide set of admissible losses in supervised learning, to which most popular choices belong (logistic, square, Matsushita, etc.). Rather than making a potentially biased ad hoc choice of the loss, there has recently been a boost in efforts to fit the loss to the domain at hand while training the model itself. The key approaches fit a canonical link, a function which monotonically relates the closed unit interval to R and can provide a proper loss via integration. In this paper, we rely on a broader view of proper composite losses and a recent construct from information geometry, source functions, whose fitting alleviates constraints faced by canonical links. We introduce a trick on squared Gaussian Processes to obtain a random process whose paths are compliant source functions with many desirable properties in the context of link estimation. Experimental results demonstrate substantial improvements over the state of the art.

paragraphs: A loss function determines how a learning algorithm penalizes its mistakes. Rather than choosing that function in advance, this paper studies learning a loss alongside the predictive model. The aim is to adapt the loss to the domain while retaining the mathematical structure of proper losses, a class grounded in statistics and Bayesian decision theory.

Previous approaches learn a canonical link, a monotonic function relating probabilities to real-valued scores, and obtain a proper loss through integration. The authors use a broader formulation of proper composite losses based on source functions from information geometry. Fitting these functions eases constraints encountered when fitting canonical links directly.

The technical construction transforms squared Gaussian processes into a random process whose paths satisfy the requirements for source functions. This provides a structured way to learn suitable functions rather than treating loss selection as an unconstrained search. Experiments report substantial improvements over the state of the art, supporting the usefulness of this more flexible route to learning losses.
summary.tldr: The paper learns proper loss functions through source functions and a Gaussian-process construction, reporting substantial improvements over prior methods.

title: All your loss are belong to Bayes

abstract: To obtain excellent deep neural architectures, a series of techniques are carefully designed in EfficientNets. The giant formula for simultaneously enlarging the resolution, depth and width provides us a Rubik's cube for neural networks. So that we can find networks with high efficiency and excellent performance by twisting the three dimensions. This paper aims to explore the twisting rules for obtaining deep neural networks with minimum model sizes and computational costs. Different from the network enlarging, we observe that resolution and depth are more important than width for tiny networks. Therefore, the original method, \ie the compound scaling in EfficientNet is no longer suitable. To this end, we summarize a tiny formula for downsizing neural architectures through a series of smaller models derived from the EfficientNet-B0 with the FLOPs constraint. Experimental results on the ImageNet benchmark illustrate that our TinyNet performs much better than the smaller version of EfficientNets using the inversed giant formula. For instance, our TinyNet-E achieves a 59.9\% Top-1 accuracy with only 24M FLOPs, which is about 1.9\% higher than that of the previous best MobileNetV3 with similar computational cost. Code will be available at {\small\url{https://github.com/huawei-noah/ghostnet/tree/master/tinynet_pytorch}}, and {\small\url{https://gitee.com/mindspore/mindspore/tree/master/model_zoo/research/cv/tinynet}}.

This paper asks how they should instead be adjusted to build very small networks with low computational costs, and finds that simply reversing the enlargement rule is unsuitable.

The authors observe that resolution and depth matter more than width for tiny networks. They use a series of smaller architectures derived from EfficientNet-B0 to develop a downsizing formula under a floating-point-operation constraint. The resulting TinyNets reflect a different allocation of limited computation across the three dimensions, guided by the behavior of small models.

On ImageNet, TinyNets outperform smaller EfficientNets obtained by reversing the original scaling formula. TinyNet-E reaches 59.9% top-1 accuracy using 24 million FLOPs, about 1.9 percentage points above the reported previous best MobileNetV3 at similar computational cost. The finding supports treating downsizing as its own architecture-design problem: scaling rules effective for larger networks need not preserve the best balance when the computational budget becomes very small.
summary.tldr: TinyNet uses a downsizing rule that prioritizes resolution and depth over width, improving ImageNet accuracy at small computational budgets.

title: Model Rubik’s Cube: Twisting Resolution, Depth and Width for TinyNets

abstract: Moiré artifacts are common in digital photography, resulting from the interference between high-frequency scene content and the color filter array of the camera. Existing deep learning-based demoiréing methods trained on large scale datasets are limited in handling various complex moiré patterns, and mainly focus on demoiréing of photos taken of digital displays. Moreover, obtaining moiré-free ground-truth in natural scenes is difficult but needed for training. In this paper, we propose a self-adaptive learning method for demoiréing a high-frequency image, with the help of an additional defocused moiré-free blur image. Given an image degraded with moiré artifacts and a moiré-free blur image, our network predicts a moiré-free clean image and a blur kernel with a self-adaptive strategy that does not require an explicit training stage, instead performing test-time adaptation. Our model has two sub-networks and works iteratively. During each iteration, one sub-network takes the moiré image as input, removing moiré patterns and restoring image details, and the other sub-network estimates the blur kernel from the blur image. The two sub-networks are jointly optimized. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods and can produce high-quality demoiréd results. It can generalize well to the task of removing moiré artifacts caused by display screens. In addition, we build a new moiré dataset, including images with screen and texture moiré artifacts. As far as we know, this is the first dataset with real texture moiré patterns.

Removing them from natural photographs is difficult partly because clean training targets are hard to obtain. This paper uses a pair of inputs: an image containing moiré and an additional defocused, moiré-free image of the scene.

The method adapts at test time without an explicit training stage. Two jointly optimized subnetworks work iteratively: one predicts a clean image from the moiré-corrupted input, while the other estimates a blur kernel from the blurred image. This setup uses the additional defocused observation to support restoration while jointly estimating the blur.

The authors also introduce a dataset containing screen and texture moiré, describing it as the first with real texture moiré patterns to their knowledge. The method's stated input requirement is central to its contribution: restoration uses both the focused corrupted image and the defocused moiré-free image.
summary.tldr: Test-time adaptation jointly estimates a clean image and blur kernel from a moiré-corrupted photograph and a defocused moiré-free companion.

title: Self-Adaptively Learning to Demoiré from Focused and Defocused Image Pairs

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is typically viewed as the problem of estimating single-step policies (for model-free RL) or single-step models (for model-based RL), leveraging the Markov property to factorize the problem in time. However, we can also view RL as a sequence modeling problem: predict a sequence of actions that leads to a sequence of high rewards. Viewed in this way, it is tempting to consider whether powerful, high-capacity sequence prediction models that work well in other supervised learning domains, such as natural-language processing, can also provide simple and effective solutions to the RL problem. To this end, we explore how RL can be reframed as "one big sequence modeling" problem, using state-of-the-art Transformer architectures to model distributions over sequences of states, actions, and rewards. Addressing RL as a sequence modeling problem significantly simplifies a range of design decisions: we no longer require separate behavior policy constraints, as is common in prior work on offline model-free RL, and we no longer require ensembles or other epistemic uncertainty estimators, as is common in prior work on model-based RL. All of these roles are filled by the same Transformer sequence model. In our experiments, we demonstrate the flexibility of this approach across imitation learning, goal-conditioned RL, and offline RL.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly breaks decision-making into single-step policies or models. This paper explores a sequence-based view: model states, actions, and rewards together, then use that representation to predict action sequences associated with high rewards. The approach brings Transformer sequence modeling to the structure of reinforcement learning trajectories.

The Transformer learns distributions over complete sequences of these quantities. In the proposed framework, the same sequence model fills roles that other approaches assign to separate components. The authors report that they do not need separate behavior-policy constraints commonly used in offline model-free learning, or ensembles and other epistemic-uncertainty estimators commonly used in model-based learning.

This consolidation simplifies a range of design decisions within their approach. Experiments demonstrate its flexibility across imitation learning, goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, and offline reinforcement learning. The stated finding is that one sequence-modeling formulation can support these different settings; the abstract does not claim a universal performance advantage. Its contribution is a unified way to represent and use the sequential structure of decision-making data.
summary.tldr: A Transformer models states, actions, and rewards jointly, providing a unified sequence-based approach across several reinforcement learning settings.

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning as One Big Sequence Modeling Problem

abstract: We consider the problem of online classification under a privacy constraint. In this setting a learner observes sequentially a stream of labelled examples $(x_t, y_t)$, for $1 \leq t \leq T$, and returns at each iteration $t$ a hypothesis $h_t$ which is used to predict the label of each new example $x_t$. The learner's performance is measured by her regret against a known hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$. We require that the algorithm satisfies the following privacy constraint: the sequence $h_1, \ldots, h_T$ of hypotheses output by the algorithm needs to be an $(\epsilon, \delta)$-differentially private function of the whole input sequence $(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_T, y_T)$.We provide the first non-trivial regret bound for the realizable setting. Specifically, we show that if the class $\mathcal{H}$ has constant Littlestone dimension then, given an oblivious sequence of labelled examples, there is a private learner that makes in expectation at most $O(\log T)$ mistakes -- comparable to the optimal mistake bound in the non-private case, up to a logarithmic factor. Moreover, for general values of the Littlestone dimension $d$, the same mistake bound holds but with a doubly-exponential in $d$ factor. A recent line of work has demonstrated a strong connection between classes that are online learnable and those that are differentially-private learnable. Our results strengthen this connection and show that an online learning algorithm can in fact be directly privatized (in the realizable setting).We also discuss an adaptive setting and provide a sublinear regret bound of $O(\sqrt{T})$.

paragraphs: This paper studies online classification when the entire sequence of released prediction rules must satisfy differential privacy with respect to the input examples. The learner receives labeled data over time, and performance is compared with a specified hypothesis class. The question is whether meaningful online learning guarantees survive this privacy requirement.

For the realizable setting, where the examples are consistent with a hypothesis in the class, the authors establish a logarithmic expected mistake bound for classes with constant Littlestone dimension. This result assumes an oblivious example sequence, rather than one chosen in response to the learner’s behavior. For general dimension d, the same logarithmic dependence on the number of rounds holds with a factor that is doubly exponential in d.

The result strengthens the connection between online learnability and private learnability by showing direct privatization in the realizable setting. The paper also treats an adaptive setting and gives an O(√T) regret bound. These guarantees preserve learning over time while making their dependence on the sequence setting and class complexity explicit.
summary.tldr: Private online classification admits logarithmic expected mistakes under realizability and an oblivious sequence, with a strong dependence on Littlestone dimension.

title: Littlestone Classes are Privately Online Learnable

abstract: Most topic modeling approaches are based on the bag-of-words assumption, where each word is required to be conditionally independent in the same document. As a result, both of the generative story and the topic formulation have totally ignored the semantic dependency among words, which is important for improving the semantic comprehension and model interpretability. To this end, in this paper, we revisit the task of topic modeling by transforming each document into a directed graph with word dependency as edges between word nodes, and develop a novel approach, namely Graph Neural Topic Model (GNTM). Specifically, in GNTM, a well-defined probabilistic generative story is designed to model both the graph structure and word sets with multinomial distributions on the vocabulary and word dependency edge set as the topics. Meanwhile, a Neural Variational Inference (NVI) approach is proposed to learn our model with graph neural networks to encode the document graphs. Besides, we theoretically demonstrate that Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) can be derived from GNTM as a special case with similar objective functions. Finally, extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets have clearly demonstrated the effectiveness and interpretability of GNTM compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

Specifically, in GNTM, a well-defined probabilistic generative story is designed to model both the graph structure and word sets with multinomial distributions on the vocabulary and word dependency edge set as the topics. Meanwhile, a Neural Variational Inference (NVI) approach is proposed to learn our model with graph neural networks to encode the document graphs. Besides, we theoretically demonstrate that Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) can be derived from GNTM as a special case with similar objective functions. Finally, extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets have clearly demonstrated the effectiveness and interpretability of GNTM compared with state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Topic models commonly represent a document through its words while setting aside dependencies among those words. This paper argues that such dependencies matter for semantic understanding and interpretability. Its Graph Neural Topic Model, or GNTM, represents each document as a directed graph whose nodes are words and whose edges encode word dependencies.

GNTM gives a probabilistic account of both the words and the graph structure. Topics include distributions over the vocabulary and over dependency edges, so they can describe relationships as well as word occurrence. A neural variational inference procedure learns the model, using graph neural networks to encode the document graphs.

The authors also establish a theoretical connection to Latent Dirichlet Allocation: LDA can be derived as a special case of GNTM with similar objective functions. This links the graph formulation to an established topic-modeling approach. Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate effectiveness and interpretability relative to state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a topic representation and learning procedure that explicitly incorporates the dependencies omitted by a bag-of-words view.
summary.tldr: GNTM models documents as word-dependency graphs, incorporating relationships into topic learning and recovering LDA as a special case.

title: Topic Modeling Revisited: A Document Graph-based Neural Network Perspective

abstract: We introduce a scalable approach to Gaussian process inference that combines spatio-temporal filtering with natural gradient variational inference, resulting in a non-conjugate GP method for multivariate data that scales linearly with respect to time. Our natural gradient approach enables application of parallel filtering and smoothing, further reducing the temporal span complexity to be logarithmic in the number of time steps. We derive a sparse approximation that constructs a state-space model over a reduced set of spatial inducing points, and show that for separable Markov kernels the full and sparse cases exactly recover the standard variational GP, whilst exhibiting favourable computational properties. To further improve the spatial scaling we propose a mean-field assumption of independence between spatial locations which, when coupled with sparsity and parallelisation, leads to an efficient and accurate method for large spatio-temporal problems.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes for data varying across space and time can be computationally demanding. This paper combines spatio-temporal filtering with natural gradient variational inference to make non-conjugate Gaussian process inference more scalable for multivariate observations. The resulting method has computational scaling that is linear in the number of time steps.

The natural gradient formulation also permits parallel filtering and smoothing. This reduces temporal span complexity—the sequential depth of the parallel calculation—to logarithmic in the number of time steps. To reduce spatial costs, the authors derive a sparse version that builds a state-space model around a smaller collection of spatial inducing points.

For separable Markov kernels, both the full and sparse constructions exactly recover the corresponding standard variational Gaussian process while offering favorable computational properties. A further mean-field approximation assumes independence between spatial locations to improve spatial scaling. Combined with sparsity and parallel computation, this produces an efficient and accurate method for large spatio-temporal problems. The exact-recovery statement and the additional independence approximation are distinct parts of the construction.
summary.tldr: Filtering, natural gradients, spatial sparsity, and parallel computation make variational Gaussian processes more scalable for spatio-temporal data.

title: Spatio-Temporal Variational Gaussian Processes

abstract: The solution of a partial differential equation can be obtained by computing the inverse operator map between the input and the solution space. Towards this end, we introduce a $\textit{multiwavelet-based neural operator learning scheme}$ that compresses the associated operator's kernel using fine-grained wavelets. By explicitly embedding the inverse multiwavelet filters, we learn the projection of the kernel onto fixed multiwavelet polynomial bases. The projected kernel is trained at multiple scales derived from using repeated computation of multiwavelet transform. This allows learning the complex dependencies at various scales and results in a resolution-independent scheme. Compare to the prior works, we exploit the fundamental properties of the operator's kernel which enable numerically efficient representation. We perform experiments on the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation, Burgers' equation, Darcy Flow, and Navier-Stokes equation. Compared with the existing neural operator approaches, our model shows significantly higher accuracy and achieves state-of-the-art in a range of datasets. For the time-varying equations, the proposed method exhibits a ($2X-10X$) improvement ($0.0018$ ($0.0033$) relative $L2$ error for Burgers' (KdV) equation). By learning the mappings between function spaces, the proposed method has the ability to find the solution of a high-resolution input after learning from lower-resolution data.

paragraphs: This paper learns mappings from the inputs of partial differential equations to their solutions. Instead of treating each solution as an unrelated prediction, it models the inverse operator between function spaces. The proposed neural operator uses multiwavelets to compress and represent the operator's kernel efficiently.

The method embeds inverse multiwavelet filters and learns the kernel's projection onto fixed polynomial bases. Repeated multiwavelet transforms create several scales at which the projected kernel is trained. This allows the model to capture dependencies at different scales and produces a resolution-independent scheme. Learning a function-space mapping also allows it to process higher-resolution inputs after training on lower-resolution data.

Experiments cover Korteweg-de Vries, Burgers', Darcy flow, and Navier-Stokes equations. The authors report higher accuracy than existing neural operator approaches and leading results across a range of datasets. For time-varying equations, they report improvements of two to ten times, including relative L2 errors of 0.0018 for Burgers' and 0.0033 for Korteweg-de Vries. These results support the value of explicitly building multiscale kernel structure into operator learning.
summary.tldr: A multiwavelet neural operator learns differential-equation solution maps across scales and supports higher-resolution prediction from lower-resolution training.

title: Multiwavelet-based Operator Learning for Differential Equations

abstract: Neural networks have been shown to outperform kernel methods in practice (including neural tangent kernels). Most theoretical explanations of this performance gap focus on learning a complex hypothesis class; in some cases, it is unclear whether this hypothesis class captures realistic data. In this work, we propose a related, but alternative, explanation for this performance gap in the image classification setting, based on finding a sparse signal in the presence of noise. Specifically, we prove that, for a simple data distribution with sparse signal amidst high-variance noise, a simple convolutional neural network trained using stochastic gradient descent learns to threshold out the noise and find the signal. On the other hand, the corresponding neural tangent kernel, with a fixed set of predetermined features, is unable to adapt to the signal in this manner. We supplement our theoretical results by demonstrating this phenomenon empirically: in CIFAR-10 and MNIST images with various backgrounds, as the background noise increases in intensity, a CNN's performance stays relatively robust, whereas its corresponding neural tangent kernel sees a notable drop in performance. We therefore propose the "local signal adaptivity" (LSA) phenomenon as one explanation for the superiority of neural networks over kernel methods.

paragraphs: This paper investigates one reason neural networks can outperform kernel methods in image classification: their ability to discover a sparse useful signal amid strong noise. The proposed explanation focuses on adapting features to local signal structure, complementing explanations based on the complexity of the functions a network can represent.

For a simple data distribution containing sparse signal and high-variance noise, the authors prove that a simple convolutional network trained with stochastic gradient descent learns to threshold away noise and identify the signal. Its corresponding neural tangent kernel uses predetermined features and cannot adapt in the same way under this analysis.

Experiments with CIFAR-10 and MNIST images placed against different backgrounds illustrate the same phenomenon. As background noise grows stronger, the convolutional network remains relatively robust, while its corresponding neural tangent kernel loses substantial performance. The authors call this local signal adaptivity and present it as one explanation of the performance gap. The theorem concerns the specified simple distribution, while the image experiments provide related empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: Theory and image experiments show how learned convolutional features can isolate sparse signals from noise more effectively than corresponding fixed kernel features.

title: Local Signal Adaptivity: Provable Feature Learning in Neural Networks Beyond Kernels

abstract: Copulas are a powerful tool for modeling multivariate distributions as they allow to separately estimate the univariate marginal distributions and the joint dependency structure. However, known parametric copulas offer limited flexibility especially in high dimensions, while commonly used non-parametric methods suffer from the curse of dimensionality. A popular remedy is to construct a tree-based hierarchy of conditional bivariate copulas.In this paper, we propose a flexible, yet conceptually simple alternative based on implicit generative neural networks.The key challenge is to ensure marginal uniformity of the estimated copula distribution.We achieve this by learning a multivariate latent distribution with unspecified marginals but the desired dependency structure.By applying the probability integral transform, we can then obtain samples from the high-dimensional copula distribution without relying on parametric assumptions or the need to find a suitable tree structure.Experiments on synthetic and real data from finance, physics, and image generation demonstrate the performance of this approach.

paragraphs: Copulas separate two aspects of a multivariate distribution: how each variable behaves individually and how the variables depend on one another. This separation is useful, but existing approaches face tradeoffs. Parametric copulas can lack flexibility in high dimensions, while common nonparametric approaches struggle as the number of dimensions grows.

The paper proposes an alternative based on implicit generative neural networks. A key requirement is that a copula’s individual marginal distributions must be uniform. The method first learns a multivariate latent distribution with the desired dependency structure while leaving its marginal distributions unspecified. It then applies the probability integral transform to obtain copula samples.

This construction allows high-dimensional dependency modeling without imposing a parametric copula family or finding a suitable tree of conditional pairwise copulas. The authors demonstrate the approach on synthetic data and real data from finance, physics, and image generation. The contribution is a conceptually simple neural sampling approach that addresses marginal uniformity while preserving the intended separation between dependencies and individual-variable distributions.
summary.tldr: Implicit generative copulas combine neural dependency modeling with a probability integral transform to produce copula samples without parametric or tree-structure choices.

title: Implicit Generative Copulas

abstract: This paper contributes a formal case study in retrospective dataset documentation and pinpoints several problems with the influential BookCorpus dataset. Recent work has underscored the importance of dataset documentation in machine learning research, including by addressing ``documentation debt'' for datasets that have been used widely but documented sparsely. BookCorpus is one such dataset. Researchers have used BookCorpus to train OpenAI's GPT-N models and Google's BERT models, but little to no documentation exists about the dataset's motivation, composition, collection process, etc. We offer a retrospective datasheet with key context and information about BookCorpus, including several notable deficiencies. In particular, we find evidence that (1) BookCorpus violates copyright restrictions for many books, (2) BookCorpus contains thousands of duplicated books, and (3) BookCorpus exhibits significant skews in genre representation. We also find hints of other potential deficiencies that call for future research, such as lopsided author contributions. While more work remains, this initial effort to provide a datasheet for BookCorpus offers a cautionary case study and adds to growing literature that urges more careful, systematic documentation of machine learning datasets.

paragraphs: A dataset can become influential before its origins and contents are adequately documented. This paper examines that problem through BookCorpus, which has been used to train GPT-N and BERT models. The authors describe its sparse documentation as documentation debt: missing context about motivation, composition, and collection that remains relevant after widespread adoption.

They produce a retrospective datasheet that gathers key information about the dataset and identifies deficiencies. Their investigation finds evidence of copyright restriction violations affecting many books, thousands of duplicated books, and substantial imbalance in genre representation. These findings concern distinct aspects of the resource: permission to use material, repeated content, and the distribution of its subject matter.

The authors distinguish these findings from tentative concerns, including hints that some authors contribute disproportionately. Those possibilities require further research. The resulting datasheet is an initial documentation effort and a cautionary case study showing how a widely used training resource can carry unresolved questions about its construction and composition.
summary.tldr: A retrospective BookCorpus datasheet finds evidence of copyright issues, extensive duplication, and genre imbalance in a widely used training dataset.

title: Addressing "Documentation Debt" in Machine Learning: A Retrospective Datasheet for BookCorpus

abstract: Zhang et al. (ICML 2020) introduced a novel modification of Goldstein's classical subgradient method, with an efficiency guarantee of $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ for minimizing Lipschitz functions. Their work, however, makes use of an oracle that is not efficiently implementable. In this paper, we obtain the same efficiency guarantee with a standard subgradient oracle, thus making our algorithm efficiently implementable. Our resulting method works on any Lipschitz function whose value and gradient can be evaluated at points of differentiability. We additionally present a new cutting plane algorithm that achieves an efficiency of $O(d\varepsilon^{-2}\log S)$ for the class of $S$-smooth (and possibly non-convex) functions in low dimensions. Strikingly, this $\epsilon$-dependence matches the lower bounds for the convex setting.

paragraphs: An optimization guarantee is useful computationally only if the information required at each step can actually be obtained efficiently. This paper addresses that issue for a previous method for minimizing Lipschitz functions: its attractive efficiency bound relied on an oracle that was not efficiently implementable.

The authors develop a gradient sampling method that preserves the O(ε⁻⁴) efficiency guarantee while using a standard subgradient oracle. The method applies to any Lipschitz function whose value and gradient can be evaluated wherever the function is differentiable. This replaces the problematic information requirement with a more practical one without worsening the stated dependence on the accuracy parameter.

A second contribution targets low-dimensional problems through a cutting-plane algorithm. For functions with smoothness parameter S, including potentially nonconvex functions, its efficiency scales as O(d ε⁻² log S), where d is dimension. Its dependence on ε matches lower bounds from the convex setting. Together, the results distinguish a broadly applicable implementable method from a sharper guarantee available with smoothness and low dimension.
summary.tldr: Gradient sampling achieves a previous Lipschitz optimization guarantee with a standard oracle, while a second method gives sharper low-dimensional rates.

title: A gradient sampling method with complexity guarantees for Lipschitz functions in high and low dimensions

abstract: In this paper, we consider the matching of multi-agent multi-armed bandit problem, i.e., while agents prefer arms with higher expected reward, arms also have preferences on agents. In such case, agents pulling the same arm may encounter collisions, which leads to a reward of zero.For this problem, we design a specific communication protocol which uses deliberate collision to transmit information among agents, and propose a layer-based algorithm that helps establish optimal stable matching between agents and arms. With this subtle communication protocol, our algorithm achieves a state-of-the-art $O(\log T)$ regret in the decentralized matching market, and outperforms existing baselines in experimental results.

In such case, agents pulling the same arm may encounter collisions, which leads to a reward of zero.For this problem, we design a specific communication protocol which uses deliberate collision to transmit information among agents, and propose a layer-based algorithm that helps establish optimal stable matching between agents and arms. With this subtle communication protocol, our algorithm achieves a state-of-the-art $O(\log T)$ regret in the decentralized matching market, and outperforms existing baselines in experimental results.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit problem in which several agents seek rewarding arms, while the arms also have preferences over agents. The task therefore involves matching participants on two sides of a market. Agents must learn which arms offer higher expected rewards while coordinating their choices with other agents.

A collision occurs when agents select the same arm and can leave them with zero reward. The authors turn this apparent obstacle into a communication mechanism: agents deliberately create collisions to transmit information. They combine the protocol with a layer-based algorithm designed to establish an optimal stable matching between agents and arms. Communication is thus built into the same interactions through which agents obtain rewards.

The resulting decentralized algorithm achieves regret growing on the order of log T, which the abstract reports as state of the art for this matching setting. Experiments also show improvements over existing baselines. The key contribution is the coordination strategy: deliberate collisions provide information that supports learning and matching, even though collisions themselves can sacrifice immediate reward.
summary.tldr: A collision-based communication protocol supports decentralized stable matching with logarithmic regret.

title: Matching in Multi-arm Bandit with Collision

abstract: Dataset distillation aims to learn a small synthetic dataset that preserves most of the information from the original dataset. Dataset distillation can be formulated as a bi-level meta-learning problem where the outer loop optimizes the meta-dataset and the inner loop trains a model on the distilled data. Meta-gradient computation is one of the key challenges in this formulation, as differentiating through the inner loop learning procedure introduces significant computation and memory costs. In this paper, we address these challenges using neural Feature Regression with Pooling (FRePo), achieving the state-of-the-art performance with an order of magnitude less memory requirement and two orders of magnitude faster training than previous methods. The proposed algorithm is analogous to truncated backpropagation through time with a pool of models to alleviate various types of overfitting in dataset distillation. FRePo significantly outperforms the previous methods on CIFAR100, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K. Furthermore, we show that high-quality distilled data can greatly improve various downstream applications, such as continual learning and membership inference defense. Please check out our webpage at https://sites.google.com/view/frepo.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation seeks a small synthetic training set that retains much of a larger dataset's useful information. One formulation repeatedly trains a model on the synthetic data, then adjusts that data based on the model's performance. Computing how changes to the data affect the entire training process can demand substantial memory and computation.

The paper introduces neural Feature Regression with Pooling, or FRePo, to address that bottleneck. Its optimization is analogous to truncated backpropagation through time, reducing the burden associated with differentiating through training. It also uses a pool of models to alleviate different forms of overfitting during distillation. Together, these choices aim to make synthetic datasets both cheaper to learn and more effective.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance with an order of magnitude less memory and two orders of magnitude faster training than previous methods. FRePo substantially improves results on CIFAR100, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K. The paper also demonstrates benefits of high-quality distilled data for continual learning and membership-inference defense, extending its value beyond dataset compression alone.
summary.tldr: FRePo learns effective synthetic datasets with substantially lower training and memory costs, while improving distillation and downstream applications.

title: Dataset Distillation using Neural Feature Regression

abstract: CLIP yielded impressive results on zero-shot transfer learning tasks and is considered as a foundation model like BERT or GPT3. CLIP vision models that have a rich representation are pre-trained using the InfoNCE objective and natural language supervision before they are fine-tuned on particular tasks. Though CLIP excels at zero-shot transfer learning, it suffers from an explaining away problem, that is, it focuses on one or few features, while neglecting other relevant features. This problem is caused by insufficiently extracting the covariance structure in the original multi-modal data. We suggest to use modern Hopfield networks to tackle the problem of explaining away. Their retrieved embeddings have an enriched covariance structure derived from co-occurrences of features in the stored embeddings. However, modern Hopfield networks increase the saturation effect of the InfoNCE objective which hampers learning. We propose to use the InfoLOOB objective to mitigate this saturation effect. We introduce the novel "Contrastive Leave One Out Boost" (CLOOB), which uses modern Hopfield networks for covariance enrichment together with the InfoLOOB objective. In experiments we compare CLOOB to CLIP after pre-training on the Conceptual Captions and the YFCC dataset with respect to their zero-shot transfer learning performance on other datasets. CLOOB consistently outperforms CLIP at zero-shot transfer learning across all considered architectures and datasets.

paragraphs: CLIP learns image representations using natural-language supervision and can transfer to new tasks without task-specific training. This paper identifies an explaining-away problem in which it focuses on a few features while overlooking other relevant ones. The authors attribute this behavior to insufficient extraction of covariance structure: information about which features occur together in the multimodal data.

CLOOB addresses that problem with modern Hopfield networks, which retrieve embeddings enriched by feature co-occurrences in stored embeddings. However, this enrichment increases a saturation effect in CLIP's InfoNCE training objective, hampering learning. After pretraining on Conceptual Captions and YFCC, the authors compare zero-shot transfer against CLIP on other datasets. CLOOB performs better across all architectures and datasets considered in those experiments, supporting the combined design within the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: CLOOB combines Hopfield-based feature enrichment with InfoLOOB training and outperforms CLIP in the reported zero-shot transfer comparisons.

title: CLOOB: Modern Hopfield Networks with InfoLOOB Outperform CLIP

abstract: Humans can perform unseen tasks by recalling relevant skills acquired previously and then generalizing them to the target tasks, even if there is no supervision at all. In this paper, we aim to improve this kind of cross-task generalization ability of massive multi-task language models, such as T0 and FLAN, in an unsupervised setting. We propose a retrieval-augmentation method named ReCross that takes a few unlabelled examples as queries to retrieve a small subset of upstream data and uses them to update the multi-task model for better generalization. ReCross is a straightforward yet effective retrieval method that combines both efficient dense retrieval and effective pair-wise reranking. Our results and analysis show that it significantly outperforms both non-retrieval methods and other baseline methods.

In this paper, we aim to improve this kind of cross-task generalization ability of massive multi-task language models, such as T0 and FLAN, in an unsupervised setting. paragraphs: A language model trained on many tasks may still struggle with a new task that has no labeled examples. This paper studies how to improve that cross-task generalization using a few unlabeled examples from the target task. Its method, ReCross, uses those examples to identify useful material from the model's upstream training data.

ReCross retrieves a small subset of that data and then uses it to update the multitask model. The unlabeled target examples guide which prior training material is selected, linking the new task to potentially relevant previous experience. Retrieval combines efficient dense search with pairwise reranking, so candidate selection is followed by a more focused relevance comparison.

The reported results and analysis show significant improvements over both non-retrieval approaches and other baseline methods. The unsupervised setting concerns the absence of target-task supervision; adaptation still draws on upstream data. The contribution is a practical way to select and reuse previous training experience for a new task, with retrieval serving as a guide to model updating.
summary.tldr: ReCross uses unlabeled target examples to retrieve upstream training data and update multitask models for better cross-task generalization.

title: Unsupervised Cross-Task Generalization via Retrieval Augmentation

abstract: In many real-world settings exact perturbation sets to be used by an adversary are not plausibly available to a learner. While prior literature has studied both scenarios with completely known and completely unknown perturbation sets, we propose an in-between setting of learning with respect to a class of perturbation sets. We show that in this setting we can improve on previous results with completely unknown perturbation sets, while still addressing the concerns of not having perfect knowledge of these sets in real life. In particular, we give the first positive results for the learnability of infinite Littlestone classes when having access to a perfect-attack oracle. We also consider a setting of learning with abstention, where predictions are considered robustness violations, only when the wrong prediction is made within the perturbation set. We show there are classes for which perturbation-set unaware learning without query access is possible, but abstention is required.

paragraphs: Robust learning often depends on knowing which changes an adversary is allowed to make to an input. In practice, a learner may have some information about these changes without knowing their exact boundaries. This paper studies that middle position by giving the learner a class of possible perturbation sets.

The authors show that this partial knowledge can improve learnability results compared with a setting where perturbation sets are completely unknown. In particular, they obtain positive results for infinite Littlestone classes when a perfect-attack oracle is available. The oracle assumption is part of the result: the learner has access to an idealized mechanism for identifying attacks.

The paper also studies learners that can abstain from predicting. In this formulation, a robustness violation occurs when the learner makes an incorrect prediction within the perturbation set. The authors identify classes where learning without knowledge of that set and without query access is possible, but requires abstention. The findings show that both partial information about attacks and the option to withhold a prediction can change what robust learning can achieve.
summary.tldr: Partial knowledge of possible adversarial perturbations and the option to abstain enable robust learnability results under the paper's stated information assumptions.

title: Adversarially Robust Learning with Uncertain Perturbation Sets

abstract: Carefully designed activation functions can improve the performance of neural networks in many machine learning tasks. However, it is difficult for humans to construct optimal activation functions, and current activation function search algorithms are prohibitively expensive. This paper aims to improve the state of the art through three steps: First, the benchmark datasets Act-Bench-CNN, Act-Bench-ResNet, and Act-Bench-ViT were created by training convolutional, residual, and vision transformer architectures from scratch with 2,913 systematically generated activation functions. Second, a characterization of the benchmark space was developed, leading to a new surrogate-based method for optimization. More specifically, the spectrum of the Fisher information matrix associated with the model's predictive distribution at initialization and the activation function's output distribution were found to be highly predictive of performance. Third, the surrogate was used to discover improved activation functions in several real-world tasks, with a surprising finding: a sigmoidal design that outperformed all other activation functions was discovered, challenging the status quo of always using rectifier nonlinearities in deep learning. Each of these steps is a contribution in its own right; together they serve as a practical and theoretical foundation for further research on activation function optimization.

paragraphs: Activation functions affect how neural networks learn, but designing them by hand is difficult and searching through candidates can be expensive. This paper develops a way to predict which functions are promising, supported by benchmarks built from training convolutional networks, residual networks, and vision transformers with 2,913 systematically generated activation functions.

Analysis of these benchmarks identifies two useful predictors of performance: the spectrum of the Fisher information matrix associated with the network’s predictions at initialization, and the activation function’s output distribution. The authors use these signals to construct a surrogate model. This model guides optimization by estimating the promise of activation choices rather than relying only on full training evaluations.

Applied to several real-world tasks, the approach discovers improved activation functions, including a sigmoidal design that outperforms the other functions considered. That result challenges the assumption that rectifier-style nonlinearities should always be preferred. The contribution combines reusable benchmark data, evidence about predictive characteristics, and a search method for finding better activations in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A surrogate model uses initialization-time signals to guide activation-function search and discovers strong alternatives to rectifier nonlinearities.

title: Efficient Activation Function Optimization through Surrogate Modeling

abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a prominent non-invasive neuroimaging technique providing insights into brain function. Unfortunately, EEG data exhibit a high degree of noise and variability across subjects hampering generalizable signal extraction. Therefore, a key aim in EEG analysis is to extract the underlying neural activation (content) as well as to account for the individual subject variability (style). We hypothesize that the ability to convert EEG signals between tasks and subjects requires the extraction of latent representations accounting for content and style. Inspired by recent advancements in voice conversion technologies, we propose a novel contrastive split-latent permutation autoencoder (CSLP-AE) framework that directly optimizes for EEG conversion. Importantly, the latent representations are guided using contrastive learning to promote the latent splits to explicitly represent subject (style) and task (content). We contrast CSLP-AE to conventional supervised, unsupervised (AE), and self-supervised (contrastive learning) training and find that the proposed approach provides favorable generalizable characterizations of subject and task. Importantly, the procedure also enables zero-shot conversion between unseen subjects. While the present work only considers conversion of EEG, the proposed CSLP-AE provides a general framework for signal conversion and extraction of content (task activation) and style (subject variability) components of general interest for the modeling and analysis of biological signals.

paragraphs: EEG signals contain both activity associated with a task and differences associated with the person being measured. Noise and variation across people make these components difficult to separate. This paper asks whether explicitly representing task content and subject style can support signal conversion and representations that generalize across subjects.

The authors propose CSLP-AE, an autoencoder framework that directly trains for EEG conversion. Its latent representation is split into components, and contrastive learning guides those components to represent subject identity and task information separately. The design draws inspiration from voice conversion, where separating what is expressed from who expresses it is also useful.

Compared with conventional supervised, autoencoder, and contrastive training approaches, CSLP-AE produces favorable generalizable characterizations of subjects and tasks. It also enables zero-shot conversion between previously unseen subjects. The reported experiments concern EEG specifically. The authors present the architecture as a broader framework for separating content and style in biological signals, but its demonstrated conversion results remain within the EEG setting studied.
summary.tldr: CSLP-AE separates task and subject information in EEG representations, enabling signal conversion between unseen subjects.

title: CSLP-AE: A Contrastive Split-Latent Permutation Autoencoder Framework for Zero-Shot Electroencephalography Signal Conversion

abstract: Many data symmetries can be described in terms of group equivariance and the most common way of encoding group equivariances in neural networks is by building linear layers that are group equivariant.In this work we investigate whether equivariance of a network implies that all layers are equivariant.On the theoretical side we find cases where equivariance implies layerwise equivariance, but alsodemonstrate that this is not the case generally.Nevertheless, we conjecture that CNNs that are trained to be equivariant will exhibit layerwise equivariance and explain how this conjecture is a weaker version of the recent permutation conjecture by Entezari et al.\ [2022].We perform quantitative experiments with VGG-nets on CIFAR10 and qualitative experiments with ResNets on ImageNet to illustrate and support our theoretical findings. These experiments are not only of interest for understanding how group equivariance is encoded in ReLU-networks, but they also give a new perspective on Entezari et al.'s permutation conjecture as we find that itis typically easier to merge a network with a group-transformed version of itself than merging two different networks.

paragraphs: A network is equivariant when transforming its input produces a corresponding transformation of its output. A common way to achieve this is to make individual layers equivariant. This paper asks whether the reverse implication holds: if an entire ReLU network respects a symmetry, must that symmetry also be respected separately by all its layers?

The theoretical answer is conditional. The authors identify cases where whole-network equivariance does imply layerwise equivariance, but also demonstrate that this is false in general. They nevertheless conjecture that convolutional networks trained to be equivariant will exhibit equivariance layer by layer. They relate this conjecture to a weaker version of an existing permutation conjecture about neural networks.

Quantitative experiments with VGG networks on CIFAR10 and qualitative experiments with ResNets on ImageNet illustrate and support the theoretical analysis. The authors also find that merging a network with a group-transformed version of itself is typically easier than merging two different networks. This provides another perspective on symmetry and network merging while leaving the proposed training-related statement as a conjecture.
summary.tldr: Whole-network equivariance does not generally imply equivariant layers, though theory and experiments motivate a conjecture about trained convolutional networks.

title: Investigating how ReLU-networks encode symmetries

abstract: We identify incremental learning dynamics in transformers, where the difference between trained and initial weights progressively increases in rank. We rigorously prove this occurs under the simplifying assumptions of diagonal weight matrices and small initialization. Our experiments support the theory and also show that phenomenon can occur in practice without the simplifying assumptions.
