paragraphs: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong results in areas such as motor control and tasks involving perceptual or stochastic inputs. The authors argue that comparable progress in algorithmic and logical reasoning needs dedicated benchmarks. PUZZLES supplies such a test environment using Simon Tatham’s Portable Puzzle Collection as its foundation.

The benchmark contains 40 different logic puzzles, with adjustable sizes and varying complexity. Those dimensions make it possible to examine more than whether an agent succeeds on one fixed problem. They provide ways to characterize an agent’s strengths and study its generalization as the reasoning problems change in size or difficulty.

The paper evaluates several reinforcement learning algorithms and supplies baseline comparisons for subsequent work. Its central contribution is therefore an evaluation resource and an initial account of agent performance across diverse reasoning tasks. The environment and associated software are available, allowing further methods to be studied using the same benchmark. The reported evaluations establish a basis for research rather than claiming that reinforcement learning has already solved the collection’s reasoning challenges.
summary.tldr: PUZZLES provides 40 adjustable logic puzzles and baseline evaluations for studying reasoning and generalization in reinforcement learning.

title: PUZZLES: A Benchmark for Neural Algorithmic Reasoning

abstract: We consider estimation of a linear functional of the treatment effect from adaptively collected data. This problem finds a variety of applications including off-policy evaluation in contextual bandits, and estimation of the average treatment effect in causal inference. While a certain class of augmented inverse propensity weighting (AIPW) estimators enjoys desirable asymptotic properties including the semi-parametric efficiency, much less is known about their non-asymptotic theory with adaptively collected data. To fill in the gap, we first present generic upper bounds on the mean-squared error of the class of AIPW estimators that crucially depends on a sequentially weighted error between the treatment effect and its estimates. Motivated by this, we propose a general reduction scheme that allows one to produce a sequence of estimates for the treatment effect via online learning to minimize the sequentially weighted estimation error. To illustrate this, we provide three concrete instantiations in (1) the tabular case; (2) the case of linear function approximation; and (3) the case of general function approximation for the outcome model. We then provide a local minimax lower bound to show the instance-dependent optimality of the AIPW estimator using no-regret online learning algorithms.

paragraphs: When data collection adapts to previous observations, evaluating a policy or estimating a treatment effect requires accounting for that changing process. This paper studies linear functionals of treatment effects, covering applications such as contextual-bandit off-policy evaluation and average treatment-effect estimation. It focuses on finite-sample understanding of augmented inverse propensity weighting estimators.

The authors derive general upper bounds on mean-squared error that depend crucially on a sequentially weighted error in treatment-effect estimates. This identifies a specific estimation target for improvement. They then reduce the construction of those estimates to online learning, using a sequence of predictions designed to minimize the weighted error appearing in the bound.

The framework is instantiated for tabular settings, linear function approximation, and general outcome-model function approximation. A local minimax lower bound establishes instance-dependent optimality for the AIPW estimator when paired with no-regret online learning algorithms. The result connects online prediction quality to statistical estimation accuracy, providing finite-sample theory for data collected through an adaptive process.
summary.tldr: Online learning supplies treatment-effect estimates that give adaptively collected-data estimators finite-sample guarantees and instance-dependent optimality.

title: Off-policy estimation with adaptively collected data: the power of online learning

abstract: This paper presents Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection (IVLOD), a novel learning task designed to incrementally adapt pre-trained Vision-Language Object Detection Models (VLODMs) to various specialized domains, while simultaneously preserving their zero-shot generalization capabilities for the generalized domain. To address this new challenge, we present the Zero-interference Reparameterizable Adaptation (ZiRa), a novel method that introduces Zero-interference Loss and reparameterization techniques to tackle IVLOD without incurring a significant increase in memory usage. Comprehensive experiments on COCO and ODinW-13 datasets demonstrate that ZiRa effectively safeguards the zero-shot generalization ability of VLODMs while continuously adapting to new tasks. Specifically, after training on ODinW-13 datasets, ZiRa exhibits superior performance compared to CL-DETR and iDETR, boosting zero-shot generalizability by substantial $\textbf{13.91}$ and $\textbf{8.74}$ AP, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/JarintotionDin/ZiRaGroundingDINO.

paragraphs: Pretrained vision-language object detectors can generalize to categories or settings without task-specific training. Adapting them sequentially to specialized domains introduces a second objective: preserving that broad zero-shot ability while learning new tasks. This paper formalizes the combined challenge as Incremental Vision-Language Object Detection.

The proposed method, ZiRa, combines a Zero-interference Loss with reparameterization techniques. It is designed to support incremental adaptation without a significant increase in memory usage. The goal brings specialized-domain learning and general-domain retention into the same adaptation procedure, so progress on new tasks is evaluated alongside continued zero-shot capability.

Experiments on COCO and ODinW-13 show that ZiRa preserves zero-shot generalization while adapting continuously to new tasks. After training on ODinW-13, its zero-shot performance exceeds CL-DETR by 13.91 AP and iDETR by 8.74 AP. These findings demonstrate the method's effectiveness on the proposed combined objective in the tested settings, highlighting the value of explicitly protecting generalization during sequential specialization.
summary.tldr: ZiRa adapts vision-language object detectors to successive specialized tasks while preserving zero-shot generalization with little additional memory.

title: Zero-shot Generalizable Incremental Learning for Vision-Language Object Detection

abstract: Face recognition is essential for identity authentication, but the rich visual clues in facial images pose significant privacy risks, highlighting the critical importance of privacy-preserving solutions. For instance, numerous studies have shown that generative models are capable of effectively performing reconstruction attacks that result in the restoration of original visual clues. To mitigate this threat, we introduce FracFace, a fractal-based privacy-preserving face recognition framework. This approach effectively weakens the visual clues that can be exploited by reconstruction attacks by disrupting the spatial structure in frequency domain features, while retaining the vital visual clues required for identity recognition. To achieve this, we craft a Frequency Channels Refining module that reduces sparsity in the frequency domain. It suppresses visual clues that could be exploited by reconstruction attacks, while preserving features indispensable for recognition, thus making these attacks more challenging. More significantly, we design a Frequency Fractal Mapping module that obfuscates deep representations by remapping refined frequency channels into a fractal-based privacy structure. By leveraging the self-similarity of fractals, this module preserves identity relevant features while enhancing defense capabilities, thereby improving the overall robustness of the protection scheme. Experiments conducted on multiple public face recognition benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed FracFace significantly reduces the visual recoverability of facial features, while maintaining high recognition accuracy, as well as the superiorities over state-of-the-art privacy protection approaches.

paragraphs: Face recognition needs information that distinguishes identities, but facial representations can also retain visual clues that help reconstruct a person's appearance. FracFace aims to weaken those reconstruction clues while preserving the information needed for recognition. Its approach modifies frequency-domain features and their spatial organization to make recovering facial appearance more difficult.

The framework first applies a Frequency Channels Refining module, which reduces sparsity in frequency-domain features. This stage suppresses reconstruction-relevant clues while preserving features useful for recognizing identity. A Frequency Fractal Mapping module then remaps the refined channels into a fractal-based structure. The authors use the self-similarity of fractals to retain identity-related information while further obscuring the deep representation.

Experiments on multiple public face recognition benchmarks show substantially reduced visual recoverability alongside high recognition accuracy. The authors also report advantages over state-of-the-art privacy protection approaches. The result supports a practical separation between recognizing someone and recovering their appearance: the representation remains useful for the former while making the tested reconstruction attacks more challenging.
summary.tldr: FracFace refines and fractally remaps frequency features to reduce facial reconstruction while maintaining high recognition accuracy on evaluated benchmarks.

title: FracFace: Breaking the Visual Clues—Fractal-Based Privacy-Preserving Face Recognition

abstract: The non-Euclidean geometry inherent in graph structures fundamentally impedes cross-graph knowledge transfer. Drawing inspiration from texture transfer in computer vision, we pioneer topological primitives as transferable semantic units for graph structural knowledge. To address three critical barriers - the absence of specialized benchmarks, aligned semantic representations, and systematic transfer methodologies - we present G²SN-Transfer, a unified framework comprising: (i) TopoGraph-Mapping that transforms non-Euclidean graphs into transferable sequences via topological primitive distribution dictionaries; (ii) G²SN, a dual-stream architecture learning text-topology aligned representations through contrastive alignment; and (iii) AdaCross-Transfer, a data-adaptive knowledge transfer mechanism leveraging cross-attention for both full-parameter and parameter-frozen scenarios. Particularly, G²SN is a dual-stream sequence network driven by ordinary differential equations, and our theoretical analysis establishes the convergence guarantee of G²SN. We construct STA-18, the first large-scale benchmark with aligned topological primitive-text pairs across 18 diverse graph datasets. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that G²SN achieves state-of-the-art performance on four structural learning tasks (average 3.2\% F1-score improvement), while our transfer method yields consistent enhancements across 13 downstream tasks (5.2\% average gains) including 10 large-scale graph datasets. The datasets and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/UGSKT-C10E/.

It proposes topological primitives as transferable units of structural meaning. The resulting G²SN-Transfer framework addresses representation, transfer, and evaluation together, creating a way to relate graph structure to aligned textual information.

G²SN then learns aligned text and topology representations through a dual-stream architecture and contrastive alignment. These results support the proposed structural units as useful carriers of knowledge across the evaluated graphs and tasks.
summary.tldr: G²SN-Transfer represents graphs through topological primitives aligned with text to improve structural learning and cross-graph transfer.

title: One for All: Universal Topological Primitive Transfer for Graph Structure Learning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential in audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR), but their high computational demands and sensitivity to token granularity limit their practicality in resource-constrained settings. Token compression methods can reduce inference cost, but they require fixing a compression rate in advance and produce a single fixed-length output, offering no flexibility to balance information density and efficiency at inference time. Matryoshka representation learning (MRL) addresses this by enabling a single model to operate across multiple token granularities, allowing compression rates to be adjusted dynamically. However, current MRL-based methods treat each scale independently during training, limiting cross-scale generalization, robustness at high compression, and interpretability. To overcome these limitations, we propose MoME (Mixture of Matryoshka Experts), a novel framework that integrates sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into MRL-based LLMs for AVSR. MoME augments a frozen LLM with top-k routed and shared experts, allowing dynamic capacity allocation across scales and modalities. A shared router promotes consistent expert activation across granularities, enabling compressed sequences to benefit from representations learned at lower compression. Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 demonstrate that MoME achieves state-of-the-art performance across AVSR, ASR, and VSR tasks, while requiring significantly fewer parameters and maintaining robustness under noise. MoME unifies the adaptability of MRL with the efficiency of MoE, offering a scalable and interpretable solution for resource-aware speech recognition.

paragraphs: Audio-visual speech recognition must balance the information retained in input tokens against the cost of processing them. Matryoshka representation learning lets one model operate at different compression levels, allowing that balance to change during inference. However, training each level independently limits knowledge sharing and can weaken performance when compression is high.

MoME adds a sparse mixture of experts to a frozen language model. A router selects a limited set of experts, alongside shared experts, to allocate capacity across modalities and compression levels. The shared router encourages consistent expert use across granularities, so heavily compressed inputs can benefit from representations learned when more information was retained.

Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 report leading performance for combined audio-visual recognition, audio-only recognition, and visual-only recognition. The method also uses significantly fewer parameters and remains robust under noise. These findings support combining adjustable representations with selective expert computation: the model can vary input detail while sharing useful learning across scales, rather than treating each compression level as an isolated training problem.
summary.tldr: MoME shares expert knowledge across token compression levels to improve efficient, noise-robust audio-visual speech recognition.

title: MoME: Mixture of Matryoshka Experts for Audio-Visual Speech Recognition

abstract: Short videos are an effective tool for promoting contents and improving knowledge accessibility. While existing extractive video summarization methods struggle to produce a coherent narrative, existing abstractive methods cannot `quote' from the input videos, i.e., inserting short video clips in their outputs. In this work, we explore novel video editing models for generating shorts that feature a coherent narrative with embedded video insertions extracted from a long input video. We propose a novel retrieval-embedded generation framework that allows a large language model to quote multimodal resources while maintaining a coherent narrative. Our proposed REGen system first generates the output story script with quote placeholders using a finetuned large language model, and then uses a novel retrieval model to replace the quote placeholders by selecting a video clip that best supports the narrative from a pool of candidate quotable video clips. We examine the proposed method on the task of documentary teaser generation, where short interview insertions are commonly used to support the narrative of a documentary. Our objective evaluations show that the proposed method can effectively insert short video clips while maintaining a coherent narrative. In a subjective survey, we show that our proposed method outperforms existing abstractive and extractive approaches in terms of coherence, alignment, and realism in teaser generation.

While existing extractive video summarization methods struggle to produce a coherent narrative, existing abstractive methods cannot `quote' from the input videos, i.e., inserting short video clips in their outputs. In this work, we explore novel video editing models for generating shorts that feature a coherent narrative with embedded video insertions extracted from a long input video. We propose a novel retrieval-embedded generation framework that allows a large language model to quote multimodal resources while maintaining a coherent narrative. Our proposed REGen system first generates the output story script with quote placeholders using a finetuned large language model, and then uses a novel retrieval model to replace the quote placeholders by selecting a video clip that best supports the narrative from a pool of candidate quotable video clips. We examine the proposed method on the task of documentary teaser generation, where short interview insertions are commonly used to support the narrative of a documentary. Our objective evaluations show that the proposed method can effectively insert short video clips while maintaining a coherent narrative. In a subjective survey, we show that our proposed method outperforms existing abstractive and extractive approaches in terms of coherence, alignment, and realism in teaser generation.

paragraphs: Creating a short video from a long one involves both selecting source material and building a coherent narrative. The paper identifies complementary weaknesses in existing approaches: extractive summaries can struggle with storytelling, while abstractive methods cannot insert quoted clips from the original video. REGen combines generated narration with retrieved video insertions.

A fine-tuned language model first writes a story script containing placeholders for quotes. A retrieval model then fills those placeholders by selecting clips from a pool of candidate excerpts, choosing material that supports the surrounding narrative. This separates the task of constructing the story from finding the source-video evidence that belongs at particular points in it.

The authors evaluate the system on documentary teaser generation, where interview excerpts commonly support the narration. Objective evaluations show that REGen can insert short clips while maintaining narrative coherence. In a subjective survey, it outperforms existing extractive and abstractive approaches on coherence, alignment, and realism. The findings support embedding retrieval into generation to produce shorts that combine an organized story with relevant material quoted from the input.
summary.tldr: REGen writes short-video narratives with quote placeholders and retrieves source clips to fill them, improving documentary teaser quality in reported evaluations.

title: REGen: Multimodal Retrieval-Embedded Generation for Long-to-Short Video Editing

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) show promise for embodied planning tasks but struggle with complex scenarios involving unfamiliar environments and multi-step goals. Current approaches rely on environment-agnostic imitation learning that disconnects instructions from environmental contexts, causing models to struggle with context-sensitive instructions and rely on supplementary cues rather than visual reasoning during long-horizon interactions. In this work, we propose World-Aware Planning Narrative Enhancement (WAP), a framework that infuses LVLMs with comprehensive environmental understanding through four cognitive capabilities (visual appearance modeling, spatial reasoning, functional abstraction, and syntactic grounding) while developing and evaluating models using only raw visual observations through curriculum learning. Evaluations on the EB-ALFRED benchmark demonstrate substantial improvements, with Qwen2.5-VL achieving a 60.7 absolute improvement in task success rates—particularly in commonsense reasoning (+60.0) and long-horizon planning (+70.0). Notably, our enhanced open-source models outperform proprietary systems like GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet by a large margin.

These findings support grounding planning training more closely in environmental understanding.
summary.tldr: WAP strengthens vision-language planning through curriculum-based environmental understanding, producing substantial gains on the EB-ALFRED benchmark.

title: World-aware Planning Narratives Enhance Large Vision-Language Model Planner

abstract: Many critical applications, from autonomous scientific discovery to personalized medicine, demand systems that can both strategically acquire the most informative data and instantaneously perform inference based upon it. While amortized methods for Bayesian inference and experimental design offer part of the solution, neither approach is optimal in the most general and challenging task, where new data needs to be collected for instant inference. To tackle this issue, we introduce the Amortized Active Learning and Inference Engine (ALINE), a unified framework for amortized Bayesian inference and active data acquisition. ALINE leverages a transformer architecture trained via reinforcement learning with a reward based on self-estimated information gain provided by its own integrated inference component. This allows it to strategically query informative data points while simultaneously refining its predictions. Moreover, ALINE can selectively direct its querying strategy towards specific subsets of model parameters or designated predictive tasks, optimizing for posterior estimation, data prediction, or a mixture thereof. Empirical results on regression-based active learning, classical Bayesian experimental design benchmarks, and a psychometric model with selectively targeted parameters demonstrate that ALINE delivers both instant and accurate inference along with efficient selection of informative points.

paragraphs: ALINE tackles a paired problem: deciding what data to collect next and quickly updating an inference after receiving it. These decisions are closely connected because the usefulness of a measurement depends on what the system is trying to learn. The paper combines Bayesian inference and active data acquisition in one trained framework.

Its transformer is trained with reinforcement learning. The reward comes from information gain estimated by its own inference component, so the mechanism that interprets observations also helps guide future queries. This connects data selection directly to the system’s evolving predictions. ALINE can also focus acquisition on selected model parameters or particular prediction tasks, rather than treating every unknown as equally important.

The authors evaluate the framework on regression active learning, Bayesian experimental design benchmarks, and a psychometric model with targeted parameters. They report fast, accurate inference alongside efficient selection of informative observations. These findings support the value of jointly learning how to ask questions and how to use their answers, including when the learning objective concerns only part of a model.
summary.tldr: ALINE jointly learns Bayesian inference and informative data selection, with the ability to target specific parameters or prediction tasks.

title: ALINE: Joint Amortization for Bayesian Inference and Active Data Acquisition

abstract: Generative data augmentation (GDA) leverages generative models to enrich training sets with entirely new samples drawn from the modeled data distribution to achieve performance gains. However, the usage of the mighty contemporary diffusion models in GDA remains impractical: *i)* their thousand-step sampling loop inflates wall-time and energy cost per image augmentation; and *ii)* the divergence between synthetic and real distributions is unknown--classifiers trained on synthetic receive biased gradients. We propose DAR-GDA, a three-stage augmentation pipeline that unites model **D**istillation, **A**dversarial alignment, and importance **R**eweighting that makes diffusion-quality augmentation both fast and optimized for improving downstream learning outcomes. In particular, a teacher diffusion model is compressed into a one-step student via score distillation, slashing the time per-image cost by $>100\times$ while preserving FID. During this distillation (D), the student model additionally undergoes adversarial alignment (A) by receiving direct training signals against real images, supplementing the teacher's guidance to better match the true data distribution. The discriminator from this adversarial process inherently learns to assess the synthetic-to-real data gap. Its calibrated probabilistic outputs are then employed in reweighting (R) by importance weights that quantify the distributional gap and adjust the classification loss when training downstream models; we show that reweighting yields an unbiased stochastic estimator of the real-data risk, fostering training dynamics akin to those of genuine samples. Experiments validate DAR-GDA's synergistic design through progressive accuracy gains with each D-A-R stage. Our approach not only surpasses conventional non-foundation-model GDA baselines but also remarkably matches or exceeds the GDA performance of large, web-pretrained text-to-image models, despite using solely in-domain data. DAR-GDA thus offers diffusion-fidelity GDA samples efficiently, while correcting synthetic-to-real bias to benefit downstream tasks.

title: Generative Data Augmentation via Diffusion Distillation, Adversarial Alignment, and Importance Reweighting

abstract: This paper addresses the scarcity of low-cost but high-dexterity platforms for collecting real-world multi-fingered robot manipulation data towards generalist robot autonomy. To achieve it, we propose the RAPID Hand, a co-optimized hardware and software platform where the compact 20-DoF hand, robust whole-hand perception, and high-DoF teleoperation interface are jointly designed. Specifically, RAPID Hand adopts a compact and practical hand ontology and a hardware-level perception framework that stably integrates wrist-mounted vision, fingertip tactile sensing, and proprioception with sub-7 ms latency and spatial alignment. Collecting high-quality demonstrations on high-DoF hands is challenging, as existing teleoperation methods struggle with precision and stability on complex multi-fingered systems. We address this by co-optimizing hand design, perception integration, and teleoperation interface through a universal actuation scheme, custom perception electronics, and two retargeting constraints. We evaluate the platform’s hardware, perception, and teleoperation interface. Training a diffusion policy on collected data shows superior performance over prior works, validating the system’s capability for reliable, high-quality data collection. The platform is constructed from low-cost and off-the-shelf components and will be made public to ensure reproducibility and ease of adoption.

The policy outperforms prior work in their evaluation, supporting the platform's ability to collect useful, high-quality data. Built from inexpensive, off-the-shelf components, RAPID Hand is intended for public release to improve reproducibility and adoption. Its contribution centers on making dexterous demonstration collection more accessible as an integrated system.
summary.tldr: RAPID Hand jointly designs an affordable dexterous hand, integrated sensing, and teleoperation for reliable robot-demonstration collection.

title: RAPID Hand: Robust, Affordable, Perception-Integrated, Dexterous Manipulation Platform for Embodied Intelligence

abstract: In this paper, we examine the impact and significance of bias terms in Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). While bias terms are known to enhance nonlinear capacity by shifting activations in typical neural networks, we discover their functionality differs markedly in neural representation networks. Our analysis reveals that INR performance neither scales with increased number of bias terms nor shows substantial improvement through bias term gradient propagation. We demonstrate that bias terms in INRs primarily serve to eliminate \textit{spatial aliasing} caused by symmetry from both coordinates and activation functions, with input-layer bias terms yielding the most significant benefits. These findings challenge the conventional practice of implementing full-bias INR architecture. We propose using freezing bias terms exclusively in input layers, which consistently outperforms fully biased networks in signal fitting tasks. Furthermore, we introduce Feature-Biased INRs~(Feat-Bias), which initialize input-layer bias with high-level features extracted from pre-trained models. This feature-biasing approach effectively addresses the limited performance in INR post-processing tasks due to neural parameter uninterpretability, achieving superior accuracy while reducing parameter count and improving reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: This paper examines what bias terms actually contribute to implicit neural representations. Although biases commonly increase a network's flexibility by shifting activations, the authors find a different dominant role here. Performance does not scale with the number of biases, and propagating gradients through those terms provides little improvement.

Their analysis shows that biases primarily remove spatial aliasing arising from symmetries in coordinates and activation functions. Input-layer biases provide the largest benefit. Based on this finding, the authors propose keeping biases only in the input layer and freezing them during training. This configuration consistently outperforms fully biased networks in the reported signal-fitting tasks.

The paper then introduces Feature-Biased INRs, which initialize input-layer biases using high-level features from pretrained models. This gives the biases a feature-based role and addresses difficulties in post-processing caused by uninterpretable neural parameters. The authors report higher accuracy, fewer parameters, and better reconstruction quality. Together, the results motivate a more targeted use of biases in these representation networks.
summary.tldr: Biases in implicit neural representations mainly counter spatial aliasing, and frozen or feature-initialized input biases improve the reported fitting and reconstruction results.

title: Understanding Bias Terms in Neural Representations

abstract: Despite remarkable progress in driving world models, their potential for autonomous systems remains largely untapped: the world models are mostly learned for world simulation and decoupled from trajectory planning. While recent efforts aim to unify world modeling and planning in a single framework, the synergistic facilitation mechanism of world modeling for planning still requires further exploration. In this work, we introduce a new driving paradigm named Policy World Model (PWM), which not only integrates world modeling and trajectory planning within a unified architecture, but is also able to benefit planning using the learned world knowledge through the proposed action-free future state forecasting scheme. Through collaborative state-action prediction, PWM can mimic the human-like anticipatory perception, yielding more reliable planning performance. To facilitate the efficiency of video forecasting, we further introduce a parallel token generation mechanism, equipped with a context-guided tokenizer and an adaptive dynamic focal loss. Despite utilizing only front camera input, our method matches or exceeds state-of-the-art approaches that rely on multi-view and multi-modal inputs. Code will be released at https://github.com/6550Zhao/Policy-World-Model.

paragraphs: Policy World Model connects driving scene prediction with trajectory planning. Its goal is to make learned knowledge about how the world evolves directly useful for planning.

PWM places world modeling and planning in one architecture and introduces action-free future-state forecasting. Through collaborative prediction of states and actions, the framework uses anticipation of future conditions to support planning. This result supports their proposed connection between forecasting and planning in the evaluated setting. The contribution combines an architectural integration with a specific forecasting mechanism intended to help world knowledge improve trajectory decisions, alongside changes that support efficient video prediction.
summary.tldr: Policy World Model integrates future-state forecasting and driving trajectory planning, reporting strong performance using only front-camera input.

title: From Forecasting to Planning: Policy World Model for Collaborative State-Action Prediction

abstract: We study the greedy (exploitation-only) algorithm in bandit problems with a known reward structure. We allow arbitrary finite reward structures, while prior work focused on a few specific ones. We fully characterize when the greedy algorithm asymptotically succeeds or fails, in the sense of sublinear vs. linear regret as a function of time. Our characterization identifies a partial identifiability property of the problem instance as the necessary and sufficient condition for the asymptotic success. Notably, once this property holds, the problem becomes easy—\emph{any} algorithm will succeed (in the same sense as above), provided it satisfies a mild non-degeneracy condition. Our characterization extends to contextual bandits and interactive decision-making with arbitrary feedback. Examples demonstrating broad applicability and extensions to infinite reward structures are provided.

paragraphs: A greedy bandit algorithm repeatedly chooses the action that currently looks best, without deliberately exploring alternatives. Whether that works depends on what the observed rewards reveal about the available choices. This paper studies the question for arbitrary finite, known reward structures, extending beyond the specific structures considered in earlier work.

The main result identifies partial identifiability as a necessary and sufficient condition for the greedy algorithm's asymptotic success. Success means sublinear regret: accumulated loss relative to optimal choices grows more slowly than time. Failure means linear regret. The characterization therefore gives a precise boundary between instances where exploitation alone eventually succeeds and instances where it does not.

A stronger consequence is that, when the property holds, any algorithm satisfying a mild non-degeneracy condition achieves success in the same asymptotic sense. The favorable structure of the instance is thus central to the guarantee. The authors extend their characterization to contextual bandits and interactive decision-making with arbitrary feedback, and provide examples and extensions involving infinite reward structures.
summary.tldr: Partial identifiability exactly characterizes when greedy learning achieves sublinear rather than linear regret in finite structured bandits.

title: Greedy Algorithms for Structured Bandits: A Sharp Characterization of Asymptotic Success / Failure

abstract: Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has become a powerful solution to extract rich representations from unlabeled data. Yet, SSL research is mostly focused on clean, curated and high-quality datasets. As a result, applying SSL on noisy data remains a challenge, despite being crucial to applications such as astrophysics, medical imaging, geophysics or finance. In this work, we present a fully self-supervised framework that enables noise-robust representation learning without requiring a denoiser at inference or downstream fine-tuning. Our method first trains an SSL denoiser on noisy data, then uses it to construct a denoised-to-noisy data curriculum (i.e., training first on denoised, then noisy samples) for pretraining a SSL backbone (e.g., DINOv2), combined with a teacher-guided regularization that anchors noisy embeddings to their denoised counterparts. This process encourages the model to internalize noise robustness. Notably, the denoiser can be discarded after pretraining, simplifying deployment. On ImageNet-1k with ViT-B under extreme Gaussian noise ($\sigma=255$, SNR = 0.72 dB), our method improves linear probing accuracy by 4.8\% over DINOv2, demonstrating that denoiser-free robustness can emerge from noise-aware pretraining. The code is available at https://github.com/wenquanlu/noisy_dinov2.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning extracts representations without labels, but much of its development assumes clean data. This paper targets representation learning under substantial noise, aiming to make the learned model robust enough that deployment requires neither a separate denoiser nor downstream fine-tuning.

The method does use a denoiser during pretraining. It first learns that denoiser from noisy data through self-supervision, then uses its outputs to create a curriculum that starts with denoised examples and progresses toward noisy ones. Teacher-guided regularization additionally encourages embeddings of noisy inputs to remain anchored to embeddings of their denoised counterparts. These two mechanisms encourage the backbone to absorb noise robustness into its representations.

After pretraining, the denoiser can be discarded, simplifying inference. On ImageNet-1k with a ViT-B backbone under extreme Gaussian noise, specified as sigma 255 and an SNR of 0.72 dB, the method reports a 4.8% improvement in linear probing accuracy over DINOv2. The result demonstrates denoiser-free inference robustness emerging from noise-aware pretraining in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: A denoised-to-noisy training curriculum helps self-supervised models internalize noise robustness so the denoiser can be discarded after pretraining.

title: Ditch the Denoiser: Emergence of Noise Robustness in Self-Supervised Learning from Data Curriculum

abstract: Fine-tuning vision language models (VLMs) has achieved remarkable performance across various downstream tasks; yet, it requires access to model gradients through backpropagation (BP), making them unsuitable for memory-constrained, inference-only edge devices. To address this limitation, previous work has explored various BP-free fine-tuning methods. However, these approaches often rely on high-variance evolutionary strategies (ES) or zeroth-order (ZO) optimization, and often fail to achieve satisfactory performance. In this paper, we propose a hybrid Sharpness-aware Zeroth-order optimization (SharpZO) approach, specifically designed to enhance the performance of ZO VLM fine-tuning via a sharpness-aware warm-up training. SharpZO features a two-stage optimization process: a sharpness-aware ES stage that globally explores and smooths the loss landscape to construct a strong initialization, followed by a fine-grained local search via sparse ZO optimization. The entire optimization relies solely on forward passes. Detailed theoretical analysis and extensive experiments on CLIP models demonstrate that SharpZO significantly improves accuracy and convergence speed, achieving up to 7\% average gain over state-of-the-art forward-only methods.

paragraphs: Adapting vision-language models usually requires backpropagation and access to gradients, which creates difficulties on memory-constrained devices designed for inference. Forward-only optimization avoids that requirement, but existing evolutionary and zeroth-order approaches can suffer from high variance and weak performance. SharpZO improves this adaptation process through a two-stage optimization design.

The first stage uses a sharpness-aware evolutionary strategy to explore broadly and smooth the loss landscape, creating a stronger initialization. The second stage applies sparse zeroth-order optimization for more detailed local search. Both stages use only forward passes. The design connects a broad warm-up phase with a focused refinement phase so that local optimization starts from a more favorable position.

The paper combines theoretical analysis with experiments on CLIP models. It reports improvements in both accuracy and convergence speed, including up to a 7% average gain over state-of-the-art forward-only methods. These findings support the staged approach for vision-language prompt tuning when gradient-based adaptation is unavailable, with sharpness-aware initialization contributing to subsequent forward-only refinement.
summary.tldr: SharpZO combines sharpness-aware evolutionary warm-up with sparse local optimization to improve vision-language prompt tuning using only forward passes.

title: SharpZO: Hybrid Sharpness-Aware Vision Language Model Prompt Tuning via Forward-Only Passes

abstract: We introduce Self Forcing, a novel training paradigm for autoregressive video diffusion models. It addresses the longstanding issue of exposure bias, where models trained on ground-truth context must generate sequences conditioned on their own imperfect outputs during inference. Unlike prior methods that denoise future frames based on ground-truth context frames, Self Forcing conditions each frame's generation on previously self-generated outputs by performing autoregressive rollout with key-value (KV) caching during training. This strategy enables supervision through a holistic loss at the video level that directly evaluates the quality of the entire generated sequence, rather than relying solely on traditional frame-wise objectives. To ensure training efficiency, we employ a few-step diffusion model along with a stochastic gradient truncation strategy, effectively balancing computational cost and performance. We further introduce a rolling KV cache mechanism that enables efficient autoregressive video extrapolation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves real-time streaming video generation with sub-second latency on a single GPU, while matching or even surpassing the generation quality of significantly slower and non-causal diffusion models.

paragraphs: Autoregressive video generators produce new frames using earlier frames as context. Training on real preceding frames creates a mismatch: during deployment, the context consists of the model’s own imperfect outputs. Self Forcing addresses this exposure bias by having the model generate its own preceding frames during training, bringing the training situation closer to actual generation.

The method performs autoregressive rollouts with key-value caching and evaluates the resulting video through a loss applied to the sequence as a whole. This allows supervision to account for the quality of the generated video beyond individual frames. A few-step diffusion model and stochastic gradient truncation keep the training procedure computationally manageable.

The authors also introduce a rolling key-value cache for efficient video extrapolation. Their experiments demonstrate real-time streaming generation with latency below one second on a single GPU. Generation quality matches or exceeds that of significantly slower non-causal diffusion models in the reported comparisons. The findings support training directly on self-generated context as a way to combine efficient sequential generation with strong overall video quality.
summary.tldr: Self Forcing trains video diffusion models on their own generated context, enabling high-quality real-time streaming with sub-second latency in the reported experiments.

title: Self Forcing: Bridging the Train-Test Gap in Autoregressive Video Diffusion

abstract: \emphDiffusion network inference and \emphmeme tracking have been two key challenges in viral diffusion. This paper shows that these two tasks can be addressed simultaneously with a probabilistic model involving a mixture of mutually exciting point processes. A fast learning algorithms is developed based on mean-field variational inference with budgeted diffusion bandwidth. The model is demonstrated with applications to the diffusion of viral texts in (1) online social networks (e.g., Twitter) and (2) the blogosphere on the Web.
originalAbstract: \emphDiffusion network inference and \emphmeme tracking have been two key challenges in viral diffusion. This paper shows that these two tasks can be addressed simultaneously with a probabilistic model involving a mixture of mutually exciting point processes. A fast learning algorithms is developed based on mean-field variational inference with budgeted diffusion bandwidth. The model is demonstrated with applications to the diffusion of viral texts in (1) online social networks (e.g., Twitter) and (2) the blogosphere on the Web.

paragraphs: Studying viral text involves two connected questions: how information spreads through a network, and how to track the memes being spread. This paper addresses diffusion-network inference and meme tracking together. Combining them in one model provides a shared probabilistic account of the spread process and the content being followed.

The model uses a mixture of mutually exciting point processes. This represents diffusion through events whose occurrence can encourage other events, with the mixture supplying multiple components in the model. The authors develop a fast learning algorithm based on mean-field variational inference and a budgeted diffusion bandwidth, connecting the probabilistic formulation to a computational procedure.

The approach is demonstrated on viral text in online social networks, including Twitter, and in the web's blogosphere. These applications illustrate the joint treatment of network inference and meme tracking across two diffusion settings. The stated contribution is the ability to address both tasks simultaneously, together with an inference approach and application demonstrations.
summary.tldr: A mixture of mutually exciting point processes jointly models diffusion networks and meme tracking, with demonstrations on social-network and blog text.

title: Mixture of Mutually Exciting Processes for Viral Diffusion

abstract: We consider a similarity-score based paradigm to address scenarios where either the class labels are only partially revealed during learning, or the training and testing data are drawn from heterogeneous sources. The learning problem is subsequently formulated as optimization over a bilinear form of fixed rank. Our paradigm bears similarity to metric learning, where the major difference lies in its aim of learning a rectangular similarity matrix, instead of a proper metric. We tackle this problem in a Riemannian optimization framework. In particular, we consider its applications in pairwise-based action recognition, and cross-domain image-based object recognition. In both applications, the proposed algorithm produces competitive performance on respective benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning when class labels are only partly available or when training and test data come from different sources. It approaches these situations through similarity scores: the learned model expresses how strongly two representations correspond. This provides a framework for using relationships between examples in settings where ordinary labeled training is less straightforward.

The learning problem is formulated as optimizing a fixed-rank bilinear form. Its similarity matrix can be rectangular, which distinguishes the formulation from learning a proper metric. The authors solve the resulting problem using Riemannian optimization, a framework that handles the geometry associated with the constrained matrix representation.

They apply the method to action recognition based on pairs and to object recognition across image domains. The algorithm achieves competitive performance on the benchmark datasets for both applications. These results support fixed-rank similarity learning as a useful approach to partial labels and heterogeneous sources, with the rectangular representation serving as a central feature of the formulation.
summary.tldr: Riemannian optimization learns fixed-rank rectangular similarity matrices for recognition with partial labels or heterogeneous data sources.

title: Riemannian Similarity Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of detecting past activities as well as anticipating which activity will happen in the future and how. We start by modeling the rich spatio-temporal relations between human poses and objects (called affordances) using a conditional random field (CRF). However, because of the ambiguity in the temporal segmentation of the sub-activities that constitute an activity, in the past as well as in the future, multiple graph structures are possible. In this paper, we reason about these alternate possibilities by reasoning over multiple possible graph structures. We obtain them by approximating the graph with only additive features, which lends to efficient dynamic programming. Starting with this proposal graph structure, we then design moves to obtain several other likely graph structures. We then show that our approach improves the state-of-the-art significantly for detecting past activities as well as for anticipating future activities, on a dataset of 120 activity videos collected from four subjects.

paragraphs: Understanding an activity involves recognizing what happened and anticipating what will happen next and how. This paper addresses both tasks using RGB-D video. It begins with a conditional random field that models spatial and temporal relationships between human poses and objects, including the affordances involved in their interaction.

An activity contains smaller subactivities, but their temporal boundaries can be ambiguous. Different segmentations imply different graph structures, for both past observations and possible futures. The method explicitly reasons over several structures. It first approximates the graph using additive features, enabling efficient dynamic programming, and then modifies the resulting proposal to generate additional likely structures.

Considering alternative structures allows ambiguity in activity decomposition to enter the inference process. The authors report significant improvements over the state of the art for both detecting past activities and anticipating future ones. These results come from a dataset of 120 activity videos collected from four subjects. The finding supports the proposed structural reasoning approach within that evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Reasoning over alternative activity graph structures improves recognition and anticipation in an RGB-D dataset of 120 videos from four subjects.

title: Learning Spatio-Temporal Structure from RGB-D Videos for Human Activity Detection and Anticipation

abstract: Bundle discounts are used by retailers in many industries. Optimal bundle pricing requires learning the joint distribution of consumer valuations for the items in the bundle, that is, how much they are willing to pay for each of the items. We suppose that a retailer has sales transaction data, and the corresponding consumer valuations are latent variables. We develop a statistically consistent and computationally tractable inference procedure for fitting a copula model over correlated valuations, using only sales transaction data for the individual items. Simulations and data experiments demonstrate consistency, scalability, and the importance of incorporating correlations in the joint distribution.

We suppose that a retailer has sales transaction data, and the corresponding consumer valuations are latent variables. We develop a statistically consistent and computationally tractable inference procedure for fitting a copula model over correlated valuations, using only sales transaction data for the individual items. Simulations and data experiments demonstrate consistency, scalability, and the importance of incorporating correlations in the joint distribution.

paragraphs: Choosing bundle prices requires understanding how much consumers value the items together. The relevant information is the joint distribution of their valuations, including how values for different items are related. The paper considers retailers who have individual-item sales transactions but cannot directly observe the consumer valuations behind those transactions.

The authors treat valuations as latent variables and fit a copula model for their correlated distribution. They develop an inference procedure that uses only the transaction records for individual items. This connects routinely observed purchase data with the unobserved joint valuation model needed for bundle pricing, making dependence between item valuations part of the inference task.

The procedure is statistically consistent and computationally tractable. Simulations and data experiments demonstrate consistency and scalability, while also showing the importance of incorporating correlations in the joint distribution. The findings support estimating relationships among valuations when building a model for bundle decisions. The contribution centers on recovering this pricing-relevant distribution from transactions rather than requiring direct observations of willingness to pay.
summary.tldr: A consistent, tractable copula inference method estimates correlated consumer valuations from individual-item sales transactions for bundle pricing.

title: Latent Variable Copula Inference for Bundle Pricing from Retail Transaction Data

abstract: We show how any binary pairwise model may be “uprooted” to a fully symmetric model, wherein original singleton potentials are transformed to potentials on edges to an added variable, and then “rerooted” to a new model on the original number of variables. The new model is essentially equivalent to the original model, with the same partition function and allowing recovery of the original marginals or a MAP configuration, yet may have very different computational properties that allow much more efficient inference. This meta-approach deepens our understanding, may be applied to any existing algorithm to yield improved methods in practice, generalizes earlier theoretical results, and reveals a remarkable interpretation of the triplet-consistent polytope.

The new model is essentially equivalent to the original model, with the same partition function and allowing recovery of the original marginals or a MAP configuration, yet may have very different computational properties that allow much more efficient inference. This meta-approach deepens our understanding, may be applied to any existing algorithm to yield improved methods in practice, generalizes earlier theoretical results, and reveals a remarkable interpretation of the triplet-consistent polytope.

paragraphs: Inference in a graphical model can depend strongly on how the model is represented. This paper introduces a transformation for any binary pairwise model, where variables have two states and interactions involve pairs. The objective is to obtain a different representation that preserves essential probabilistic information but may be much easier to compute with.

The first step, called uprooting, adds a variable and turns the original single-variable potentials into edge potentials connected to it. This creates a fully symmetric model. Rerooting then produces a model with the original number of variables. The transformed model has the same partition function, and its results allow recovery of the original marginals or a maximum-probability configuration.

Although these quantities are preserved, the computational properties can change substantially, potentially enabling more efficient inference. The authors present the transformation as a meta-approach that can be applied with existing algorithms to improve methods in practice. It also generalizes earlier theory and provides an interpretation of the triplet-consistent polytope. The efficiency benefit is a possibility enabled by representation change, rather than a universal speedup.
summary.tldr: Uprooting and rerooting transform binary pairwise models while preserving key inference quantities and potentially making computation much more efficient.

title: Uprooting and Rerooting Graphical Models

abstract: We consider the Max K-Armed Bandit problem, where a learning agent is faced with several stochastic arms, each a source of i.i.d. rewards of unknown distribution. At each time step the agent chooses an arm, and observes the reward of the obtained sample. Each sample is considered here as a separate item with the reward designating its value, and the goal is to find an item with the highest possible value. Our basic assumption is a known lower bound on the \em tail function of the reward distributions. Under the PAC framework, we provide a lower bound on the sample complexity of any (ε,δ)-correct algorithm, and propose an algorithm that attains this bound up to logarithmic factors. We provide an analysis of the robustness of the proposed algorithm to the model assumptions, and further compare its performance to the simple non-adaptive variant, in which the arms are chosen randomly at each stage.

paragraphs: The Max K-Armed Bandit problem treats each sampled reward as the value of a separate item. The learner chooses among several stochastic sources and seeks an item with the highest possible value. Each source produces independent, identically distributed rewards from an unknown distribution, so choosing where to sample is part of the search.

The paper assumes a known lower bound on the reward distributions' tail functions. Under this assumption, the authors derive a lower bound on the number of samples required by any algorithm satisfying the specified accuracy and confidence requirements. They then propose an algorithm that reaches this bound up to logarithmic factors.

This connects an information requirement with an achievable sampling procedure, showing near-matching sample complexity within the stated framework. The authors also analyze robustness to the modeling assumptions and compare the algorithm with a non-adaptive procedure that selects arms randomly. Those analyses examine both the role of the tail assumption and the consequences of adapting source selection during the search.
summary.tldr: Under a known tail lower bound, a Max K-Armed Bandit algorithm matches the sample-complexity lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: PAC Lower Bounds and Efficient Algorithms for The Max K-Armed Bandit Problem

abstract: We estimate stochastic processes that govern the dynamics of evolving populations such as cell differentiation. The problem is challenging since longitudinal trajectory measurements of individuals in a population are rarely available due to experimental cost and/or privacy. We show that cross-sectional samples from an evolving population suffice for recovery within a class of processes even if samples are available only at a few distinct time points. We provide a stratified analysis of recoverability conditions, and establish that reversibility is sufficient for recoverability. For estimation, we derive a natural loss and regularization, and parameterize the processes as diffusive recurrent neural networks. We demonstrate the approach in the context of uncovering complex cellular dynamics known as the ‘epigenetic landscape’ from existing biological assays.

paragraphs: Studying an evolving population is difficult when researchers can observe snapshots but cannot track the same individuals over time. Experimental cost or privacy can make individual trajectories unavailable. This paper asks whether those cross-sectional observations can reveal the stochastic process governing population dynamics, including processes involved in cell differentiation.

The authors show that recovery is possible within a class of processes even when samples come from only a few distinct times. They analyze different recoverability conditions and establish reversibility as a sufficient condition. This is a conditional recovery result: reversibility provides one route to recoverability, rather than being presented as a necessary requirement for every recoverable process.

For estimation, the paper derives a loss function and regularization and represents the processes as diffusive recurrent neural networks. The approach is demonstrated using existing biological assays to uncover complex cellular dynamics described as an epigenetic landscape. The contribution connects a theoretical account of what population snapshots can reveal with a trainable model for estimating those dynamics.
summary.tldr: Diffusive recurrent networks estimate population dynamics from snapshots, with recovery guarantees for a class of processes and reversibility as a sufficient condition.

title: Learning Population-Level Diffusions with Generative RNNs

abstract: We study the problem of using i.i.d. samples from an unknown multivariate probability distribution p to estimate the mutual information of p. This problem has recently received attention in two settings: (1) where p is assumed to be Gaussian and (2) where p is assumed only to lie in a large nonparametric smoothness class. Estimators proposed for the Gaussian case converge in high dimensions when the Gaussian assumption holds, but are brittle, failing dramatically when p is not Gaussian, while estimators proposed for the nonparametric case fail to converge with realistic sample sizes except in very low dimension. Hence, there is a lack of robust mutual information estimators for many realistic data. To address this, we propose estimators for mutual information when p is assumed to be a nonparanormal (or Gaussian copula) model, a semiparametric compromise between Gaussian and nonparametric extremes. Using theoretical bounds and experiments, we show these estimators strike a practical balance between robustness and scalability.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate mutual information from independent samples of an unknown multivariate distribution. Mutual information describes statistical dependence. Existing approaches face a tradeoff: Gaussian estimators can work in high dimensions when their assumption is correct, but can fail badly when it is wrong.

More flexible nonparametric estimators avoid that narrow distributional assumption, yet the abstract reports that realistic sample sizes are generally insufficient outside very low dimensions. The authors propose a middle ground by assuming a nonparanormal, or Gaussian copula, model. This semiparametric choice lies between a fully Gaussian model and a broad nonparametric class.

The contribution is a set of mutual-information estimators designed for that intermediate model. Theoretical bounds and experiments support a practical balance between robustness and scalability. The approach matters because flexibility and high-dimensional estimation are being addressed together, through a deliberate modeling compromise. Its robustness claim remains tied to the nonparanormal setting; the results do not remove the need for a distributional assumption.
summary.tldr: Nonparanormal mutual-information estimators balance robustness and scalability between restrictive Gaussian models and data-hungry nonparametric approaches.

title: Nonparanormal Information Estimation

abstract: Machine learning models (e.g., speech recognizers) trained on average loss suffer from representation disparity—minority groups (e.g., non-native speakers) carry less weight in the training objective, and thus tend to suffer higher loss. Worse, as model accuracy affects user retention, a minority group can shrink over time. In this paper, we first show that the status quo of empirical risk minimization (ERM) amplifies representation disparity over time, which can even turn initially fair models unfair. To mitigate this, we develop an approach based on distributionally robust optimization (DRO), which minimizes the worst case risk over all distributions close to the empirical distribution. We prove that this approach controls the risk of the minority group at each time step, in the spirit of Rawlsian distributive justice, while remaining oblivious to the identity of the groups. We demonstrate that DRO prevents disparity amplification on examples where ERM fails, and show improvements in minority group user satisfaction in a real-world text autocomplete task.

paragraphs: Training to minimize average error gives smaller groups less influence over the objective. If those groups receive worse predictions and consequently stop using a service, their influence can shrink further during subsequent training. This paper studies that feedback loop and shows how repeated empirical risk minimization can amplify representation disparity, including making an initially fair model unfair.

The proposed response is distributionally robust optimization. Instead of considering only the empirical distribution, it minimizes the worst risk among distributions close to it. This changes which errors drive learning without requiring the algorithm to know users' group identities. The authors prove that their approach controls minority-group risk at each time step in the setting they analyze.

The paper demonstrates examples where this method prevents disparity amplification while ordinary empirical risk minimization fails. It also reports improved minority-group user satisfaction in a real text autocomplete task. The findings make retention part of the fairness problem: a model's errors can reshape the population that supplies its future training data.
summary.tldr: Distributionally robust training can counter feedback loops that worsen minority-group performance without requiring demographic group identities.

title: Fairness Without Demographics in Repeated Loss Minimization

abstract: Program synthesis is a class of regression problems where one seeks a solution, in the form of a source-code program, mapping the inputs to their corresponding outputs exactly. Due to its precise and combinatorial nature, program synthesis is commonly formulated as a constraint satisfaction problem, where input-output examples are encoded as constraints and solved with a constraint solver. A key challenge of this formulation is scalability: while constraint solvers work well with a few well-chosen examples, a large set of examples can incur significant overhead in both time and memory. We describe a method to discover a subset of examples that is both small and representative: the subset is constructed iteratively, using a neural network to predict the probability of unchosen examples conditioned on the chosen examples in the subset, and greedily adding the least probable example. We empirically evaluate the representativeness of the subsets constructed by our method, and demonstrate such subsets can significantly improve synthesis time and stability.

paragraphs: Program synthesis seeks a source-code program that exactly maps supplied inputs to their outputs. A common approach turns each example into a constraint and asks a solver to find a satisfying program. This becomes expensive when many examples are included, even though a small, carefully selected set can be effective.

The paper proposes an iterative method for constructing a compact, representative subset. A neural network estimates the probability of each unselected example conditional on the examples already chosen. The algorithm then adds the least probable example. This selection rule uses the current subset to identify which remaining example is least anticipated and should be included next.

The authors empirically assess how representative the resulting subsets are and demonstrate significant improvements in synthesis time and stability. The contribution addresses which constraints to present to the solver, linking learned example selection to the cost of exact program construction. The reported gains show that selecting informative examples can make the constraint-solving stage more manageable.
summary.tldr: A neural selection method builds small representative example sets that improve program synthesis time and stability.

title: Selecting Representative Examples for Program Synthesis

abstract: We present DL2, a system for training and querying neural networks with logical constraints. Using DL2, one can declaratively specify domain knowledge constraints to be enforced during training, as well as pose queries on the model to find inputs that satisfy a set of constraints. DL2 works by translating logical constraints into a loss function with desirable mathematical properties. The loss is then minimized with standard gradient-based methods. We evaluate DL2 by training networks with interesting constraints in unsupervised, semi-supervised and supervised settings. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that DL2 is more expressive than prior approaches combining logic and neural networks, and its loss functions are better suited for optimization. Further, we show that for a number of queries, DL2 can find the desired inputs in seconds (even for large models such as ResNet-50 on ImageNet).

paragraphs: DL2 provides a way to express desired neural-network behavior using logical constraints. During training, these constraints encode domain knowledge that the model should satisfy. Afterward, the same system can query a model by searching for inputs that meet a specified collection of requirements, making logic useful for both learning and examining behavior.

The mechanism translates logical statements into a loss function with mathematical properties suited to optimization. Standard gradient-based methods then minimize that loss. This connects a declarative description of requirements with the numerical procedures already used to train neural networks, allowing constraints to become part of the optimization problem.

The authors evaluate constrained training in unsupervised, semi-supervised, and supervised settings. They report greater expressiveness than prior approaches combining neural networks with logic, along with losses better suited to optimization. For a number of queries, DL2 finds satisfying inputs within seconds, including queries involving ResNet-50 on ImageNet. These results demonstrate both the training interface and the practical feasibility of constraint-based input searches for the evaluated queries.
summary.tldr: DL2 translates logical constraints into optimizable losses for neural-network training and searches for inputs satisfying model queries.

title: DL2: Training and Querying Neural Networks with Logic

abstract: When observing the actions of others, humans make inferences about why they acted as they did, and what this implies about the world; humans also use the fact that their actions will be interpreted in this manner, allowing them to act informatively and thereby communicate efficiently with others. Although learning algorithms have recently achieved superhuman performance in a number of two-player, zero-sum games, scalable multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms that can discover effective strategies and conventions in complex, partially observable settings have proven elusive. We present the Bayesian action decoder (BAD), a new multi-agent learning method that uses an approximate Bayesian update to obtain a public belief that conditions on the actions taken by all agents in the environment. BAD introduces a new Markov decision process, the public belief MDP , in which the action space consists of all deterministic partial policies, and exploits the fact that an agent acting only on this public belief state can still learn to use its private information if the action space is augmented to be over all partial policies mapping private information into environment actions. The Bayesian update is closely related to the theory of mind reasoning that humans carry out when observing others’ actions. We first validate BAD on a proof-of-principle two-step matrix game, where it outperforms policy gradient methods; we then evaluate BAD on the challenging, cooperative partial-information card game Hanabi, where, in the two-player setting, it surpasses all previously published learning and hand-coded approaches, establishing a new state of the art.

The Bayesian Action Decoder, or BAD, builds this interpretation of actions into multi-agent reinforcement learning. It uses an approximate Bayesian update to maintain a public belief informed by the actions of all agents.

The central construction is a public-belief Markov decision process. Its actions are deterministic partial policies: rules mapping an agent's private information to environment actions. Choosing among these rules allows decisions based on the public belief to still make use of private information. Observing the resulting action can then inform the shared belief, supporting the discovery of informative conventions.

The authors first test BAD in a two-step matrix game, where it outperforms policy-gradient methods. They then evaluate it on Hanabi, a cooperative card game with partial information. In the two-player setting, BAD surpasses previously published learned and hand-coded approaches. These results demonstrate the method's effectiveness in the tested settings, with the strongest reported benchmark claim specifically concerning two-player Hanabi.
summary.tldr: BAD learns cooperative conventions by interpreting actions through a shared Bayesian belief and achieves a reported state of the art in two-player Hanabi.

title: Bayesian Action Decoder for Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent progress in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have enabled a simple paradigm of architecture design: larger models typically achieve better accuracy. Due to this, in modern CNN architectures, it becomes more important to design models that generalize well under certain resource constraints, e.g. the number of parameters. In this paper, we propose a simple way to improve the capacity of any CNN model having large-scale features, without adding more parameters. In particular, we modify a standard convolutional layer to have a new functionality of channel-selectivity, so that the layer is trained to select important channels to re-distribute their parameters. Our experimental results under various CNN architectures and datasets demonstrate that the proposed new convolutional layer allows new optima that generalize better via efficient resource utilization, compared to the baseline.

paragraphs: Larger convolutional neural networks often achieve better accuracy, but increasing parameter counts may conflict with resource constraints. This paper asks how to improve the capacity of a CNN with large-scale features while keeping its parameter budget fixed. Its approach changes how a convolutional layer allocates its existing resources.

The proposed layer learns channel selectivity: it selects important channels and redistributes their parameters. This introduces a learned allocation decision within a standard convolutional layer. The goal is to make the available parameters more useful, so that model improvement can come from how resources are assigned as well as from how many parameters exist.

Experiments across multiple CNN architectures and datasets show that the modified layer reaches solutions that generalize better than the baseline. The authors attribute this improvement to efficient resource use and access to new optima during training. The evidence supports channel selection and parameter redistribution as a way to improve the evaluated networks without adding parameters to obtain those gains.
summary.tldr: A channel-selective convolutional layer reallocates existing parameters and improves generalization in the evaluated CNNs without increasing parameter count.

title: Training CNNs with Selective Allocation of Channels

abstract: Recent work showed that overparameterized autoencoders can be trained to implement associative memory via iterative maps, when the trained input-output Jacobian of the network has all of its eigenvalue norms strictly below one. Here, we theoretically analyze this phenomenon for sigmoid networks by leveraging recent developments in deep learning theory, especially the correspondence between training neural networks in the infinite-width limit and performing kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). We find that overparameterized sigmoid autoencoders can have attractors in the NTK limit for both training with a single example and multiple examples under certain conditions. In particular, for multiple training examples, we find that the norm of the largest Jacobian eigenvalue drops below one with increasing input norm, leading to associative memory.
