paragraphs: An autoencoder can do more than reconstruct an input once: repeatedly feeding its output back into itself can create a memory-retrieval process. The relevant behavior is attraction, where repeated applications move inputs toward a stored example. This paper analyzes when overparameterized networks with sigmoid activations can exhibit that behavior.

The analysis uses the connection between infinitely wide neural networks and kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel. This gives the authors a theoretical way to study the trained network’s input-output Jacobian, which describes how small input changes affect its output. Earlier work identified eigenvalue magnitudes strictly below one as a condition supporting associative memory through iteration.

The authors show that attractors can exist in this infinite-width setting for both single-example and multiple-example training, under specified conditions. With multiple examples, they find that increasing input norm can push the largest Jacobian eigenvalue magnitude below one. The result connects input scale and local stability to memory behavior; it does not claim that every trained sigmoid autoencoder automatically becomes an associative memory.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies conditions under which infinitely wide sigmoid autoencoders can retrieve memories through repeated application.

title: Associative Memory in Iterated Overparameterized Sigmoid Autoencoders

abstract: Deep autoregressive models compute point likelihood estimates of individual data points. However, many applications (i.e., database cardinality estimation), require estimating range densities, a capability that is under-explored by current neural density estimation literature. In these applications, fast and accurate range density estimates over high-dimensional data directly impact user-perceived performance. In this paper, we explore a technique for accelerating range density estimation over deep autoregressive models. This technique, called variable skipping, exploits the sparse structure of range density queries to avoid sampling unnecessary variables during approximate inference. We show that variable skipping provides 10-100x efficiency improvements when targeting challenging high-quantile error metrics, enables complex applications such as text pattern matching, and can be realized via a simple data augmentation procedure without changing the usual maximum likelihood objective.

paragraphs: Autoregressive density models assign likelihoods to individual data points, but some applications need the probability mass of an entire range. Database cardinality estimation is one example, where estimating how many records meet query conditions affects user-visible performance. This paper studies how to make those range estimates faster over high-dimensional data.

The proposed technique, variable skipping, exploits the sparse structure of range queries to avoid sampling variables that are unnecessary during approximate inference. The key opportunity comes from the query itself: not every variable needs the same processing for a particular requested range. The technique can be introduced through a simple data augmentation procedure while retaining the usual maximum likelihood training objective.

The authors report efficiency improvements of 10 to 100 times when targeting challenging high-quantile error metrics, which emphasize the larger errors in the evaluation distribution. They also demonstrate support for applications such as text pattern matching. The contribution connects query-aware inference savings with a training procedure that fits the existing autoregressive learning objective.
summary.tldr: Variable skipping avoids unnecessary sampling in autoregressive range queries, delivering reported efficiency gains of 10 to 100 times.

title: Variable Skipping for Autoregressive Range Density Estimation

abstract: Meta-learning aims to perform fast adaptation on a new task through learning a “prior” from multiple existing tasks. A common practice in meta-learning is to perform a train-validation split (\emph{train-val method}) where the prior adapts to the task on one split of the data, and the resulting predictor is evaluated on another split. Despite its prevalence, the importance of the train-validation split is not well understood either in theory or in practice, particularly in comparison to the more direct \emph{train-train method}, which uses all the per-task data for both training and evaluation. We provide a detailed theoretical study on whether and when the train-validation split is helpful in the linear centroid meta-learning problem. In the agnostic case, we show that the expected loss of the train-val method is minimized at the optimal prior for meta testing, and this is not the case for the train-train method in general without structural assumptions on the data. In contrast, in the realizable case where the data are generated from linear models, we show that both the train-val and train-train losses are minimized at the optimal prior in expectation. Further, perhaps surprisingly, our main result shows that the train-train method achieves a \emph{strictly better} excess loss in this realizable case, even when the regularization parameter and split ratio are optimally tuned for both methods. Our results highlight that sample splitting may not always be preferable, especially when the data is realizable by the model. We validate our theories by experimentally showing that the train-train method can indeed outperform the train-val method, on both simulations and real meta-learning tasks.

The findings make the usefulness of splitting conditional on the relationship between the data and the model.
summary.tldr: Train-validation splitting helps align meta-learning objectives in general, but reusing all task data can be provably better in a realizable linear setting.

title: How Important is the Train-Validation Split in Meta-Learning?

abstract: With graphs rapidly growing in size and deeper graph neural networks (GNNs) emerging, the training and inference of GNNs become increasingly expensive. Existing network weight pruning algorithms cannot address the main space and computational bottleneck in GNNs, caused by the size and connectivity of the graph. To this end, this paper first presents a unified GNN sparsification (UGS) framework that simultaneously prunes the graph adjacency matrix and the model weights, for effectively accelerating GNN inference on large-scale graphs. Leveraging this new tool, we further generalize the recently popular lottery ticket hypothesis to GNNs for the first time, by defining a graph lottery ticket (GLT) as a pair of core sub-dataset and sparse sub-network, which can be jointly identified from the original GNN and the full dense graph by iteratively applying UGS. Like its counterpart in convolutional neural networks, GLT can be trained in isolation to match the performance of training with the full model and graph, and can be drawn from both randomly initialized and self-supervised pre-trained GNNs. Our proposal has been experimentally verified across various GNN architectures and diverse tasks, on both small-scale graph datasets (Cora, Citeseer and PubMed), and large-scale datasets from the challenging Open Graph Benchmark (OGB). Specifically, for node classification, our found GLTs achieve the same accuracies with 20% 98% MACs saving on small graphs and 25% 85% MACs saving on large ones. For link prediction, GLTs lead to 48% 97% and 70% MACs saving on small and large graph datasets, respectively, without compromising predictive performance. Codes are at https://github.com/VITA-Group/Unified-LTH-GNN.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks become expensive as both their models and input graphs grow. Removing model weights alone leaves a major source of cost intact: the graph’s size and connectivity. This paper introduces unified GNN sparsification, which removes graph connections and model weights together to accelerate inference.

The framework also extends the lottery ticket idea to graph learning. A graph lottery ticket consists of a core portion of the graph data paired with a sparse neural network. Repeated sparsification identifies this pair from the full graph and model. The authors report that these tickets can be trained separately to match full training performance, starting from either random initialization or self-supervised pretraining.

Experiments span different architectures, node classification, and link prediction on small and large graph datasets. For node classification, reported multiply-accumulate savings range from 20% to 98% on small graphs and 25% to 85% on large graphs, with matching accuracy. Link prediction also shows substantial savings without reduced predictive performance. These results support treating graph structure and model parameters as a joint compression problem.
summary.tldr: Jointly pruning graph connections and neural-network weights identifies smaller graph models that match full-model performance in the reported experiments.

title: A Unified Lottery Ticket Hypothesis for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The Dual Principal Component Pursuit (DPCP) method has been proposed to robustly recover a subspace of high-relative dimension from corrupted data. Existing analyses and algorithms of DPCP, however, mainly focus on finding a normal to a single hyperplane that contains the inliers. Although these algorithms can be extended to a subspace of higher co-dimension through a recursive approach that sequentially finds a new basis element of the space orthogonal to the subspace, this procedure is computationally expensive and lacks convergence guarantees. In this paper, we consider a DPCP approach for simultaneously computing the entire basis of the orthogonal complement subspace (we call this a holistic approach) by solving a non-convex non-smooth optimization problem over the Grassmannian. We provide geometric and statistical analyses for the global optimality and prove that it can tolerate as many outliers as the square of the number of inliers, under both noiseless and noisy settings. We then present a Riemannian regularity condition for the problem, which is then used to prove that a Riemannian subgradient method converges linearly to a neighborhood of the orthogonal subspace with error proportional to the noise level.

paragraphs: Recovering a subspace from corrupted data requires identifying shared structure despite observations that do not belong to it. Earlier Dual Principal Component Pursuit methods largely focused on finding one direction perpendicular to a hyperplane containing the inliers. Extending that procedure by finding perpendicular directions sequentially is computationally expensive and lacks convergence guarantees.

This paper instead estimates an entire basis for the orthogonal complement simultaneously. It formulates that task as a nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization problem on the Grassmannian, a space whose elements represent subspaces. The holistic formulation treats the perpendicular directions as one geometric object, allowing the analysis to address recovery of the full subspace directly.

Geometric and statistical analyses establish global optimality results and show tolerance for outlier counts scaling as the square of the inlier count in the analyzed noiseless and noisy settings. A Riemannian regularity condition then supports linear convergence of a subgradient method to a neighborhood of the desired orthogonal subspace. The remaining error is proportional to the noise level, explicitly linking recovery precision to data corruption.
summary.tldr: A holistic DPCP formulation estimates the full orthogonal subspace with robustness guarantees and linear convergence to noise-dependent accuracy.

title: Dual Principal Component Pursuit for Robust Subspace Learning: Theory and Algorithms for a Holistic Approach

abstract: The early phase of training a deep neural network has a dramatic effect on the local curvature of the loss function. For instance, using a small learning rate does not guarantee stable optimization because the optimization trajectory has a tendency to steer towards regions of the loss surface with increasing local curvature. We ask whether this tendency is connected to the widely observed phenomenon that the choice of the learning rate strongly influences generalization. We first show that stochastic gradient descent (SGD) implicitly penalizes the trace of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), a measure of the local curvature, from the start of training. We argue it is an implicit regularizer in SGD by showing that explicitly penalizing the trace of the FIM can significantly improve generalization. We highlight that poor final generalization coincides with the trace of the FIM attaining a large value early in training, to which we refer as catastrophic Fisher explosion. Finally, to gain insight into the regularization effect of penalizing the trace of the FIM, we show that it limits memorization by reducing the learning speed of examples with noisy labels more than that of the examples with clean labels.

paragraphs: The first phase of neural-network training can change the geometry of the loss surface substantially. A small learning rate does not necessarily make optimization stable: training can move toward regions with greater local curvature. This paper investigates whether that tendency helps explain why learning-rate choices strongly influence how well a network generalizes.

The authors show that stochastic gradient descent implicitly penalizes the trace of the Fisher Information Matrix from the beginning of training. This trace serves as a measure of local curvature. They support its interpretation as an implicit regularizer by showing that adding an explicit penalty on the same quantity can significantly improve generalization.

Poor final generalization coincides with a large early increase in this trace, which the authors call catastrophic Fisher explosion. They also investigate how penalizing the trace affects memorization: it slows learning of examples with noisy labels more than learning of clean examples. These findings connect early training geometry with selective resistance to label noise, while the reported coincidence does not itself establish a universal causal rule.
summary.tldr: Large early Fisher-matrix traces coincide with poor generalization, while explicitly penalizing the trace can improve generalization and limit noisy-label memorization.

title: Catastrophic Fisher Explosion: Early Phase Fisher Matrix Impacts Generalization

abstract: Certifiable robustness is a highly desirable property for adopting deep neural networks (DNNs) in safety-critical scenarios, but often demands tedious computations to establish. The main hurdle lies in the massive amount of non-linearity in large DNNs. To trade off the DNN expressiveness (which calls for more non-linearity) and robustness certification scalability (which prefers more linearity), we propose a novel solution to strategically manipulate neurons, by "grafting" appropriate levels of linearity. The core of our proposal is to first linearize insignificant ReLU neurons, to eliminate the non-linear components that are both redundant for DNN performance and harmful to its certification. We then optimize the associated slopes and intercepts of the replaced linear activations for restoring model performance while maintaining certifiability. Hence, typical neuron pruning could be viewed as a special case of grafting a linear function of the fixed zero slopes and intercept, that might overly restrict the network flexibility and sacrifice its performance. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets and network backbones show that our linearity grafting can (1) effectively tighten certified bounds; (2) achieve competitive certifiable robustness without certified robust training (i.e., over 30% improvements on CIFAR-10 models); and (3) scale up complete verification to large adversarially trained models with 17M parameters. Codes are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/Linearity-Grafting.

paragraphs: Certifying a neural network’s robustness can be computationally difficult because large networks contain many nonlinear operations. This paper studies how to reduce that burden while preserving predictive performance. Its approach, linearity grafting, selectively replaces insignificant ReLU activations with linear functions.

After choosing which neurons to linearize, the method learns the slopes and intercepts of their replacement functions. This gives the network room to recover performance while retaining the certification benefits of greater linearity. Ordinary neuron pruning fits within this view as the special case where both slope and intercept are fixed to zero, leaving less flexibility.

Experiments across datasets and network architectures report tighter certified bounds and competitive certifiable robustness without certified robust training, including improvements exceeding 30% on CIFAR-10 models. The method also scales complete verification to large adversarially trained models with 17 million parameters. These findings support selective linearization as a way to manage the tension between expressive nonlinear models and tractable robustness certification, with learned replacements preserving more flexibility than simply removing neurons.
summary.tldr: Linearity grafting replaces selected ReLUs with learned linear functions to make robustness certification more scalable while preserving model performance.

title: Linearity Grafting: Relaxed Neuron Pruning Helps Certifiable Robustness

abstract: In this paper, we consider nonconvex minimax optimization, which is gaining prominence in many modern machine learning applications, such as GANs. Large-scale edge-based collection of training data in these applications calls for communication-efficient distributed optimization algorithms, such as those used in federated learning, to process the data. In this paper, we analyze local stochastic gradient descent ascent (SGDA), the local-update version of the SGDA algorithm. SGDA is the core algorithm used in minimax optimization, but it is not well-understood in a distributed setting. We prove that Local SGDA has order-optimal sample complexity for several classes of nonconvex-concave and nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems, and also enjoys linear speedup with respect to the number of clients. We provide a novel and tighter analysis, which improves the convergence and communication guarantees in the existing literature. For nonconvex-PL and nonconvex-one-point-concave functions, we improve the existing complexity results for centralized minimax problems. Furthermore, we propose a momentum-based local-update algorithm, which has the same convergence guarantees, but outperforms Local SGDA as demonstrated in our experiments.

paragraphs: Minimax learning involves optimizing competing objectives, as in generative adversarial networks. When training data are distributed across clients, the optimization must also account for communication costs. This paper studies Local SGDA, a version of stochastic gradient descent–ascent that performs local updates in a federated setting.

The authors establish order-optimal sample complexity for several classes of nonconvex–concave and nonconvex–nonconcave problems. Their analysis also shows linear speedup with the number of clients in the analyzed settings. A tighter treatment improves existing convergence and communication guarantees, clarifying how efficiently local updates can solve these distributed minimax problems.

The theoretical contributions extend to centralized optimization, where the paper improves complexity results for nonconvex–PL and nonconvex–one-point-concave objectives. The authors additionally introduce a momentum-based local-update method. It shares Local SGDA’s convergence guarantees but performs better in their experiments. Thus, the paper contributes both stronger understanding of an established algorithm and an empirically improved alternative within the same guarantee level.
summary.tldr: Tighter analysis establishes efficient Local SGDA guarantees for several minimax classes, while a momentum variant improves experimental performance.

title: Federated Minimax Optimization: Improved Convergence Analyses and Algorithms

abstract: We consider the problem of computing bounds for causal inference problems with unobserved confounders, where identifiability does not hold. Existing non-parametric approaches for computing such bounds use linear programming (LP) formulations that quickly become intractable for existing solvers because the size of the LP grows exponentially in the number of edges in the underlying causal graph. We show that this LP can be significantly pruned by carefully considering the structure of the causal query, allowing us to compute bounds for significantly larger causal inference problems as compared to what is possible using existing techniques. This pruning procedure also allows us to compute the bounds in closed form for a special class of causal graphs and queries, which includes a well-studied family of problems where multiple confounded treatments influence an outcome. We also propose a very efficient greedy heuristic that produces very high quality bounds, and scales to problems that are several orders of magnitude larger than those for which the pruned LP can be solved.

paragraphs: When unobserved confounders prevent a causal quantity from being uniquely identified, bounds can still describe the range of possible answers. Computing those bounds is often expensive. Existing nonparametric linear-programming formulations grow exponentially with the number of edges in the causal graph, quickly exceeding what available solvers can handle.

This paper shows that examining the structure of the particular causal query allows much of the linear program to be pruned. The smaller formulation makes bounds computable for substantially larger problems. For a special class of graphs and queries, the same reasoning produces closed-form bounds, including problems in which multiple confounded treatments affect an outcome.

The authors additionally propose a greedy heuristic for problems beyond the reach of the pruned linear program. They report very high-quality bounds and scalability to problems several orders of magnitude larger. These contributions provide complementary ways to make causal bounding more tractable: query-specific pruning, closed-form results in a special class, and an efficient heuristic for larger cases.
summary.tldr: Query-aware pruning and a greedy heuristic make causal bounds computable for much larger problems with unobserved confounding.

title: Scalable Computation of Causal Bounds

abstract: We generalize the multiple-play multi-armed bandits (MP-MAB) problem with a shareable arms setting, in which several plays can share the same arm. Furthermore, each shareable arm has a finite reward capacity and a “per-load” reward distribution, both of which are unknown to the learner. The reward from a shareable arm is load-dependent, which is the “per-load” reward multiplying either the number of plays pulling the arm, or its reward capacity when the number of plays exceeds the capacity limit. When the “per-load” reward follows a Gaussian distribution, we prove a sample complexity lower bound of learning the capacity from load-dependent rewards and also a regret lower bound of this new MP-MAB problem. We devise a capacity estimator whose sample complexity upper bound matches the lower bound in terms of reward means and capacities. We also propose an online learning algorithm to address the problem and prove its regret upper bound. This regret upper bound’s first term is the same as regret lower bound’s, and its second and third terms also evidently correspond to lower bound’s. Extensive experiments validate our algorithm’s performance and also its gain in 5G & 4G base station selection.

title: Multiple-Play Stochastic Bandits with Shareable Finite-Capacity Arms

abstract: In this paper, we present a model-based offline reinforcement learning method that integrates count-based conservatism, named $\texttt{Count-MORL}$. Our method utilizes the count estimates of state-action pairs to quantify model estimation error, marking the first algorithm of demonstrating the efficacy of count-based conservatism in model-based offline deep RL to the best of our knowledge. For our proposed method, we first show that the estimation error is inversely proportional to the frequency of state-action pairs. Secondly, we demonstrate that the learned policy under the count-based conservative model offers near-optimality performance guarantees. Through extensive numerical experiments, we validate that $\texttt{Count-MORL}$ with hash code implementation significantly outperforms existing offline RL algorithms on the D4RL benchmark datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/oh-lab/Count-MORL.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from previously collected experience. In a model-based approach, the learner also uses an estimated model, making errors in that model relevant to policy quality. Count-MORL uses estimates of how often state-action pairs occur to determine how conservatively the learned model should be treated.

The paper first shows an inverse relationship between model-estimation error and the frequency of state-action pairs. This connects conservatism to data coverage: less frequently observed pairs provide weaker support for the estimated model. The authors then establish near-optimal performance guarantees for the policy learned using their count-based conservative model. Counts thus provide a common basis for both the algorithm and its theoretical analysis.

For implementation, the method uses hash codes to obtain count estimates. Numerical experiments on D4RL benchmark datasets report significant improvements over existing offline reinforcement-learning algorithms. The authors present this as, to their knowledge, the first demonstration that count-based conservatism is effective in model-based offline deep reinforcement learning. The empirical results support the usefulness of frequency information in the evaluated benchmark settings.
summary.tldr: Count-MORL uses state-action frequency estimates to guide model conservatism, combining near-optimality guarantees with strong D4RL results.

title: Model-based Offline Reinforcement Learning with Count-based Conservatism

abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has been gaining popularity for the deployment of deep neural networks on resource-limited devices since unlike quantization-aware training, neither a full training dataset nor end-to-end training is required at all. As PTQ schemes based on reconstructing each layer or block output turn out to be effective to enhance quantized model performance, recent works have developed algorithms to devise and learn a new weight-rounding scheme so as to better reconstruct each layer or block output. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective new weight-rounding mechanism for PTQ, coined FlexRound, based on element-wise division instead of typical element-wise addition such that FlexRound enables jointly learning a common quantization grid size as well as a different scale for each pre-trained weight. Thanks to the reciprocal rule of derivatives induced by element-wise division, FlexRound is inherently able to exploit pre-trained weights when updating their corresponding scales, and thus, flexibly quantize pre-trained weights depending on their magnitudes. We empirically validate the efficacy of FlexRound on a wide range of models and tasks. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to carry out comprehensive experiments on not only image classification and natural language understanding but also natural language generation, assuming a per-tensor uniform PTQ setting. Moreover, we demonstrate, for the first time, that large language models can be efficiently quantized, with only a negligible impact on performance compared to half-precision baselines, achieved by reconstructing the output in a block-by-block manner.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization reduces the numerical precision of a trained network for deployment on devices with limited resources. It avoids requiring a full training dataset or end-to-end training. A central challenge is deciding how to round weights while preserving model behavior, often by reconstructing the outputs of individual layers or blocks.

FlexRound introduces a rounding mechanism based on element-wise division. It jointly learns a shared quantization grid size and a separate scale for each pretrained weight. The derivatives produced by division allow weight values to influence updates to their corresponding scales. This lets the rounding process respond flexibly to differences in weight magnitude.

The authors evaluate the method across image classification, natural language understanding, and natural language generation under a per-tensor uniform quantization setting. They also report that reconstructing outputs block by block can efficiently quantize large language models with negligible performance impact relative to half-precision baselines in their experiments. The contribution connects a particular rounding parameterization to broad empirical evidence that post-training compression can preserve useful model behavior.
summary.tldr: FlexRound learns division-based weight rounding and reports effective post-training quantization across vision and language tasks, including large language models.

title: FlexRound: Learnable Rounding based on Element-wise Division for Post-Training Quantization

abstract: In the context of adversarial robustness, we make three strongly related contributions. First, we prove that while attacking ReLU classifiers is $\mathit{NP}$-hard, ensuring their robustness at training time is $\Sigma^2_P$-hard (even on a single example). This asymmetry provides a rationale for the fact that robust classifications approaches are frequently fooled in the literature. Second, we show that inference-time robustness certificates are not affected by this asymmetry, by introducing a proof-of-concept approach named Counter-Attack (CA). Indeed, CA displays a reversed asymmetry: running the defense is $\mathit{NP}$-hard, while attacking it is $\Sigma_2^P$-hard. Finally, motivated by our previous result, we argue that adversarial attacks can be used in the context of robustness certification, and provide an empirical evaluation of their effectiveness. As a byproduct of this process, we also release UG100, a benchmark dataset for adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: This paper examines a computational imbalance between attacking a classifier and making it robust. For ReLU classifiers, the authors prove that finding attacks is NP-hard, while ensuring robustness during training is hard for a higher level of the polynomial hierarchy, even for a single example. The result provides a complexity-based rationale for why robustness methods can still be defeated.

The authors then show that this particular imbalance does not carry over to all inference-time certification methods. Their proof-of-concept defense, Counter-Attack, reverses the direction: running the defense is NP-hard, while attacking it is hard for the higher complexity class. These are computational hardness statements, rather than claims that the defense is inexpensive to run.

Motivated by this reversal, the paper explores using adversarial attacks as components of robustness certification and evaluates their effectiveness empirically. It also releases the UG100 attack benchmark. Together, the contributions distinguish the computational demands of robust training from those of certification and show how attack procedures can contribute to a defensive objective.
summary.tldr: The paper proves computational asymmetries between attack and defense and introduces an inference-time certification approach that reverses their direction.

title: Computational Asymmetries in Robust Classification

abstract: Improving and guaranteeing the robustness of deep learning models has been a topic of intense research. Ensembling, which combines several classifiers to provide a better model, has been shown to be beneficial for generalisation, uncertainty estimation, calibration, and mitigating the effects of concept drift. However, the impact of ensembling on certified robustness is less well understood. In this work, we generalise Lipschitz continuity by introducing S-Lipschitz classifiers, which we use to analyse the theoretical robustness of ensembles. Our results are precise conditions when ensembles of robust classifiers are more robust than any constituent classifier, as well as conditions when they are less robust.

paragraphs: Combining several classifiers into an ensemble can benefit generalization, uncertainty estimation, calibration, and adaptation to changing concepts. This paper examines a separate question: what does combining classifiers do to certified robustness? The focus is on mathematical robustness guarantees, so benefits in other aspects of prediction do not automatically settle the question.

The authors introduce S-Lipschitz classifiers as a generalization of Lipschitz continuity. This supplies a framework for analyzing robustness when multiple classifiers are combined. The purpose of the new mathematical description is to identify how ensemble behavior relates to the robustness of the individual classifiers that make it up.

The resulting theory gives precise conditions under which an ensemble of robust classifiers is more robust than every constituent classifier. It also gives conditions under which ensembling reduces robustness. These two directions are central to the contribution: assembling robust components can strengthen a guarantee, but the outcome depends on the conditions governing their combination. The paper makes that dependence explicit through a general certification framework.
summary.tldr: A generalized Lipschitz framework identifies conditions under which ensembling robust classifiers improves or reduces certified robustness.

title: Certifying Ensembles: A General Certification Theory with S-Lipschitzness

abstract: Even for known nonlinear dynamical systems, feedback controller synthesis is a difficult problem that often requires leveraging the particular structure of the dynamics to induce a stable closed-loop system. For general nonlinear models, including those fit to data, there may not be enough known structure to reliably synthesize a stabilizing feedback controller. In this paper, we discuss a state-dependent nonlinear tracking controller formulation based on a state-dependent Riccati equation for general nonlinear control-affine systems. This formulation depends on a nonlinear factorization of the system of vector fields defining the control-affine dynamics, which always exists under mild smoothness assumptions. We propose a method for learning this factorization from a finite set of data. On a variety of simulated nonlinear dynamical systems, we empirically demonstrate the efficacy of learned versions of this controller in stable trajectory tracking. Alongside our learning method, we evaluate recent ideas in jointly learning a controller and stabilizability certificate for known dynamical systems; we show experimentally that such methods can be frail in comparison.

paragraphs: A learned model of a nonlinear system does not automatically provide the structure needed to design a stabilizing controller. Even when the dynamics are known, constructing feedback that produces stable behavior can be difficult. This paper focuses on learning a particular representation of the dynamics because that representation is directly useful for controller construction.

The controller is a state-dependent nonlinear tracking formulation based on a state-dependent Riccati equation. It applies to nonlinear control-affine systems and relies on a nonlinear factorization of the vector fields describing their dynamics. The authors state that this factorization exists under mild smoothness assumptions, and propose learning it from a finite dataset.

Experiments on several simulated nonlinear systems show that controllers built from the learned factorization can track trajectories stably. The authors also test approaches that jointly learn a controller and a stabilizability certificate for known dynamics, finding them comparatively fragile in their experiments. The broader lesson is supported empirically: learning structure tailored to control can be useful beyond simply fitting a general dynamical model.
summary.tldr: Learning a control-relevant factorization of nonlinear dynamics enables effective trajectory tracking in simulated systems.

title: Learning Control-Oriented Dynamical Structure from Data

abstract: Unsupervised learning with functional data is an emerging paradigm of machine learning research with applications to computer vision, climate modeling and physical systems. A natural way of modeling functional data is by learning operators between infinite dimensional spaces, leading to discretization invariant representations that scale independently of the sample grid resolution. Here we present Variational Autoencoding Neural Operators (VANO), a general strategy for making a large class of operator learning architectures act as variational autoencoders. For this purpose, we provide a novel rigorous mathematical formulation of the variational objective in function spaces for training. VANO first maps an input function to a distribution over a latent space using a parametric encoder and then decodes a sample from the latent distribution to reconstruct the input, as in classic variational autoencoders. We test VANO with different model set-ups and architecture choices for a variety of benchmarks. We start from a simple Gaussian random field where we can analytically track what the model learns and progressively transition to more challenging benchmarks including modeling phase separation in Cahn-Hilliard systems and real world satellite data for measuring Earth surface deformation.

paragraphs: Functional data are naturally viewed as functions rather than fixed arrays of measurements. Neural operators model relationships between such functions, enabling representations that do not depend on a particular discretization grid. This paper introduces VANO, a general strategy for turning a broad class of operator-learning architectures into variational autoencoders.

VANO encodes an input function as a distribution in latent space. It then samples from that distribution and decodes the sample to reconstruct the function. The authors provide a rigorous formulation of the variational training objective in function spaces, giving this familiar encoding-and-reconstruction pattern a mathematical foundation suited to functional data.

The evaluation spans different architectures and model setups. It begins with a Gaussian random field, where the learned behavior can be tracked analytically, then moves to phase separation in Cahn-Hilliard systems and satellite measurements of Earth-surface deformation. These tests examine the framework from a mathematically interpretable example through more demanding physical and real-world data, illustrating the range of functional modeling problems it targets.
summary.tldr: VANO gives neural operators a variational autoencoder formulation for learning probabilistic representations of functional data.

title: Variational Autoencoding Neural Operators

abstract: Training deep neural networks for classification often includes minimizing the training loss beyond the zero training error point. In this phase of training, a "neural collapse" behavior has been observed: the variability of features (outputs of the penultimate layer) of within-class samples decreases and the mean features of different classes approach a certain tight frame structure. Recent works analyze this behavior via idealized unconstrained features models where all the minimizers exhibit exact collapse. However, with practical networks and datasets, the features typically do not reach exact collapse, e.g., because deep layers cannot arbitrarily modify intermediate features that are far from being collapsed. In this paper, we propose a richer model that can capture this phenomenon by forcing the features to stay in the vicinity of a predefined features matrix (e.g., intermediate features). We explore the model in the small vicinity case via perturbation analysis and establish results that cannot be obtained by the previously studied models. For example, we prove reduction in the within-class variability of the optimized features compared to the predefined input features (via analyzing gradient flow on the "central-path" with minimal assumptions), analyze the minimizers in the near-collapse regime, and provide insights on the effect of regularization hyperparameters on the closeness to collapse. We support our theory with experiments in practical deep learning settings.

paragraphs: After a classifier reaches zero training error, further training often makes examples from the same class have increasingly similar internal features. Class means also approach a structured geometric arrangement. Idealized models can predict exact neural collapse, but practical networks commonly stop short because later layers cannot freely reshape all earlier features.

This paper introduces a model that requires optimized features to remain near a predefined feature matrix, such as intermediate network features. The authors study small neighborhoods through perturbation analysis. This constraint represents limited freedom to change the input features and allows the model to describe departures from exact collapse.

The contribution explains aspects of partial collapse that unconstrained feature models, whose minimizers collapse exactly, cannot capture.
summary.tldr: Constraining features to stay near an initial representation enables a perturbation analysis of incomplete neural collapse and regularization effects.

title: Perturbation Analysis of Neural Collapse

abstract: Research in the field of hyperparameter optimization (HPO) has been greatly accelerated by existing HPO benchmarks. Nonetheless, existing efforts in benchmarking all focus on HPO for traditional learning paradigms while ignoring federated learning (FL), a promising paradigm for collaboratively learning models from dispersed data. In this paper, we first identify some uniqueness of federated hyperparameter optimization (FedHPO) from various aspects, showing that existing HPO benchmarks no longer satisfy the need to study FedHPO methods. To facilitate the research of FedHPO, we propose and implement a benchmark suite FedHPO-Bench that incorporates comprehensive FedHPO problems, enables flexible customization of the function evaluations, and eases continuing extensions. We conduct extensive experiments based on FedHPO-Bench to provide the community with more insights into FedHPO. We open-sourced FedHPO-Bench at https://github.com/alibaba/FederatedScope/tree/master/benchmark/FedHPOBench.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization selects the settings used to train a model, and benchmarks make it easier to study methods for performing that selection. This paper focuses on federated learning, where models are learned collaboratively from dispersed data. The authors argue that benchmarks built for traditional learning do not adequately serve this setting.

They first examine what distinguishes federated hyperparameter optimization from its conventional counterpart. Based on those differences, they implement FedHPO-Bench, a benchmark suite containing a broad collection of federated optimization problems. The suite permits flexible customization of function evaluations and is designed to accommodate further extensions as research needs develop.

The authors also conduct extensive experiments using the suite to provide insights into federated hyperparameter optimization. The contribution combines a study of the setting with shared experimental infrastructure. Customizable evaluations and extensibility matter because a useful benchmark must support investigation of the federated problem itself, rather than simply reuse an evaluation setup intended for a different learning paradigm. The suite is released as open-source software.
summary.tldr: FedHPO-Bench provides customizable, extensible benchmarks for studying hyperparameter optimization in federated learning.

title: FedHPO-Bench: A Benchmark Suite for Federated Hyperparameter Optimization

abstract: High-quality machine learning models are dependent on access to high-quality training data. When the data are not already available, it is tedious and costly to obtain them. Data markets help with identifying valuable training data: model consumers pay to train a model, the market uses that budget to identify data and train the model (the budget allocation problem), and finally the market compensates data providers according to their data contribution (revenue allocation problem). For example, a bank could pay the data market to access data from other financial institutions to train a fraud detection model. Compensating data contributors requires understanding data’s contribution to the model; recent efforts to solve this revenue allocation problem based on the Shapley value are inefficient to lead to practical data markets. In this paper, we introduce a new algorithm to solve budget allocation and revenue allocation problems simultaneously in linear time. The new algorithm employs an adaptive sampling process that selects data from those providers who are contributing the most to the model. Better data means that the algorithm accesses those providers more often, and more frequent accesses corresponds to higher compensation. Furthermore, the algorithm can be deployed in both centralized and federated scenarios, boosting its applicability. We provide theoretical guarantees for the algorithm that show the budget is used efficiently and the properties of revenue allocation are similar to Shapley’s. Finally, we conduct an empirical evaluation to show the performance of the algorithm in practical scenarios and when compared to other baselines. Overall, we believe that the new algorithm paves the way for the implementation of practical data markets.

paragraphs: A data market must make two connected decisions: which providers’ data to spend a customer’s training budget on, and how to divide the resulting revenue among those providers. Assessing each provider’s contribution separately can be expensive. The paper addresses both decisions together through an algorithm that the authors describe as running in linear time.

The central mechanism is adaptive sampling. As training proceeds, the algorithm accesses providers whose data contribute more to the model more frequently. Those access frequencies also determine compensation. This connects purchasing and payment through the same process: data that prove more useful receive both more attention during training and greater compensation.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for efficient budget use and revenue allocation with properties similar to those associated with Shapley values. This is a similarity in allocation properties, rather than a claim that the algorithm computes identical payments. The method supports centralized and federated settings, and an empirical evaluation examines practical scenarios and baseline comparisons. Together, these contributions offer a computationally practical approach to coordinating data acquisition and contributor rewards.
summary.tldr: An adaptive sampling algorithm jointly allocates training budgets and provider payments by accessing and compensating more useful data providers more often.

title: Addressing Budget Allocation and Revenue Allocation in Data Market Environments Using an Adaptive Sampling Algorithm

abstract: Large Language Models are prone to biased predictions and hallucinations, underlining the paramount importance of understanding their model-internal reasoning process. However, achieving faithful attributions for the entirety of a black-box transformer model and maintaining computational efficiency is an unsolved challenge. By extending the Layer-wise Relevance Propagation attribution method to handle attention layers, we address these challenges effectively. While partial solutions exist, our method is the first to faithfully and holistically attribute not only input but also latent representations of transformer models with the computational efficiency similar to a single backward pass. Through extensive evaluations against existing methods on LLaMa 2, Mixtral 8x7b, Flan-T5 and vision transformer architectures, we demonstrate that our proposed approach surpasses alternative methods in terms of faithfulness and enables the understanding of latent representations, opening up the door for concept-based explanations. We provide an LRP library at https://github.com/rachtibat/LRP-eXplains-Transformers.

paragraphs: Understanding which parts of a transformer contribute to a prediction is valuable when investigating biased outputs or hallucinations. Attribution methods aim to assign relevance to those contributing parts, but covering an entire transformer faithfully and efficiently is difficult. This paper extends Layer-wise Relevance Propagation so that it can handle attention layers.

The resulting method, AttnLRP, attributes predictions to both model inputs and internal representations. That second capability matters because an explanation can examine intermediate features as well as the information originally supplied to the model. The reported computational cost is similar to a single backward pass, making broad attribution less expensive than a procedure requiring many such computations.

Evaluations span LLaMa 2, Mixtral 8x7b, Flan-T5, and vision transformers. The authors report greater faithfulness than alternative attribution methods and show that the approach enables investigation of latent representations. This opens a route toward explanations based on internal concepts. The contribution is an efficient attribution tool for studying model behavior, rather than a demonstrated remedy for the problematic outputs motivating the work.
summary.tldr: AttnLRP extends relevance propagation through attention to explain transformer inputs and internal representations at roughly backward-pass cost.

title: AttnLRP: Attention-Aware Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Transformers

abstract: The recent surge in contrastive learning has intensified the interest in understanding the generalization of non-pointwise learning paradigms. While information-theoretic analysis achieves remarkable success in characterizing the generalization behavior of learning algorithms, its applicability is largely confined to pointwise learning, with extensions to the simplest pairwise settings remaining unexplored due to the challenges of non-i.i.d losses and dimensionality explosion. In this paper, we develop the first series of information-theoretic bounds extending beyond pointwise scenarios, encompassing pointwise, pairwise, triplet, quadruplet, and higher-order scenarios, all within a unified framework. Specifically, our hypothesis-based bounds elucidate the generalization behavior of iterative and noisy learning algorithms via gradient covariance analysis, and our prediction-based bounds accurately estimate the generalization gap with computationally tractable low-dimensional information metrics. Comprehensive numerical studies then demonstrate the effectiveness of our bounds in capturing the generalization dynamics across diverse learning scenarios.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives evaluate examples in pairs or larger groups instead of assigning a separate loss to each individual example. Understanding generalization in these settings is difficult because the losses are not independent and identically distributed, and the quantities being analyzed can become very high-dimensional. This paper develops a unified information-theoretic treatment of that problem.

The framework covers individual examples, pairs, triplets, quadruplets, and higher-order groupings. It provides two kinds of bounds. Hypothesis-based bounds analyze iterative, noisy learning algorithms through gradient covariance. Prediction-based bounds use low-dimensional information measures to estimate the generalization gap in a computationally tractable way.

These two perspectives connect generalization to both the learning process and the predictions it produces. Numerical studies across diverse learning settings show that the bounds capture generalization dynamics effectively. The contribution broadens the reach of information-theoretic analysis to objectives built from relationships among examples, giving a common framework for settings that are difficult to address through pointwise analysis alone.
summary.tldr: A unified information-theoretic framework bounds generalization for learning objectives involving individual examples, pairs, and larger groups.

title: Towards Generalization beyond Pointwise Learning: A Unified Information-theoretic Perspective

abstract: In this work, we develop a new theory and method for sufficient dimension reduction (SDR) in single-index models, where SDR is a sub-field of supervised dimension reduction based on conditional independence. Our work is primarily motivated by the recent introduction of the Hellinger correlation as a dependency measure. Utilizing this measure, we have developed a method capable of effectively detecting the dimension reduction subspace, complete with theoretical justification. Through extensive numerical experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed method significantly enhances and outperforms existing SDR methods. This improvement is largely attributed to our proposed method’s deeper understanding of data dependencies and the refinement of existing SDR techniques.

paragraphs: Supervised dimension reduction seeks a smaller description of the inputs that preserves information relevant to predicting an outcome. Sufficient dimension reduction formalizes this aim through conditional independence: the reduced representation should account for the predictive relationship. This paper develops a new theory and method for that task in single-index models.

The method builds on Hellinger correlation, a measure of statistical dependence. The authors use it to identify the dimension reduction subspace and provide theoretical justification for doing so. The choice of dependence measure is central because the reduction must retain the relationship between inputs and the outcome, rather than merely find a compact description of the inputs themselves.

Extensive numerical experiments report significant improvements over existing sufficient dimension reduction methods. The authors attribute these gains largely to better characterization of data dependencies and refinements to existing techniques. The contribution combines a theoretically supported subspace detection method with numerical evidence of improved performance, within the single-index modeling setting studied in the paper.
summary.tldr: A Hellinger-correlation method identifies sufficient dimension reduction subspaces in single-index models and outperforms existing methods in numerical experiments.

title: Enhancing Sufficient Dimension Reduction via Hellinger Correlation

abstract: This paper investigates projection-free algorithms for stochastic constrained multi-level optimization. In this context, the objective function is a nested composition of several smooth functions, and the decision set is closed and convex. Existing projection-free algorithms for solving this problem suffer from two limitations: 1) they solely focus on the gradient mapping criterion and fail to match the optimal sample complexities in unconstrained settings; 2) their analysis is exclusively applicable to non-convex functions, without considering convex and strongly convex objectives. To address these issues, we introduce novel projection-free variance reduction algorithms and analyze their complexities under different criteria. For gradient mapping, our complexities improve existing results and match the optimal rates for unconstrained problems. For the widely-used Frank-Wolfe gap criterion, we provide theoretical guarantees that align with those for single-level problems. Additionally, by using a stage-wise adaptation, we further obtain complexities for convex and strongly convex functions. Finally, numerical experiments on different tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems whose objective nests several smooth functions inside one another, with decisions restricted to a closed, convex set. It focuses on stochastic, projection-free methods. Existing methods had weaker sample-complexity results and analyses concentrated on non-convex objectives and a single measure of optimization progress.

The main contribution is a stronger collection of complexity guarantees, showing that nested stochastic objectives can be handled without the previously reported gaps under the stated criteria.
summary.tldr: New projection-free variance-reduction methods strengthen complexity guarantees for nested stochastic optimization across several objective classes and progress criteria.

title: Projection-Free Variance Reduction Methods for Stochastic Constrained Multi-Level Compositional Optimization

abstract: Blind Image Quality Assessment (BIQA) mirrors subjective made by human observers. Generally, humans favor comparing relative qualities over predicting absolute qualities directly. However, current BIQA models focus on mining the "local" context, i.e., the relationship between information among individual images and the absolute quality of the image, ignoring the "global" context of the relative quality contrast among different images in the training data. In this paper, we present the Perceptual Context and Sensitivity BIQA (CSIQA), a novel contrastive learning paradigm that seamlessly integrates "global” and "local” perspectives into the BIQA. Specifically, the CSIQA comprises two primary components: 1) A Quality Context Contrastive Learning module, which is equipped with different contrastive learning strategies to effectively capture potential quality correlations in the global context of the dataset. 2) A Quality-aware Mask Attention Module, which employs the random mask to ensure the consistency with visual local sensitivity, thereby improving the model’s perception of local distortions. Extensive experiments on eight standard BIQA datasets demonstrate the superior performance to the state-of-the-art BIQA methods.

paragraphs: Blind image quality assessment aims to predict perceived image quality. This paper starts from the observation that people often find relative comparisons easier than assigning absolute scores. The authors argue that existing models emphasize information within individual images while underusing quality relationships across different images in the training set.

CSIQA combines two components to address these perspectives together. A Quality Context Contrastive Learning module uses contrastive strategies to capture quality correlations across the dataset. A Quality-aware Mask Attention Module uses random masking to align the model with local visual sensitivity and improve its perception of localized distortions. One component supplies comparative context; the other strengthens attention to image-level evidence of degraded quality.

Experiments on eight standard blind image quality datasets report performance above the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining relationships between images with sensitivity to distortions within images. The approach makes relative quality information part of learning while retaining the local detail needed to assess each individual image.
summary.tldr: CSIQA combines cross-image quality comparisons with masking-based sensitivity to local distortions for better blind image quality assessment.

title: Integrating Global Context Contrast and Local Sensitivity for Blind Image Quality Assessment

abstract: We tackle the common challenge of inter-concept visual confusion in compositional concept generation using text-guided diffusion models (TGDMs). It becomes even more pronounced in the generation of customized concepts, due to the scarcity of user-provided concept visual examples. By revisiting the two major stages leading to the success of TGDMs—1) contrastive image-language pre-training (CLIP) for text encoder that encodes visual semantics, and 2) training TGDM that decodes the textual embeddings into pixels—we point that existing customized generation methods only focus on fine-tuning the second stage while overlooking the first one. To this end, we propose a simple yet effective solution called CLIF: contrastive image-language fine-tuning. Specifically, given a few samples of customized concepts, we obtain non-confusing textual embeddings of a concept by fine-tuning CLIP via contrasting a concept and the over-segmented visual regions of other concepts. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CLIF in preventing the confusion of multi-customized concept generation. Project page: https://clif-official.github.io/clif.

paragraphs: Text-guided diffusion models can visually confuse concepts when generating several together. The problem becomes more pronounced for customized concepts because users provide only a few visual examples. This paper examines the two stages behind generation: encoding visual meaning into text representations and decoding those representations into image pixels.

The authors argue that existing customization methods concentrate on fine-tuning the image-generation stage while overlooking the text encoder. Their method, contrastive image-language fine-tuning, or CLIF, instead fine-tunes CLIP to produce more distinct textual representations. Given a few examples, it contrasts a concept with visual regions obtained by over-segmenting other concepts, helping separate their encoded visual meanings.

Experiments demonstrate that CLIF is effective at preventing confusion when generating multiple customized concepts. The approach matters because it locates part of the problem upstream of pixel generation, in the representations supplied to the diffusion model. Improving those representations gives the generator a clearer distinction between the concepts it is being asked to combine.
summary.tldr: CLIF fine-tunes CLIP to separate customized concept representations, reducing visual confusion when diffusion models generate them together.

title: Non-confusing Generation of Customized Concepts in Diffusion Models

abstract: This paper studies decentralized optimization problem, where the local objective on each node is an average of a finite set of convex functions and the global function is strongly convex. We propose an efficient stochastic variance reduced first-order method that allows the different nodes to establish their stochastic local gradient estimator with different mini-batch sizes per iteration. We prove the upper bound on the computation time of the proposed method contains the dependence on the global condition number, which is sharper than the previous results that only depend on the local condition numbers. Compared with the state-of-the-art methods, we also show that our method requires less local incremental first-order oracle calls and comparable communication cost. We further perform numerical experiments to validate the advantage of our method.

We prove the upper bound on the computation time of the proposed method contains the dependence on the global condition number, which is sharper than the previous results that only depend on the local condition numbers. paragraphs: This paper studies optimization spread across multiple nodes. Each node holds an objective that averages finitely many convex functions, and their combined global objective is strongly convex. The goal is to reduce the computation required at individual nodes while keeping the communication needed for cooperation competitive.

The proposed method uses stochastic gradients with variance reduction, improving the reliability of estimates built from subsets of local functions. It allows different nodes to use different mini-batch sizes in the same iteration. This flexibility is part of a first-order method designed for the decentralized finite-sum setting.

The theoretical computation-time bound depends on the global condition number, giving a sharper result than previous bounds based only on local condition numbers. The method also requires fewer local incremental first-order oracle calls while retaining comparable communication cost relative to state-of-the-art methods. Numerical experiments support its advantage. The result matters because an analysis based on the combined objective can give a more favorable account of difficulty than one governed only by the individual local objectives.
summary.tldr: A decentralized variance-reduced method improves computation bounds through global conditioning while allowing node-specific mini-batch sizes.

title: Decentralized Convex Finite-Sum Optimization with Better Dependence on Condition Numbers

abstract: Despite their groundbreaking performance for many generative modeling tasks, diffusion models have fallen short on discrete data domains such as natural language. Crucially, standard diffusion models rely on the well-established theory of score matching, but efforts to generalize this to discrete structures have not yielded the same empirical gains. In this work, we bridge this gap by proposing score entropy, a novel loss that naturally extends score matching to discrete spaces, integrates seamlessly to build discrete diffusion models, and significantly boosts performance. Experimentally, we test our Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion models (SEDD) on standard language modeling tasks. For comparable model sizes, SEDD beats existing language diffusion paradigms (reducing perplexity by $25$-$75$%) and is competitive with autoregressive models, in particular outperforming GPT-2. Furthermore, compared to autoregressive mdoels, SEDD generates faithful text without requiring distribution annealing techniques like temperature scaling (around $6$-$8\times$ better generative perplexity than un-annealed GPT-2), can trade compute and quality (similar quality with $32\times$ fewer network evaluations), and enables controllable infilling (matching nucleus sampling quality while enabling other strategies besides left to right prompting).

paragraphs: Diffusion models have been less successful on discrete data such as language than on many other generation tasks. The paper attributes a key difficulty to extending score matching, the theory underlying standard diffusion training, to discrete structures. It introduces score entropy, a loss designed to bring that training principle into discrete spaces by estimating distribution ratios.

The resulting Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion models, or SEDD, are evaluated on language modeling. At comparable model sizes, the authors report perplexity reductions of 25–75% against existing language diffusion approaches and competitive performance with autoregressive models, including improvements over GPT-2. Its controllable infilling supports generation arrangements beyond left-to-right prompting and matches nucleus sampling quality in the reported comparison. These findings make the contribution both a discrete diffusion training objective and a demonstration of more flexible language generation.
summary.tldr: SEDD uses a new discrete score-matching loss to improve language diffusion performance while supporting flexible infilling and compute–quality tradeoffs.

title: Discrete Diffusion Modeling by Estimating the Ratios of the Data Distribution

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved notable success in image generation, but they remain highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, which compromise their integrity by producing specific undesirable outputs when presented with a pre-defined trigger. In this paper, we investigate how to protect diffusion models from this dangerous threat. Specifically, we propose TERD, a backdoor defense framework that builds unified modeling for current attacks, which enables us to derive an accessible reversed loss. A trigger reversion strategy is further employed: an initial approximation of the trigger through noise sampled from a prior distribution, followed by refinement through differential multi-step samplers. Additionally, with the reversed trigger, we propose backdoor detection from the noise space, introducing the first backdoor input detection approach for diffusion models and a novel model detection algorithm that calculates the KL divergence between reversed and benign distributions. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TERD secures a 100% True Positive Rate (TPR) and True Negative Rate (TNR) across datasets of varying resolutions. TERD also demonstrates nice adaptability to other Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE)-based models. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-ML/TERD.

paragraphs: Backdoored diffusion models produce specific unwanted outputs when a predefined trigger is present. TERD addresses this threat by building a unified model of current attacks, which the authors use to derive a reversed loss. This supplies a basis for recovering the trigger and detecting backdoor behavior.

Trigger recovery proceeds in two stages. First, the framework obtains an initial approximation using noise sampled from a prior distribution. It then refines that approximation with differential multi-step samplers. The recovered trigger supports detection in noise space, including an input detector and a model detector that measures KL divergence between recovered and benign distributions.

Across evaluations involving datasets at different resolutions, the authors report 100% true positive and true negative rates. They also demonstrate adaptability to other models based on stochastic differential equations. These reported detection rates describe the evaluated cases. The broader contribution is a framework connecting unified attack modeling, trigger reconstruction, and detection at both the input and model levels.
summary.tldr: TERD reconstructs diffusion-model backdoor triggers and uses them for input and model detection, achieving 100% detection rates in the reported evaluations.

title: TERD: A Unified Framework for Safeguarding Diffusion Models Against Backdoors

abstract: Given two weighted graphs $G = (V, E, w_G)$ and $H = (V, F, w_H)$ defined on the same vertex set, the constrained clustering problem seeks to find a subset $S \subset V$ that minimises the cut ratio between $w_G(S, V \setminus S)$ and $w_H(S, V \setminus S)$. In this work, we establish a Cheeger-type inequality that relates the solution of the constrained clustering problem to the spectral properties of $ G$ and $H$. To reduce computational complexity, we utilise the signed Laplacian of $H$, streamlining calculations while maintaining accuracy. By solving a generalised eigenvalue problem, our proposed algorithm achieves notable performance improvements, particularly in challenging scenarios where traditional spectral clustering methods struggle. We demonstrate its practical effectiveness through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering defined by two weighted graphs over the same vertices. A candidate split cuts edges in both graphs, and the objective is to minimize the ratio of the cut weight in the first graph to that in the second. The second graph therefore changes how the quality of a partition is judged.

The authors establish a Cheeger-type inequality connecting the best constrained clustering solution with spectral properties of the two graphs. Such a connection makes matrix-based calculations relevant to the partitioning objective. They use the signed Laplacian of the second graph to reduce computational complexity while maintaining accuracy.

The resulting algorithm solves a generalized eigenvalue problem to obtain a clustering solution. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate practical effectiveness, with notable improvements in difficult settings where traditional spectral clustering struggles. The paper’s contribution combines a theoretical relationship between cuts and spectra with a computational formulation intended to make constrained clustering more effective.
summary.tldr: A Cheeger-type inequality and signed-Laplacian formulation support an efficient spectral algorithm for constrained graph clustering.

title: Signed Laplacians for Constrained Graph Clustering

abstract: Learning diffusion bridge models is easy; making them fast and practical is an art. Diffusion bridge models (DBMs) are a promising extension of diffusion models for applications in image-to-image translation. However, like many modern diffusion and flow models, DBMs suffer from the problem of slow inference. To address it, we propose a novel distillation technique based on the inverse bridge matching formulation and derive the tractable objective to solve it in practice. Unlike previously developed DBM distillation techniques, the proposed method can distill both conditional and unconditional types of DBMs, distill models in a one-step generator, and use only the corrupted images for training. We evaluate our approach for both conditional and unconditional types of bridge matching on a wide set of setups, including super-resolution, JPEG restoration, sketch-to-image, and other tasks, and show that our distillation technique allows us to accelerate the inference of DBMs from 4x to 100x and even provide better generation quality than used teacher model depending on particular setup. We provide the code at https://github.com/ngushchin/IBMD

paragraphs: Diffusion bridge models are promising tools for image-to-image translation, but their slow inference can make them difficult to use in practice. This paper develops a distillation method that transfers a bridge model's behavior into a faster generator. The goal is to preserve useful generation capability while reducing the computation needed for each output.

The method starts from an inverse bridge matching formulation and derives a tractable training objective. It supports both conditional and unconditional bridge models and can distill them into a one-step generator. Another stated capability is training using only corrupted images, broadening the circumstances in which this form of distillation can be applied.

The authors evaluate the approach across tasks including super-resolution, JPEG restoration, and sketch-to-image generation. They report inference speedups ranging from 4 to 100 times. In some setups, the distilled generator also produces better-quality results than its teacher. The quality improvement is explicitly setup-dependent, while the range of evaluations demonstrates the method's applicability to several kinds of bridge-based image translation.
summary.tldr: Inverse bridge matching distills diffusion bridge models into faster generators, reporting 4–100× speedups and sometimes better quality than the teacher.

title: Inverse Bridge Matching Distillation

abstract: Optimal allocation of scarce resources is a common problem for decision makers faced with choosing a limited number of locations for intervention. Spatiotemporal prediction models could make such decisions data-driven. A recent performance metric called fraction of best possible reach (BPR) measures the impact of using a model’s recommended size K subset of sites compared to the best possible top-K in hindsight. We tackle two open problems related to BPR. First, we explore how to rank all sites numerically given a probabilistic model that predicts event counts jointly across sites. Ranking via the per-site mean is suboptimal for BPR. Instead, we offer a better ranking for BPR backed by decision theory. Second, we explorehow to train a probabilistic model’s parameters to maximize BPR. Discrete selection of K sites implies all-zero parameter gradients which prevent standard gradient training. We overcome this barrier via advances in perturbed optimizers. We further suggest a training objective that combines likelihood with a BPR constraint to deliver high-quality top-K rankings as well as good forecasts for all sites. We demonstrate our approach on two where-to-intervene applications: mitigating opioid-related fatal overdoses for public health and monitoring endangered wildlife.

paragraphs: When resources permit intervention at only K locations, a forecast must support a selection decision. This paper studies fraction of best possible reach, or BPR, which compares the impact of the recommended locations with the best selection in hindsight. The authors address both how to rank locations and how to train models for this objective.

For probabilistic models that jointly predict event counts across locations, ranking by each location's mean is suboptimal for BPR. The paper develops a better ranking using decision theory. The proposed solution uses perturbed optimizers to make decision-aware training possible. A further objective combines likelihood with a BPR constraint, seeking useful forecasts across all locations alongside strong top-K choices. Applications concern opioid-related fatal overdose mitigation and endangered-wildlife monitoring. The contribution connects the forecasting objective to the particular resource-allocation measure used to judge decisions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops ranking and training methods that align probabilistic forecasts with the impact of selecting K intervention sites.

title: Decision-aware Training of Spatiotemporal Forecasting Models to Select a Top-K Subset of Sites for Intervention

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) optimizes Traffic Signal Control (TSC) to reduce congestion and emissions, but real-world TSC systems face challenges like adversarial attacks and missing data, leading to incorrect signal decisions and increased congestion. Existing methods, limited to offline data predictions, address only one issue and fail to meet TSC’s dynamic, real-time needs. We propose RobustLight, a novel framework with an enhanced, plug-and-play diffusion model to improve TSC robustness against noise, missing data, and complex patterns by restoring attacked data. RobustLight integrates two algorithms to recover original data states without altering existing TSC platforms. Using a dynamic state infilling algorithm, it trains the diffusion model online. Experiments on real-world datasets show RobustLight improves recovery performance by up to 50.43% compared to baseline scenarios. It effectively counters diverse adversarial attacks and missing data. The relevant datasets and code are available at Github.
