paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning traffic controllers depend on accurate information about current traffic conditions. Attacks, noise, and missing observations can distort that information and lead to poor signal decisions. The paper argues that existing recovery approaches are too restricted by offline prediction and often address only one failure type, leaving them poorly matched to dynamic traffic-control requirements.

RobustLight adds an enhanced diffusion model that restores corrupted traffic data. The framework integrates two recovery algorithms and is designed to work with existing traffic-signal platforms without changing them. A dynamic state infilling algorithm supports online training of the diffusion model, allowing the recovery process to operate within the changing conditions of the control setting.

Experiments using real-world datasets report recovery-performance improvements of up to 50.43% relative to baseline scenarios. The framework also counters diverse adversarial attacks and missing data in the evaluations. That figure concerns recovery performance, and its maximum wording matters: the reported improvement reaches that level in the tested scenarios rather than establishing a uniform gain for every condition.
summary.tldr: RobustLight uses online diffusion-based data restoration to improve traffic-signal control robustness to attacks, noise, and missing observations.

title: RobustLight: Improving Robustness via Diffusion Reinforcement Learning for Traffic Signal Control

abstract: Activation sparsity denotes the existence of substantial weakly-contributed neurons within feed-forward networks of large language models (LLMs), providing wide potential benefits such as computation acceleration. However, existing works lack thorough quantitative studies on this useful property, in terms of both its measurement and influential factors. In this paper, we address three underexplored research questions: (1) How can activation sparsity be measured more accurately? (2) How is activation sparsity affected by the model architecture and training process? (3) How can we build a more sparsely activated and efficient LLM? Specifically, we develop a generalizable and performance-friendly metric, named CETT-PPL-1%, to measure activation sparsity. Based on CETT-PPL-1%, we quantitatively study the influence of various factors and observe several important phenomena, such as the convergent power-law relationship between sparsity and training data amount, the higher competence of ReLU activation than mainstream SiLU activation, the potential sparsity merit of a small width-depth ratio, and the scale insensitivity of activation sparsity. Finally, we provide implications for building sparse and effective LLMs, and demonstrate the reliability of our findings by training a 2.4B model with a sparsity ratio of 93.52%, showing 4.1$\times$ speedup compared with its dense version. The codes and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/thunlp/SparsingLaw/.

paragraphs: Many neurons in a language model's feed-forward networks contribute only weakly, creating opportunities to avoid unnecessary computation. This paper studies activation sparsity quantitatively: how to measure it, how architecture and training affect it, and how those findings can guide the construction of more efficient models. It introduces CETT-PPL-1% as a generalizable, performance-friendly measurement.

Using that metric, the authors observe a convergent power-law relationship between sparsity and the amount of training data. They also find greater sparsity capability with ReLU than with the widely used SiLU activation, potential benefits from a smaller width-to-depth ratio, and insensitivity of activation sparsity to model scale. These are reported observations from the study.

The authors apply the findings to train a 2.4-billion-parameter model with a sparsity ratio of 93.52%. It achieves a 4.1-fold speedup relative to its dense version. This demonstration connects the measurement and architectural analysis to practical acceleration, showing how deliberate choices during model development can support highly sparse activation.
summary.tldr: A quantitative study of activation sparsity guides a 2.4-billion-parameter model with 93.52% sparsity and a 4.1-fold speedup over its dense version.

title: Sparsing Law: Towards Large Language Models with Greater Activation Sparsity

abstract: Evolutionary neural architecture search (ENAS) is a key part of evolutionary machine learning, which commonly utilizes evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to automatically design high-performing deep neural architectures. During past years, various ENAS methods have been proposed with exceptional performance. However, the theory research of ENAS is still in the infant. In this work, we step for the runtime analysis, which is an essential theory aspect of EAs, of ENAS upon multiclass classification problems. Specifically, we first propose a benchmark to lay the groundwork for the analysis. Furthermore, we design a two-level search space, making it suitable for multiclass classification problems and consistent with the common settings of ENAS. Based on both designs, we consider (1+1)-ENAS algorithms with one-bit and bit-wise mutations, and analyze their upper and lower bounds on the expected runtime. We prove that the algorithm using both mutations can find the optimum with the expected runtime upper bound of $O(rM\ln{rM})$ and lower bound of $\Omega(rM\ln{M})$. This suggests that a simple one-bit mutation may be greatly considered, given that most state-of-the-art ENAS methods are laboriously designed with the bit-wise mutation. Empirical studies also support our theoretical proof.

paragraphs: Evolutionary neural architecture search uses evolutionary algorithms to design neural networks automatically. Although many methods perform well empirically, their theoretical behavior is less developed. This paper studies expected runtime for multiclass classification, asking how long particular evolutionary search procedures take to reach an optimum in a constructed analytical setting.

The authors first introduce a benchmark and a two-level search space designed for multiclass classification and aligned with common evolutionary architecture-search settings. They then analyze (1+1)-ENAS algorithms using one-bit and bit-wise mutations. Establishing both upper and lower runtime bounds helps characterize the search effort instead of relying only on observed experimental performance.

Within the paper’s setup and notation, the reported expected-runtime bounds are O(rM ln(rM)) above and Ω(rM ln M) below for the studied mutation approaches. These results motivate considering simple one-bit mutation, despite the prevalence of more elaborate bit-wise mutation designs. Empirical studies support the theoretical analysis. The contribution is a tractable foundation for comparing mutation choices, with the runtime conclusions attached to the benchmark and search space developed.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes expected-runtime bounds for evolutionary architecture search on a multiclass benchmark, supporting consideration of simple one-bit mutation.

title: Runtime Analysis of Evolutionary NAS for Multiclass Classification

abstract: This paper proposes a novel concept of natural perturbations for black-box training of neural networks by zeroth-order optimization. When a neural network is implemented directly in hardware, training its parameters by backpropagation ends up with an inaccurate result due to the lack of detailed internal information. We instead employ zeroth-order optimization, where the sampling of parameter perturbations is of great importance. The sampling strategy we propose maximizes the entropy of perturbations with a regularization that the probability distribution conditioned by the neural network does not change drastically, by inheriting the concept of natural gradient. Experimental results show the superiority of our proposal on diverse datasets, tasks, and architectures.

We instead employ zeroth-order optimization, where the sampling of parameter perturbations is of great importance. Experimental results show the superiority of our proposal on diverse datasets, tasks, and architectures.

paragraphs: Training a neural network implemented directly in hardware can be difficult when its internal behavior is not known in sufficient detail. The paper identifies this lack of information as a source of inaccurate backpropagation results. It instead studies black-box training through zeroth-order optimization, where the choice of parameter perturbations becomes especially important.

The proposed natural perturbations adapt an idea from the natural gradient. Their sampling distribution maximizes perturbation entropy while regularizing how much the network’s conditional probability distribution changes. This combines broad exploration of parameter changes with a preference against changes that drastically alter the model’s probabilistic behavior. The sampling rule is the central contribution.

Experiments across diverse datasets, tasks, and architectures show superior performance for the proposed approach. These findings support the value of considering the network’s resulting probability distribution when choosing perturbations. The method addresses how to make black-box parameter exploration more effective in the hardware-motivated setting where detailed internal information is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Natural perturbations improve black-box neural-network training by balancing diverse parameter exploration with controlled changes in model behavior.

title: Natural Perturbations for Black-box Training of Neural Networks by Zeroth-Order Optimization

abstract: Scalable sampling of molecular states in thermodynamic equilibrium is a long-standing challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators tackle this problem by pairing normalizing flows with importance sampling to obtain uncorrelated samples under the target distribution. In this paper, we extend the Boltzmann generator framework with two key contributions, denoting our framework Sequential Boltzmann Generators (SBG). The first is a highly efficient Transformer-based normalizing flow operating directly on all-atom Cartesian coordinates. In contrast to the equivariant continuous flows of prior methods, we leverage exactly invertible non-equivariant architectures which are highly efficient during both sample generation and likelihood evaluation. This efficiency unlocks more sophisticated inference strategies beyond standard importance sampling. In particular, we perform inference-time scaling of flow samples using a continuous-time variant of sequential Monte Carlo, in which flow samples are transported towards the target distribution with annealed Langevin dynamics. SBG achieves state-of-the-art performance w.r.t. all metrics on peptide systems, demonstrating the first equilibrium sampling in Cartesian coordinates of tri-, tetra- and hexa-peptides that were thus far intractable for prior Boltzmann generators.

paragraphs: Sampling molecular states at thermodynamic equilibrium requires producing configurations with the right target distribution. Boltzmann generators approach this through normalizing flows and importance sampling. Sequential Boltzmann Generators extend that framework with a faster flow architecture and a more elaborate inference procedure, aiming to make harder molecular systems tractable.

The flow uses a Transformer and works directly with all-atom Cartesian coordinates. Its architecture is exactly invertible and non-equivariant, providing efficient sample generation and likelihood evaluation. That efficiency makes room for additional work during inference. A continuous-time sequential Monte Carlo procedure transports flow-generated samples toward the target distribution using annealed Langevin dynamics.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated metrics on peptide systems. They also report the first equilibrium sampling in Cartesian coordinates for tri-, tetra-, and hexa-peptides that previous Boltzmann generators could not handle. The result illustrates how cheaper generation and likelihood computation can support stronger downstream sampling procedures, expanding the molecular systems accessible within this framework.
summary.tldr: Sequential Boltzmann Generators combine an efficient invertible Transformer flow with sequential Monte Carlo to scale equilibrium sampling of peptides.

title: Scalable Equilibrium Sampling with Sequential Boltzmann Generators

abstract: Federated Active Learning (FAL) aims to learn an effective global model, while minimizing label queries. Owing to privacy requirements, it is challenging to design effective active data selection schemes due to the lack of cross-client query information. In this paper, we bridge this important gap by proposing the Federated Active data selection by LEverage score sampling (FALE) method. It is designed for regression tasks in the presence of non-i.i.d. client data to enable the server to select data globally in a privacy-preserving manner. Based on FedSVD, FALE aims to estimate the utility of unlabeled data and perform data selection via leverage score sampling. Besides, a secure model learning framework is designed for federated regression tasks to exploit supervision. FALE can operate without requiring an initial labeled set and select the instances in a single pass, significantly reducing communication overhead. Theoretical analyze establishes the query complexity for FALE to achieve constant factor approximation and relative error approximation. Extensive experiments on 11 benchmark datasets demonstrate significant improvements of FALE over existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Federated active learning aims to train a shared model while requesting as few labels as possible. Selecting useful examples across clients is difficult when privacy requirements prevent access to cross-client query information. FALE addresses this problem for regression tasks in which clients have different data distributions, so local selection decisions must account for a heterogeneous overall dataset.

The method builds on FedSVD to estimate the usefulness of unlabeled examples and select them through leverage score sampling. Its design lets the server coordinate global selection in a privacy-preserving way. The authors also introduce a secure regression-learning framework to use the resulting supervision. FALE needs no initially labeled dataset and selects examples in one pass, reducing communication overhead.

The theoretical analysis establishes label-query requirements for constant-factor and relative-error approximation guarantees. Experiments on 11 benchmark datasets report significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. The combined contribution is a selection procedure with approximation analysis and a practical communication advantage, developed specifically for federated regression with non-identically distributed client data.
summary.tldr: FALE uses leverage score sampling to select useful regression labels across heterogeneous clients in a single privacy-preserving pass.

title: Efficient Heterogeneity-Aware Federated Active Data Selection

abstract: Food systems are responsible for a third of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions. We investigate what Large Language Models (LLMs) can contribute to reducing the environmental impacts of food production. We define a typology of design and prediction tasks based on the sustainable food literature and collaboration with domain experts, and evaluate six LLMs on four tasks in our typology. For example, for a sustainable protein design task, food science experts estimated that collaboration with an LLM can reduce time spent by 45% on average, compared to 22% for collaboration with another expert human food scientist. However, for a sustainable menu design task, LLMs produce suboptimal solutions when instructed to consider both human satisfaction and climate impacts. We propose a general framework for integrating LLMs with combinatorial optimization to improve reasoning capabilities. Our approach decreases emissions of food choices by 79% in a hypothetical restaurant while maintaining participants’ satisfaction with their set of choices. Our results demonstrate LLMs’ potential, supported by optimization techniques, to accelerate sustainable food development and adoption.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how language models might help reduce the environmental impact of food systems. The authors develop a typology of design and prediction tasks using sustainable-food research and domain-expert input, then evaluate six language models on four tasks. This task-based approach examines where assistance is useful and where difficult tradeoffs remain.

For sustainable protein design, food scientists estimate that collaboration with a language model could reduce time spent by 45% on average, compared with 22% for collaboration with another expert. These are expert estimates. For menu design, however, language models produce suboptimal solutions when asked to balance human satisfaction with climate impact.

The authors respond with a framework combining language models and combinatorial optimization. In a hypothetical restaurant setting, their approach reduces emissions associated with food choices by 79% while maintaining participants’ satisfaction with their available choices. The results indicate potential for language models to assist sustainable food development, with optimization providing support when choices require balancing competing objectives. The emissions finding retains its hypothetical-restaurant scope.
summary.tldr: Language models show promise for sustainable food design, while combining them with optimization improves menu tradeoffs in a hypothetical restaurant setting.

title: What can large language models do for sustainable food?

abstract: Model merging aims to integrate the strengths of multiple fine-tuned models into a unified model while preserving task-specific capabilities. Existing methods, represented by task arithmetic, are typically classified into global- and local-aware methods. However, global-aware methods inevitably cause parameter interference, while local-aware methods struggle to maintain the effectiveness of task-specific details in the merged model. To address these limitations, we propose a Consensus Aware Localized Merging (CALM) method which incorporates localized information aligned with global task consensus, ensuring its effectiveness post-merging. CALM consists of three key components: (1) class-balanced entropy minimization sampling, providing a more flexible and reliable way to leverage unsupervised data; (2) an efficient-aware framework, selecting a small set of tasks for sequential merging with high scalability; (3) a consensus-aware mask optimization, aligning localized binary masks with global task consensus and merging them conflict-free. Experiments demonstrate the superiority and robustness of our CALM, significantly outperforming existing methods and achieving performance close to traditional MTL.

paragraphs: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models into one model while trying to retain their individual task capabilities. The paper identifies a tension between two approaches: global merging can create interference between parameters, while localized merging can lose the usefulness of task-specific details. CALM addresses this tension by aligning local merging decisions with agreement across tasks.

The method has three parts. Class-balanced entropy minimization sampling uses unlabeled data to support merging decisions. An efficiency-oriented framework chooses a small set of tasks for sequential merging, supporting scalability. Finally, mask optimization aligns localized binary masks with global task consensus, aiming to combine their contributions without conflicts.

The central idea is that a useful local contribution should remain compatible with the combined model's broader task behavior. Experiments report that CALM significantly outperforms existing merging methods, shows robustness, and approaches traditional multi-task learning performance. The findings support consensus-guided local selection as a way to preserve specialized capabilities when assembling a unified model.
summary.tldr: CALM aligns local model-merging decisions with agreement across tasks to reduce interference and preserve task-specific capabilities.

title: CALM: Consensus-Aware Localized Merging for Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Understanding human mental states—such as intentions and desires—is crucial for natural AI-human collaboration. However, this is challenging because human actions occur irregularly over time, and the underlying mental states that drive these actions are unobserved. To tackle this, we propose a novel framework that combines a logic-informed temporal point process (TPP) with amortized variational Expectation-Maximization (EM). Our key innovation is integrating logic rules as priors to guide the TPP’s intensity function, allowing the model to capture the interplay between actions and mental events while reducing dependence on large datasets. To handle the intractability of mental state inference, we introduce a discrete-time renewal process to approximate the posterior. By jointly optimizing model parameters, logic rules, and inference networks, our approach infers entire mental event sequences and adaptively predicts future actions. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that our method outperforms existing approaches in accurately inferring mental states and predicting actions, demonstrating its effectiveness in modeling human cognitive processes.

paragraphs: Inferring intentions and desires from behavior is difficult because actions happen at irregular times and the mental events behind them are unobserved. This paper models both the timing of actions and their relationship to hidden mental events. Its goal is to recover sequences of those events while predicting how a person may act next.

The framework combines a temporal point process with logic rules used as prior guidance. The rules influence the process's intensity function, which describes when events are likely to occur. This gives the model structured guidance about relationships between actions and mental events and reduces its dependence on large datasets. Learning uses amortized variational Expectation-Maximization to jointly optimize the model, logic rules, and inference networks.

Because directly inferring the hidden mental states is intractable, the method approximates their posterior distribution with a discrete-time renewal process. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report better mental-state inference and action prediction than existing approaches. The contribution is a combined account of irregular timing, logical structure, and hidden event sequences for modeling human behavior.
summary.tldr: The framework combines logical guidance and temporal event modeling to infer hidden mental-event sequences and predict actions.

title: Evolving Minds: Logic-Informed Inference from Temporal Action Patterns

abstract: An efficient attention implementation is essential for large models due to its quadratic time complexity. Fortunately, attention commonly exhibits sparsity, i.e., many values in the attention map are near zero, allowing for the omission of corresponding computations. Many studies have utilized the sparse pattern to accelerate attention. However, most existing works focus on optimizing attention within specific models by exploiting certain sparse patterns of the attention map. A universal sparse attention that guarantees both the speedup and end-to-end performance of diverse models remains elusive. In this paper, we propose SpargeAttn, a universal sparse and quantized attention for any model. Our method uses a two-stage online filter: in the first stage, we rapidly and accurately predict the attention map, enabling the skip of some matrix multiplications in attention. In the second stage, we design an online softmax-aware filter that incurs no extra overhead and further skips some matrix multiplications. Experiments show that our method significantly accelerates diverse models, including language, image, and video generation, without sacrificing end-to-end metrics.

paragraphs: Attention is expensive because its computation grows quadratically, even though many entries in an attention map are close to zero. Those small values create opportunities to omit work. Existing sparse methods often depend on patterns specific to particular models, motivating a more broadly applicable way to find computations that can be skipped.

SpargeAttn combines sparse and quantized attention with two filtering stages during computation. The first rapidly predicts the attention map and uses that prediction to skip some matrix multiplications. The second applies a softmax-aware online filter to skip additional multiplications without extra filtering overhead. The method is training-free, so its acceleration does not depend on retraining the model.

Experiments demonstrate significant acceleration across language, image-generation, and video-generation models without sacrificing the reported end-to-end metrics. This supports the method’s applicability across diverse model types. The key contribution is a shared filtering mechanism that identifies opportunities to reduce attention computation, with the practical performance claim grounded in the models evaluated.
summary.tldr: SpargeAttn uses two training-free filters to skip attention computations, accelerating diverse evaluated models without degrading end-to-end metrics.

title: SpargeAttention: Accurate and Training-free Sparse Attention Accelerating Any Model Inference

abstract: AI for software engineering has made remarkable progress, becoming a notable success within generative AI. Despite this, achieving fully automated software engineering is still a significant challenge, requiring research efforts across both academia and industry. In this position paper, our goal is threefold. First, we provide a taxonomy of measures and tasks to categorize work towards AI software engineering. Second, we outline the key bottlenecks permeating today's approaches. Finally, we highlight promising paths towards making progress on these bottlenecks to guide future research in this rapidly maturing field.

paragraphs: This position paper takes stock of AI for software engineering as an area with substantial progress and substantial unfinished work. The authors describe it as a prominent success of generative AI, while emphasizing that fully automated software engineering remains difficult. They frame further progress as a research challenge shared by academic and industrial communities.

The paper first supplies a taxonomy of tasks and measures. This provides an organizing structure for categorizing research according to the work being addressed and how progress is assessed. The authors then identify bottlenecks that run through current approaches, placing these obstacles within a broader account of what the field still needs to accomplish.

Finally, the paper highlights promising research directions aimed at those bottlenecks. Its contribution is therefore a map linking categories of work, persistent obstacles, and possible routes forward. The distinction between demonstrated progress and full automation is central: success within AI-assisted software engineering does not, in the authors’ assessment, mean the larger goal has already been reached.
summary.tldr: The paper organizes AI software-engineering research around tasks, evaluation measures, bottlenecks, and directions toward fuller automation.

title: Position: Future Research and Challenges Remain Towards AI for Software Engineering

abstract: Designing sampling algorithms for multimodal targets that remain stable under refinement of the finite-dimensional approximation of an underlying function-space problem is a central challenge. Annealed Langevin dynamics (ALD) is a natural alternative to classical Langevin in this context, since it is often observed to improve exploration across modes. Yet a gap remains between its empirical success and existing theory: under which conditions can ALD be guaranteed to remain stable across dimensions? In this paper, we bridge this gap by providing a uniform-in-dimension analysis of continuous-time ALD for Gaussian-mixture targets. Along an explicit annealing path obtained by gradually removing Gaussian smoothing from the target, we identify spectral conditions linking the smoothing covariance to the component covariances under which ALD achieves a prescribed accuracy in Kullback-Leibler divergence within a dimension-uniform time horizon. We then establish stability in a perturbative regime with imperfect initialization and approximate scores. Under a misspecified-mixture score model, we show that preconditioning ALD with an operator whose spectrum decays sufficiently fast prevents error terms from accumulating across coordinates and thereby preserves dimension-uniform control.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution with several separated regions of high probability becomes especially challenging when adding coordinates refines an underlying function-space model. An algorithm should ideally remain controlled as that approximation grows. This paper investigates when continuous-time annealed Langevin dynamics can achieve such stability for targets that are mixtures of Gaussians.

The analysis follows an explicit path that gradually removes Gaussian smoothing from the target distribution. The authors identify spectral conditions connecting the smoothing covariance with the covariances of the mixture components. Under those conditions, the process reaches a prescribed Kullback–Leibler divergence accuracy within a time horizon that is uniform across dimensions. The result gives conditions for dimension-independent control rather than an unconditional guarantee for multimodal targets.

The paper also analyzes a perturbative setting with imperfect initialization and approximate scores. For a particular misspecified-mixture score model, a preconditioning operator with sufficiently fast spectral decay prevents coordinatewise errors from accumulating. This explains how appropriately chosen preconditioning can preserve the dimension-uniform guarantee despite those approximation errors.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditions under which continuous-time annealed Langevin sampling of Gaussian mixtures maintains accuracy uniformly across dimensions.

title: Dimension-Free Multimodal Sampling via Preconditioned Annealed Langevin Dynamics

abstract: AI model hubs provide access to a rapidly growing collection of powerful pre-trained models, enabling off-the-shelf mixture-of-experts systems with different routing strategies. However, this rapid growth poses two fundamental challenges: scaling model selection across thousands of experts and continually updating routing mechanisms as new models and tasks are introduced. In this paper, we formalise this setting as Continual Model Routing (CMR) and propose CMRBench, a new large-scale benchmark simulating realistic hub expansion and including over 2,000 candidate models. Finally, we introduce CARvE, a contrastive embedding approach for efficient continual model routing via domain-stratified coreset replay and checkpoint-based anchoring. Extensive empirical results and ablations show that CARvE significantly outperforms zero-shot retrieval, fine-tuning, and adapter-merging baselines in model, family, and domain-level accuracy.

paragraphs: A model hub can supply many pretrained experts, but using that collection requires deciding which model suits a task. This becomes harder as the hub grows: selection must scale across thousands of candidates, and the routing mechanism must keep adapting as new models and tasks arrive.

The paper formalizes this changing setting as Continual Model Routing and introduces CMRBench to evaluate it. The benchmark simulates hub expansion and includes more than 2,000 candidate models. This makes ongoing adaptation part of the evaluation, alongside the ability to select suitable models from a large collection.

The proposed method, CARvE, learns contrastive embeddings for routing. It combines replay of a compact selection organized by domain with anchoring based on checkpoints. These mechanisms support learning as the routing setting changes. Experiments and ablations show significant improvements over zero-shot retrieval, fine-tuning, and adapter-merging baselines in accuracy at the individual-model, model-family, and domain levels. The findings support studying routing as a continuing learning problem.
summary.tldr: CARvE improves continual model selection as hubs expand, evaluated on a new benchmark containing over 2,000 candidate models.

title: Continual Model Routing in Evolving Model Hubs

abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values typically relies on post-training or inference-time steering that directly manipulates the backbone’s parameters or representation space. However, a critical gap exists: the model’s residual stream is highly dynamic, in which values exist as fragile, low-dimensional properties, inherently incompatible with the stability required for consistent value expression. In this paper, we propose the Stable Value Guidance Transformer (SVGT), which addresses this gap through an independent value module incorporating two key designs: (1) independent value modeling, maintaining normative representations in a dedicated value space isolated from the backbone, and (2) explicit behavioral guidance, transducing these stable signals into learnable latent Bridge Tokens. These tokens serve as dynamic value anchors to explicitly steer the generative trajectory, ensuring robust adherence across diverse contexts without disrupting the backbone’s internal representations. Experiments across multiple backbones and safety benchmarks show that SVGT generally reduces harmful scores by over 70% while maintaining generation fluency, demonstrating the efficacy of architecturally grounded value modeling.

paragraphs: This paper examines architectural support for consistent value alignment in language models. The authors argue that value representations are fragile, low-dimensional properties within a rapidly changing residual stream. Steering values directly through that stream therefore faces a mismatch between dynamic internal processing and the stability needed for consistent behavior.

The Stable Value Guidance Transformer introduces an independent value module. It maintains normative representations in a dedicated space separated from the backbone, then translates those signals into learnable latent Bridge Tokens. These tokens guide the generation trajectory, providing an explicit route from the independent value representation to the model’s behavior without disrupting the backbone’s internal representations.

Across multiple backbones and safety benchmarks, SVGT generally reduces harmful scores by more than 70% while preserving generation fluency. These results support independent value modeling as an effective architectural approach in the evaluated settings. The reported reduction is a qualified empirical finding, demonstrating improved guidance rather than establishing universal adherence to human values.
summary.tldr: SVGT uses an independent value module and Bridge Tokens to reduce harmful outputs while maintaining fluency in reported evaluations.

title: Toward Stable Value Alignment: Introducing Independent Modules for Consistent Value Guidance

abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate content that is fluent yet unsupported by the image, limiting their reliability in real-world deployment. We show that a key failure mode arises from route competition: even when visual tokens receive attention, the final token decision can be dominated by the textual pathway, causing the decoder to follow linguistic priors over visual evidence. To mitigate this, we propose a training-free, decision-aligned intervention that decomposes each attention head into a visual route and a text route, and estimates their token-level effects using an efficient one-forward/one-gradient approximation. These estimates reveal route conflict within heads and identify prior-dominant ones, enabling selective suppression of only the text route while keeping the visual route intact. Across five benchmarks spanning discriminative and generative settings, our method consistently reduces hallucination-related errors across models with limited impact on overall multimodal performance, while incurring a modest inference-time overhead.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can attend to an image and still generate claims unsupported by it. This paper identifies route competition as a key failure mode: the textual pathway can dominate the final token decision even when visual tokens receive attention. Consequently, observing visual attention alone does not establish that the image determined the answer.

The proposed intervention separates each attention head into visual and text routes. An efficient approximation using one forward pass and one gradient estimates their effects on individual token decisions. Those estimates expose conflicts between routes and identify heads dominated by linguistic priors. The method then selectively suppresses the text route in those heads while leaving the visual route intact.

This intervention requires no training and acts during inference. Across five benchmarks covering discriminative and generative tasks, it consistently reduces hallucination-related errors across models, with limited effects on overall multimodal performance and modest inference overhead. The findings support targeting how text and visual evidence influence the actual decision, making the intervention more selective than suppressing an entire attention head.
summary.tldr: A training-free intervention reduces visual hallucinations by selectively suppressing text pathways that overpower image evidence during token decisions.

title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via Causal Route Gating

abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) seek transferable representations across graph domains but are limited by structural heterogeneity and incompatible node feature spaces. We propose Structure-Centric Graph Foundation Models (SCGFM), which treat graph topology as the primary source of transferable knowledge. Modeling graphs as metric measure spaces, SCGFM introduces learnable geometric bases that define a shared structural coordinate system. Graphs are aligned to these bases via Gromov–Wasserstein distances, yielding structure-aligned latent representations that accommodate heterogeneous graph topologies. To address feature incompatibility, SCGFM employs a structure-aware feature re-encoding mechanism that unifies node representations without assuming a fixed feature dimensionality or requiring dataset-specific preprocessing. Experiments on graph- and node-level tasks demonstrate strong in-domain and cross-domain generalization, outperforming existing GFM approaches.

paragraphs: Transferring a graph model between domains is difficult when graphs differ both in connection patterns and in the features attached to nodes. SCGFM makes topology the main source of transferable knowledge. Its goal is to create a shared representation of structure while accommodating incompatible node-feature spaces.

The method treats graphs as metric measure spaces and learns geometric bases that serve as a common structural coordinate system. It aligns graphs to these bases using Gromov–Wasserstein distances, producing latent representations organized around structural correspondence. This gives heterogeneous graph topologies a shared reference through which their representations can be related.

A structure-aware re-encoding mechanism also unifies node representations without requiring a fixed input-feature dimension or dataset-specific preprocessing. Experiments on both node-level and graph-level tasks report strong generalization within and across domains, outperforming existing graph foundation models. The findings support using structural alignment and feature re-encoding together: a common topology-based representation handles differences in connectivity, while the feature mechanism addresses differences in what each dataset records about its nodes.
summary.tldr: SCGFM aligns graphs to learned geometric bases and re-encodes node features to transfer knowledge across structurally different graph domains.

title: Structure-Centric Graph Foundation Model via Geometric Bases

abstract: Infrared and visible image fusion aims to integrate complementary modalities, while existing Euclidean methods impose rigid distance metrics that distort multi-modal interactions and parent-to-child semantic hierarchies. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a text-driven fusion framework empowered by hyperbolic manifold learning. During training, BLIP-extracted text prompts serve as topological anchors within the hyperbolic space, guiding vision-attribute alignment through hyperbolic embeddings that naturally accommodate varying semantic granularities. By exploiting the exponential volume growth dictated by the Poincaré ball’s negative curvature, this approach seamlessly embeds hierarchical trees to encode coarse-to-fine semantics without metric saturation, while the vast peripheral space prevents texture distortion during cross-modal fusion. At inference, the fusion process autonomously adapts to input content using the learned text-attribute priors, completely eliminating the need for textual input. Experimental results show our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on benchmark datasets, with code available at https://github.com/Shaoyun2023/TEDFusion.

paragraphs: Infrared and visible images contain complementary information, but combining them requires preserving both texture and semantic relationships. This paper argues that Euclidean distance structures can distort interactions between modalities and hierarchies from broad scene concepts to detailed attributes. It develops a text-guided fusion framework in hyperbolic space.

During training, text prompts extracted with BLIP act as anchors that align visual attributes within hyperbolic embeddings. The Poincaré ball’s negative curvature provides exponentially growing space, which supports hierarchical structures spanning coarse and fine semantic levels. The authors use this geometry to avoid saturation of semantic distances and to preserve texture during fusion across modalities.

At inference, the method uses the text–attribute relationships learned during training to adapt fusion to the image content. It therefore requires no textual input when producing a fused image. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art approaches on benchmark datasets. The contribution combines language-guided training with a geometry designed for hierarchical relationships, while keeping the deployed fusion process driven by the input images.
summary.tldr: Text-guided hyperbolic embeddings improve infrared–visible image fusion, with learned scene adaptation requiring no text at inference.

title: Text-Driven Fusion for Infrared and Visible Images: Achieving Image Scene Adaptation on Hyperbolic Space

abstract: This work demonstrates how increasing the number of neurons in a network without increasing its total number of non-zero parameters improves performance. We show that this gain corresponds with a decrease in interference between multiple features that would otherwise share the same neurons. On symbolic Boolean tasks, splitting each neuron into sparser sub-neurons with knowledge of the clauses systematically reduces polysemanticity metrics and yields higher task accuracy. Notably, even random splits of neuron weights approximate these gains, indicating that reduced collisions, not precise assignment, are a primary driver. Consistent with the superposition hypothesis, the benefits of this framework grow with increasing interference: when polysemantic load is high, accuracy improvements are the largest. Transferring these insights to more realistic models, including classifiers over CLIP embeddings, convolutional neural networks, and deeper multilayer networks, we find that widening networks while maintaining a constant non-zero parameter count consistently increases accuracy. These results identify an interpretability-grounded mechanism to leverage width against superposition, improving performance without increasing the number of non-zero parameters. Such a direction is well matched to modern accelerators, where memory movement of non-zero parameters, rather than raw compute, is often a dominant bottleneck.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a network can benefit from more neurons while keeping the same number of nonzero parameters. The proposed explanation concerns interference: when several features share neurons, they can compete within the same representation. Spreading the available weights across more, sparser neurons can reduce those collisions without increasing the count of active weights.

On symbolic Boolean tasks, the authors split neurons into sparse sub-neurons using knowledge of the task’s clauses. This lowers measures of polysemanticity and improves accuracy. Random weight splits approximate these gains, suggesting that reducing collisions is a primary driver rather than requiring a precise feature-to-neuron assignment. The benefits are largest when the original representations have high interference.

The authors also find accuracy improvements in classifiers over CLIP embeddings, convolutional networks, and deeper multilayer networks under a fixed nonzero parameter budget. These findings connect representation interpretability with architectural performance. The paper further argues that this direction suits accelerators where moving nonzero parameters through memory is often a major bottleneck, without claiming that the accuracy results themselves establish hardware speedups.
summary.tldr: Widening networks while holding the number of nonzero parameters fixed improves accuracy in the studied models, with evidence linking the gains to reduced feature interference.

title: Expand Neurons, Not Parameters

abstract: Training large language models via self-play often suffers from a persistent iteration-collapse, where performance initially improves but subsequently regresses as training iterations increase. We analyze this phenomenon as arising from cross-iteration degeneration, where the task-generation distribution becomes increasingly confined to a narrow subset of familiar (seen) problems, weakening the effective learning signal and destabilizing training. To address this issue, we propose a plug-in approach that augments existing self-play pipelines with a one-class novelty reward. A Seen Detector trained on a historical buffer of previously used training problems identifies in-support instances and discourages redundant generation by the questioner, thereby steering exploration toward under-explored yet learnable regions. Experimental results show that the proposed method mitigates iteration-collapse during iterative training and yields consistent improvements.

paragraphs: Language models trained through self-play can improve initially and then lose performance as training continues. This paper analyzes that pattern as degeneration across iterations: the system generating training tasks increasingly concentrates on familiar problems. As the task distribution narrows, the learning signal becomes less useful and training becomes less stable.

The proposed approach adds a one-class novelty reward to an existing self-play pipeline. A Seen Detector learns from a historical buffer of previously used problems and identifies new candidates that fall within that familiar distribution. The reward discourages the question-generating model from repeatedly producing such problems, directing exploration toward less explored regions that remain learnable.

Experiments show that this addition mitigates iteration-collapse and produces consistent improvements during iterative training. The intervention acts on which problems the system generates, making the evolving training distribution an explicit part of stabilization. Its stated benefit is reducing the observed collapse rather than guaranteeing that every self-play process will improve indefinitely.
summary.tldr: OCNR rewards less familiar training problems to reduce task-distribution narrowing and mitigate performance collapse during language-model self-play.

title: OCNR: Stabilizing Self-Play by Mitigating Iteration-Collapse With One-Class Novelty Rewards

abstract: Despite their impressive performance on a wide variety of tasks, modern language models remain susceptible to distribution shifts, exhibiting brittle behavior when evaluated on data that differs in distribution from their training data. In this paper, we describe how distribution shifts in language models can be separated into observable and unobservable components, and we discuss how established approaches for dealing with distribution shift address only the former. Importantly, we identify that the resulting omitted variable bias from unobserved variables can compromise both evaluation and optimization in language models. To address this challenge, we introduce a framework that maps the strength of the omitted variables to bounds on the worst-case generalization performance of language models under distribution shift. In empirical experiments, we show that using these bounds directly in language model evaluation and optimization provides more principled measures of out-of-distribution performance, improves true out-of-distribution performance relative to standard distribution shift adjustment methods, and further enables inference about the strength of the omitted variables when target distribution labels are available.

paragraphs: Language models can behave unpredictably when evaluation data differ from their training distribution. This paper separates such changes into observable and unobservable components. It argues that established distribution-shift adjustments address the observable part, leaving omitted-variable bias that can distort both assessments of model quality and the objectives used to improve it.

The proposed framework relates the strength of omitted variables to bounds on worst-case generalization performance. This turns hidden influences into an explicit sensitivity question: how unfavorable could performance become at a given level of unobserved shift? The bounds can then be used directly in evaluation and optimization rather than treating observable adjustments as sufficient.

Empirical experiments show more principled measures of out-of-distribution performance and improved actual performance compared with standard shift-adjustment methods. When labels from the target distribution are available, the framework also supports inference about omitted-variable strength. That label requirement matters for this additional inference result, while the broader contribution is incorporating unobserved shifts into the evaluation and optimization problem.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds language-model performance under unobserved distribution shifts and uses those bounds to improve evaluation and optimization.

title: Omitted Variable Bias in Language Models Under Distribution Shift

abstract: Estimating the quality of register transfer level (RTL) designs is crucial in the electronic design automation (EDA) workflow, as it enables instant feedback on key performance metrics like area and delay without the need for time-consuming logic synthesis. While recent approaches have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to derive embeddings from RTL code and achieved promising results, they overlook the structural semantics essential for accurate quality estimation. In contrast, the control data flow graph (CDFG) view exposes the design’s structural characteristics more explicitly, offering richer cues for representation learning. In this work, we introduce StructRTL, a novel structure-aware graph self-supervised learning framework for improved RTL design quality estimation. By learning structure-informed representations from CDFGs, StructRTL significantly outperforms prior art on various quality estimation tasks. To further boost performance, we incorporate a knowledge distillation strategy that transfers low-level insights from post-mapping netlists into the CDFG-based predictor. Experimental results demonstrate that StructRTL establishes new state-of-the-art results, highlighting the effectiveness of combining structural learning with cross-stage supervision.

paragraphs: Hardware designers need early estimates of properties such as circuit area and delay, without repeatedly running time-consuming logic synthesis. Models that represent register transfer level designs through code embeddings have shown promise, but the paper argues that they overlook structural information needed for accurate estimates. StructRTL makes that structure central to its learned representations.

The framework learns from control data flow graphs, which explicitly expose structural relationships within an RTL design. Its graph-based self-supervised learning approach builds representations informed by those relationships. It then adds knowledge distillation from post-mapping netlists, transferring lower-level design insights into the predictor that operates on the earlier graph representation.

This connects two stages of hardware design: structural information available in RTL and information revealed after mapping. The latter supplies additional training guidance for the former. Experiments report that StructRTL significantly outperforms prior methods across quality estimation tasks and establishes state-of-the-art results. The findings support using both graph structure and supervision from later design stages to improve early quality prediction.
summary.tldr: StructRTL improves early hardware quality estimates by learning circuit structure and distilling knowledge from post-mapping netlists.

title: Beyond Tokens: Enhancing RTL Quality Estimation via Structural Graph Learning

abstract: AI predictive systems increasingly support high-stakes decision making, yet robust decisions under uncertainty often rely on human capabilities beyond AI alone. This motivates collaborative approaches that combine human judgment with AI predictions. We study this problem through the lens of uncertainty quantification and introduce Human-AI Collaborative Uncertainty Quantification, a framework in which an AI system refines a human expert’s proposed prediction set subject to two principles: counterfactual harm, requiring that the AI not degrade correct human judgments, and complementarity, requiring recovery of correct outcomes the human missed. At the population level, we show that the optimal collaborative prediction set has a simple two-threshold structure over a single score function, governing pruning and augmentation relative to the human proposal. Building on this characterization, we develop offline and online calibration algorithms with distribution-free finite-sample guarantees. The online algorithm adapts to arbitrary distribution shifts, including settings where human behavior evolves through interaction with the AI. Empirically, we show that collaborative prediction sets outperform human-only and AI-only baselines, achieving improved coverage–efficiency tradeoffs across image classification, regression, and text-based medical decision making.

At the population level, we show that the optimal collaborative prediction set has a simple two-threshold structure over a single score function, governing pruning and augmentation relative to the human proposal. Building on this characterization, we develop offline and online calibration algorithms with distribution-free finite-sample guarantees. Empirically, we show that collaborative prediction sets outperform human-only and AI-only baselines, achieving improved coverage–efficiency tradeoffs across image classification, regression, and text-based medical decision making.

paragraphs: This paper studies how AI can refine a human expert's set of plausible predictions while preserving useful human judgment. Two principles govern the collaboration: counterfactual harm concerns degrading correct human judgments, while complementarity concerns recovering correct outcomes the human omitted. The aim is to improve the joint prediction set under both requirements.

At the population level, the authors characterize the optimal collaborative set using two thresholds applied to one score function. One threshold governs pruning the human proposal, and the other governs adding outcomes. This gives a simple structural description of how a system can make a human-provided set more selective while also correcting omissions.

The paper develops offline and online calibration algorithms with distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees. The online method adapts to arbitrary distribution shifts, including changes in human behavior during interaction. Across image classification, regression, and text-based medical decisions, collaborative sets improve the tradeoff between covering correct outcomes and keeping predictions efficient compared with human-only and AI-only baselines.
summary.tldr: Calibrated AI refinement of human prediction sets improves coverage–efficiency tradeoffs while accounting for harm and complementary corrections.

title: Human-AI Collaborative Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: Video editing has evolved toward In-Context Learning (ICL) paradigms, yet the resulting quadratic attention costs create a critical computational bottleneck. In this work, we propose In-context Sparse Attention (ISA), the first experimentally lossless sparse framework tailored for ICL video editing. Our design is grounded in two key insights: first, context tokens exhibit significantly lower saliency than source tokens; second, we theoretically prove and empirically validate that Query sharpness correlates with approximation error. Motivated by these findings, ISA implements an efficient pre-selection strategy to prune redundant context, followed by a dynamic query grouping mechanism that routes high-error queries to full attention and low-error ones to a computationally efficient 0-th order Taylor sparse attention. Furthermore, we construct a scalable pipeline to curate a 1M-sample dataset and train LIVEditor-14B, a novel lightning video editing model via ISA. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIVEditor-14B achieves a 60% reduction in latency while surpassing state-of-the-art methods across EditVerseBench, IVE-Bench, and VIE-Bench, delivering experimentally lossless acceleration without compromising visual fidelity.
originalAbstract: Video editing has evolved toward In-Context Learning (ICL) paradigms, yet the resulting quadratic attention costs create a critical computational bottleneck. In this work, we propose In-context Sparse Attention (ISA), the first experimentally lossless sparse framework tailored for ICL video editing. Our design is grounded in two key insights: first, context tokens exhibit significantly lower saliency than source tokens; second, we theoretically prove and empirically validate that Query sharpness correlates with approximation error. Motivated by these findings, ISA implements an efficient pre-selection strategy to prune redundant context, followed by a dynamic query grouping mechanism that routes high-error queries to full attention and low-error ones to a computationally efficient 0-th order Taylor sparse attention. Furthermore, we construct a scalable pipeline to curate a 1M-sample dataset and train LIVEditor-14B, a novel lightning video editing model via ISA. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIVEditor-14B achieves a 60% reduction in latency while surpassing state-of-the-art methods across EditVerseBench, IVE-Bench, and VIE-Bench, delivering experimentally lossless acceleration without compromising visual fidelity.

paragraphs: In-context video editing faces a substantial attention cost as the amount of information grows. This paper introduces In-context Sparse Attention, or ISA, to reduce that computation while preserving editing quality in experiments. Its design draws on observations about which tokens matter and which attention queries are difficult to approximate.

The authors find that context tokens have lower saliency than source tokens. ISA therefore first removes redundant context through pre-selection. They also theoretically and empirically connect query sharpness with approximation error. A dynamic grouping mechanism uses this insight to send high-error queries through full attention while processing low-error queries with a cheaper zeroth-order Taylor sparse approximation.

The team builds a one-million-sample dataset and uses ISA to train LIVEditor-14B. Across EditVerseBench, IVE-Bench, and VIE-Bench, the model reports a 60% latency reduction while outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The description of acceleration as lossless is explicitly experimental: the reported evaluations find preserved visual fidelity. The approach concentrates expensive computation on queries where approximation is most consequential.
summary.tldr: LIVEditor-14B uses selective sparse attention to reduce video-editing latency by 60% while preserving visual fidelity in the reported experiments.

title: LIVEditor-14B: Lightning Unified Video Editing via In-Context Sparse Attention

abstract: Many reinforcement learning (RL) problems admit multiple terminal solutions of comparable quality, where the goal is not to identify a single optimum but to represent a diverse set of high-quality outcomes. Nevertheless, policies trained by standard expected-return maximization routinely collapse onto a small subset of outcomes, a phenomenon commonly attributed to insufficient exploration or weak regularization. We show that this explanation is incomplete: outcome-level mode collapse is a structural consequence of the expected-return objective itself. Under idealized learning dynamics, the log-probability ratio between any two outcomes evolves linearly in their reward difference, implying exponential ratio divergence and inevitable collapse—independent of the exploration strategy, entropy regularization, or optimization algorithm. We identify the source of this pathology as the probability multiplier inside the expectation and propose a minimal correction: inverse probability scaling, which removes outcome-frequency amplification from the learning signal, fundamentally changes the learning dynamics, and provably yields reward-proportional terminal distributions, preventing collapse in multimodal settings. We instantiate this principle in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) as a drop-in modification, IPS-GRPO, requiring no auxiliary models or architectural changes. Across different reasoning and molecular generation tasks, IPS-GRPO consistently reduces outcome-level mode collapse while matching or exceeding baseline performance, suggesting that correcting the objective rather than adding exploration heuristics is key to reliable multimodal policy optimization.

Yet expected-return training often concentrates probability on only a few outcomes. This paper argues that limited exploration is an incomplete explanation: the objective itself can amplify outcomes that are already more likely.

Under idealized learning dynamics, the authors show that the log-probability ratio between two outcomes changes linearly with their reward difference. The results support changing the learning objective when diverse high-quality outcomes matter.
summary.tldr: Inverse probability scaling counters expected-return-driven outcome collapse and improves diversity in tested reasoning and molecular generation tasks.

title: Expected Return Causes Outcome-Level Mode Collapse in Reinforcement Learning and How to Fix It with Inverse Probability Scaling

abstract: Automated methods for discovering mechanistic simulator models from observational data offer a promising path toward accelerating scientific progress. Such methods often take the form of agentic-style iterative workflows that repeatedly propose and revise candidate models by imitating human discovery processes. However, existing LLM-based approaches typically implement such workflows via hand-crafted heuristic procedures, without an explicit probabilistic formulation. We recast model discovery as probabilistic inference, i.e., as sampling from an unknown distribution over mechanistic models capable of explaining the data. This perspective provides a unified way to reason about model proposal, refinement, and selection within a single inference framework. As a concrete instantiation of this view, we introduce ModelSMC, an algorithm based on Sequential Monte Carlo sampling. ModelSMC represents candidate models as particles which are iteratively proposed and refined by an LLM, and weighted using likelihood-based criteria. Experiments on real-world scientific systems illustrate that this formulation discovers models with interpretable mechanisms and improves posterior predictive checks. More broadly, this perspective provides a probabilistic lens for understanding and developing LLM-based approaches to model discovery.

paragraphs: Discovering a mechanistic simulator means finding a model whose internal processes can explain observed data. LLM-based discovery systems often propose a model, inspect its performance, and revise it through a manually designed workflow. This paper gives that process a probabilistic interpretation: discovery becomes sampling from a distribution over possible explanatory models.

The proposed algorithm, ModelSMC, implements this perspective using Sequential Monte Carlo. It maintains candidate models as particles, with an LLM proposing and refining those candidates over successive iterations. Likelihood-based weights assess how well candidates explain the observations. Proposal, revision, and selection therefore become connected parts of an inference procedure, with multiple possible explanations represented within the same framework.

Experiments on real scientific systems illustrate that ModelSMC finds models with interpretable mechanisms and improves posterior predictive checks, which assess how well inferred models account for observed behavior. The contribution is both an algorithm and a way to reason about discovery workflows. Its reported results support probabilistic organization of model search without claiming that a discovered mechanism must be the unique true explanation.
summary.tldr: ModelSMC organizes LLM-driven scientific model discovery as probabilistic inference over candidate mechanistic explanations.

title: A Probabilistic Framework for LLM-Based Model Discovery

abstract: Natural language data follows a power-law distribution, with most knowledge and skills appearing at very low frequency. While a common intuition suggests that reweighting or curating data toward a uniform distribution may help models better learn these long-tail skills, we find a counterintuitive result: across a wide range of compositional reasoning tasks, such as state tracking and multi-step arithmetic, training under power-law distributions consistently outperforms training under uniform distributions. To understand this advantage, we introduce a minimalist skill-composition task and show that learning under a power-law distribution provably requires significantly less training data. Our theoretical analysis reveals that power law sampling induces a beneficial asymmetry that improves the pathological loss landscape, which enables models to first acquire high-frequency skill compositions with low data complexity, which in turn serves as a stepping stone to efficiently learn rare long-tailed skills. Our results offer an alternative perspective on what constitutes an effective data distribution for training models.

paragraphs: Natural language contains a few frequent skills and many rare ones. It may therefore seem helpful to flatten the training distribution so that rare skills appear more often. This paper reports the opposite result across a range of compositional reasoning tasks: power-law sampling consistently outperforms uniform sampling, including in state tracking and multi-step arithmetic.

To investigate why, the authors introduce a minimal skill-composition task and prove that learning under a power-law distribution requires substantially less training data in that setting. Their analysis attributes the advantage to an asymmetry in sampling that improves a problematic loss landscape, making the learning process more favorable.

Frequent skill combinations become easier to acquire first, and those learned combinations provide a stepping stone toward rare skills. This mechanism offers an explanation for why unequal frequencies can help compositional learning rather than simply disadvantage the long tail. The empirical results and simplified theoretical task challenge the intuition that uniformity is always preferable, without establishing that every training problem benefits from a power-law distribution.
summary.tldr: Power-law training distributions improve compositional reasoning in the studied tasks by letting frequent skill combinations support learning of rarer ones.

title: The Power of Power Law: Asymmetry Enables Compositional Reasoning

abstract: Active mapping enables embodied agents to understand and interact in previously unseen environments. However, most methods struggle to achieve zero-shot generalization to large-scale scenes and lack support for language instructions. We propose a VLM-based active mapping method that achieves zero-shot mapping while facilitating language-driven human–agent interaction. First, we introduce a 360-BEV representation that integrates omnidirectional semantics with BEV-aligned geometric structure to enhance scene understanding. Second, we develop a candidate waypoint generation strategy that allows the VLM-driven agent to select informative 2D waypoints in image space and back-project them into executable metric actions in 3D space, enabling the VLM to plan in its strongest modality. Third, we design a VLM-based depth-first exploration agent that decomposes the scenes into explorable regions, selects informative waypoints within each region, and organizes them into a topological tree. The agent follows the depth-first exploration policy to achieve thorough coverage of large-scale scenes. Without task-specific training, our method outperforms the strongest baseline, improving coverage and AUC by approximately 13.25% and 14.00%, respectively, while enabling language-conditioned interaction.

paragraphs: Active mapping requires an embodied agent to choose where to explore while building an understanding of an unfamiliar environment. This paper uses a vision-language model to support mapping without task-specific training and to accept language-driven interaction. Its central representation combines omnidirectional semantic information with geometry aligned to a bird’s-eye view.

The agent selects informative candidate waypoints in two-dimensional image space, then back-projects them into executable three-dimensional metric actions. This lets the vision-language model make spatial choices through visual inputs while connecting those choices to movement. A depth-first exploration agent divides the scene into regions and organizes the selected waypoints into a topological tree.

Following that tree supports thorough exploration of large scenes. Without task-specific training, the method improves coverage by approximately 13.25% and AUC by approximately 14.00% over the strongest evaluated baseline, while enabling language-conditioned interaction. The findings support combining a fused visual representation, image-space waypoint selection, and structured exploration for the evaluated zero-shot mapping setting.
summary.tldr: A vision-language mapping agent combines panoramic semantics, bird’s-eye geometry, and depth-first exploration to improve zero-shot scene coverage.

title: Zero-shot Active Mapping via Fused 360-BEV Representations and Vision–Language Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with billions of parameters have transformed AI applications but require immense computational and memory resources during inference. Adaptive sparse activation inference, which activates only a small number of neurons for each token, offers a novel way to accelerate model inference without degrading performance, showing great potential for resource-constrained hardware devices. Yet existing token-level MLP-based methods frequently alter activation maps, reducing efficiency gains. In this paper, we introduce SparseInfer, an MLP-free adaptive sparse activation inference method based on sentence-level prediction. We first propose the concept of core neurons and empirically demonstrate that, for an input sentence, LLMs only need the core neurons to maintain performance. Remarkably, we discovered that core neurons exhibit both stability and similarity in relation to the sentence’s semantics—an insight overlooked by previous studies. Building on this finding, we design two semantic-based methods for predicting core neurons to fit different input scenarios, which enables core neurons to be determined during the pre-filling stage and fixed during the encoding stage. Our experiments verify SparseInfer exhibits good performance in various tasks and achieve 10.33$\times$ speed up.

paragraphs: Sparse activation can reduce language-model inference costs by using only a subset of neurons for each token. However, repeatedly changing the active subset can erode efficiency gains. SparseInfer investigates whether sentence-level meaning provides a more stable basis for selecting neurons, avoiding frequent changes associated with existing token-level, MLP-based selection methods.

The authors identify core neurons that empirically suffice to maintain performance for an input sentence. They find that these neurons exhibit stability and similarity related to sentence semantics. Using this observation, they design two semantic prediction methods for different input scenarios. The active neurons are selected during prefilling and kept fixed during the encoding stage, using an MLP-free selection approach.

Experiments report good performance across various tasks and a 10.33-times speedup. The central finding is that semantic regularity can support a more stable activation pattern, reducing the overhead of repeatedly deciding which neurons to use. The reported preservation of performance and acceleration are empirical results from the evaluated settings, rather than a universal speed or quality guarantee.
summary.tldr: SparseInfer predicts stable, sentence-dependent core neurons to accelerate sparse inference, reporting a 10.33-times speedup in its experiments.

title: SparseInfer: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference with Semantics-Inspired Adaptive Sparse Activation

abstract: Flow matching models (FMs) have revolutionized text-to-image (T2I) generation, with reinforcement learning (RL) serving as a critical post-training strategy. We show that current RL pipelines for FMs suffer from two underappreciated limitations: sample inefficiency from collapsed generation diversity, and prompt overfitting, where models memorize training phrasings and collapse on semantically equivalent paraphrases. We present PromptRL (Prompt Matters in RL for Flow-Based Image Generation), a framework that incorporates language models (LMs) as trainable prompt refinement agents directly within the flow-based RL loop, yielding both a learned prompt rewriter and a synergistic training regime that reshapes optimization dynamics. PromptRL attains state-of-the-art scores of 0.97 on GenEval, 0.98 on OCR accuracy, and 24.05 on PickScore, and on instructional editing it improves FLUX.1-Kontext from 1.19 to 1.43 EditReward with only 0.06M rollouts, surpassing Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (Nano Banana, 1.37) and matching ReasonEdit-Think (1.44), which relied on fine-grained data annotations and a multi-stage pipeline. Our experiments show that PromptRL achieves higher performance ceilings with approximately 50% fewer rollouts than naive flow-only RL. Our code is available at https://github.com/G-U-N/UniRL.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can improve flow-based image generators, but the paper identifies two weaknesses in current training pipelines. Collapsed generation diversity wastes samples, and prompt overfitting makes models depend on particular training phrasings. A model may consequently perform poorly when the same meaning is expressed through a different paraphrase.

PromptRL places a trainable language-model prompt refiner inside the reinforcement learning loop. Training produces both a learned prompt rewriter and a coupled optimization process for image generation. This makes prompt refinement part of how the generator learns, addressing the role of wording within the training process itself.

The authors report scores of 0.97 on GenEval, 0.98 OCR accuracy, and 24.05 PickScore. For instructional editing, FLUX.1-Kontext improves from 1.19 to 1.43 EditReward with 0.06 million rollouts, surpassing the reported Gemini 2.5 Flash Image score and approximately matching ReasonEdit-Think. summary.tldr: PromptRL trains prompt refinement inside the image-generation reinforcement learning loop, improving reported performance with approximately half as many rollouts.

title: PromptRL: Prompt Matters in RL for Flow-Based Image Generation

abstract: We study learning multi-task, multi-agent policies for cooperative, temporal objectives, under centralized training, decentralized execution. In this setting, using automata to represent tasks assigned to agents enables breaking down a team-level objective into simpler, smaller sub-tasks. However, existing approaches remain sample-inefficient and are limited to the single-task case, requiring retraining policies for each new task. In this work, we present Automata-Conditioned Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (ACC-MARL), a framework for learning task-conditioned, decentralized team policies. We identify challenges to the feasibility of ACC-MARL, propose solutions, and prove that our approach is optimal. We further show that learned value functions can be used to assign tasks optimally at test time. Experiments demonstrate emergent task-aware, multi-step coordination among agents, such as pressing a button to unlock a door, holding the door, and short-circuiting tasks.
