paragraphs: Cooperative tasks often require agents to coordinate actions over time, rather than simply act toward the same immediate reward. Automata provide a structured way to represent these objectives and divide a team task into smaller assignments. Existing approaches described in the paper are sample-inefficient and typically learn a policy for only one task, requiring retraining when the task changes.

ACC-MARL learns decentralized team policies conditioned on automata that represent the assigned tasks. Training is centralized, but agents execute their policies in a decentralized manner. This arrangement makes task structure part of what the policy responds to, rather than tying each policy to a single objective. The authors identify feasibility challenges, propose solutions, and prove optimality for their approach within the studied formulation.

The paper also shows that learned value functions can support optimal task assignment at test time. Experiments demonstrate coordinated sequences such as one agent pressing a button to unlock a door and another holding it open. These behaviors illustrate why representing task progress matters: useful cooperation can depend on actions whose contribution becomes apparent only through later steps.
summary.tldr: ACC-MARL conditions cooperative agents on task automata, enabling decentralized multi-step coordination and optimal task assignment within its formulation.

title: Automata-Conditioned Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Estimating full-hand grasp pressure from egocentric video is critical for immersive VR and robotic manipulation, yet dense tactile sensing often relies on intrusive hardware. Existing vision-based methods predominantly rely on planar surfaces or fingertip contacts, failing to generalize to complex 3D object interactions. Therefore, we introduce EgoTactile, a benchmark pairing egocentric video with full-hand pressure supervision for diverse everyday objects, incorporating a bare-hand transfer subset to enable generalization to natural scenarios. Leveraging this benchmark, we first establish EgoPressureFormer as a discriminative baseline. Beyond this, to explicitly address the uncertainty in partial observations, we propose EgoPressureDiff, a conditional diffusion framework that adapts a large-scale pre-trained video diffusion backbone. By combining rich world knowledge priors with a Physically-Informed Feature Rectification layer to inject semantic constraints, our approach effectively hallucinates plausible contact patterns and resolves visual-physical ambiguities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance on the benchmark and robust transferability to in-the-wild scenarios. Our project page is at https://egotactile.github.io/.

paragraphs: Estimating full-hand grasp pressure from a wearable camera could reduce reliance on intrusive tactile hardware. Existing visual methods often focus on fingertips or planar contacts, missing complex interactions with everyday objects. EgoTactile introduces data and models for that richer estimation problem.

The benchmark pairs egocentric video with full-hand pressure supervision and includes a bare-hand transfer subset. The authors establish EgoPressureFormer as a discriminative baseline, then propose EgoPressureDiff to represent uncertainty from partial views. The diffusion model adapts a pretrained video backbone and adds physically informed feature rectification to guide plausible contact patterns.

Experiments show stronger benchmark performance and transfer to in-the-wild scenarios. The contribution combines a dataset with an uncertainty-aware pressure predictor. Because hidden contacts are inferred from incomplete visual information, plausible generated patterns should be distinguished from direct tactile measurement; the abstract does not claim that every individual pressure estimate is physically exact.
summary.tldr: EgoTactile pairs egocentric video with full-hand pressure labels and uses conditional diffusion to infer plausible grasp patterns.

title: EgoTactile: Learning Grasp Pressure for Everyday Objects from Egocentric Video

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are emerging as versatile foundations for mixed-modality retrieval. Yet, they often require heavy post-hoc training to convert them into contrastive encoders for retrieval. This work asks: Can off-the-shelf MLLMs serve as powerful retrievers without additional training? We present FreeRet, a plug-and-play framework that turns any MLLM into a two-stage retriever. FreeRet first derives semantically grounded embeddings directly from the model for fast candidate search, and then exploits its reasoning ability for precise reranking. The framework contributes three advances: bypassing lexical alignment layers to obtain semantically faithful embeddings, conditioning representation generation with explicit priors, and mitigating framing effect in reranking via neutral choice framing. On the MMEB and MMEB-V2, FreeRet substantially outperforms models trained on millions of pairs. Beyond benchmarks, FreeRet is model-agnostic and scales seamlessly across MLLM families and sizes, preserves their generative abilities, supports arbitrary modality combinations, and unifies retrieval, reranking, and generation into end-to-end RAG within a single model. Our findings demonstrate that pretrained MLLMs, when carefully harnessed, can serve as strong retrieval engines without training, closing a critical gap in their role as generalists.

paragraphs: FreeRet investigates whether an existing multimodal language model can retrieve relevant material without additional training. Converting such models into retrieval encoders often requires substantial training after pretraining. The proposed framework instead organizes retrieval into two stages: a fast search using embeddings from the model, followed by more precise reranking using its reasoning abilities.

Three design choices support this conversion. FreeRet bypasses lexical alignment layers to extract representations that better preserve semantics, uses explicit priors to condition representation generation, and presents reranking choices neutrally to reduce framing effects. Together, these choices address both how candidates are represented and how the model compares them after the initial search.

On MMEB and MMEB-V2, the authors report substantial gains over models trained on millions of pairs. They describe the framework as applicable across model families, sizes, and modality combinations while retaining generative capabilities. This allows one model to handle retrieval, reranking, and generation within a retrieval-augmented generation workflow, reducing the need to train a separate retrieval capability.
summary.tldr: FreeRet turns pretrained multimodal language models into two-stage retrievers without additional training.

abstract: Large margin learning of Continuous Density Hidden Markov Models with a partially labeled dataset has been extensively studied in the speech and handwriting recognition fields. Yet due to the non convexity of the optimization problem, previous works usually rely on severe approximations so that it is still an open problem. We propose a new learning algorithm that relies on non convex optimization and bundle methods and allows tackling the original optimization problem as is. It is proved to converge to a solution with accuracy $\epsilon$ with a rate $O(1/\epsilon)$. We provide experimental results gained on speech recognition and on handwriting recognition that demonstrate the potential of the method.

paragraphs: Training continuous-density hidden Markov models with only partially labeled states creates a difficult large-margin optimization problem. This setting occurs in speech and handwriting recognition, where the available labels do not fully specify the underlying states. The abstract identifies nonconvexity as the obstacle that has led earlier approaches to use severe approximations.

The paper proposes an algorithm based on nonconvex optimization and bundle methods. Its purpose is to tackle the original training objective directly, preserving the problem that the large-margin formulation asks the learner to solve. This makes the optimization method itself the central contribution to learning from partially observed sequences.

The authors prove convergence to a solution with accuracy epsilon at a rate of O(1/epsilon). The abstract does not characterize this as a guarantee of global optimality, so the convergence result should retain that distinction. Experiments in speech recognition and handwriting recognition demonstrate the method's potential. Together, the theory and evaluations support addressing the original nonconvex objective with a dedicated algorithm.
summary.tldr: A nonconvex bundle-method algorithm directly trains partially labeled hidden Markov models and has a stated O(1/epsilon) convergence rate.

title: Large margin training for hidden Markov models with partially observed states

abstract: A nonparametric model is introduced that allows multiple related regression tasks to take inputs from a common data space. Traditional transfer learning models can be inappropriate if the dependence among the outputs cannot be fully resolved by known input-specific and task-specific predictors. The proposed model treats such output responses as conditionally independent, given known predictors and appropriate unobserved random effects. The model is nonparametric in the sense that the dimensionality of random effects is not specified a priori but is instead determined from data. An approach to estimating the model is presented uses an EM algorithm that is efficient on a very large scale collaborative prediction problem. The obtained prediction accuracy is competitive with state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: The paper considers several related regression tasks whose inputs come from a common data space. Known predictors may describe both individual inputs and the tasks themselves, yet still leave dependence among the outputs unexplained. The authors identify this situation as one in which traditional transfer-learning models can be inappropriate.

Their model adds unobserved random effects to account for that remaining dependence. Its stated assumption is conditional independence: once the known predictors and appropriate hidden random effects are given, the output responses are treated as independent. The model is nonparametric specifically because the number of dimensions used for the random effects is determined from data rather than fixed beforehand.

The authors estimate the model with an expectation-maximization algorithm and report that it is efficient on a very large collaborative prediction problem. Prediction accuracy is competitive with state-of-the-art results. The contribution connects a flexible representation of unexplained output dependence with an estimation method demonstrated at large scale, without claiming that the reported accuracy exceeds all competing methods.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric random-effects model learns hidden dependence across related regression tasks and supports efficient large-scale collaborative prediction.

title: Large-scale collaborative prediction using a nonparametric random effects model

abstract: We provide a novel view of learning an approximate model of a partially observable environment from data and present a simple implementation of the idea. The learned model abstracts away unnecessary details of the agent's experience and focuses only on making certain predictions of interest. We illustrate our approach empirically in small computational examples, demonstrating the data efficiency of the algorithm.
originalAbstract: We provide a novel view of learning an approximate model of a partially observable environment from data and present a simple implementation of the idea. The learned model abstracts away unnecessary details of the agent's experience and focuses only on making certain predictions of interest. We illustrate our approach empirically in small computational examples, demonstrating the data efficiency of the algorithm.

paragraphs: An agent in a partially observable environment has access to only part of what is happening. Learning from its experience therefore involves deciding what information a model should retain. This paper proposes a perspective on approximate modeling in which the model is organized around selected predictions of interest, rather than every detail appearing in the agent's experience.

The approach deliberately abstracts away details that are unnecessary for those predictions. Its purpose is to build a representation whose retained information serves the predictive questions being asked. The authors also provide a simple implementation, turning this perspective into an algorithm that can be learned from data. The approximation is thus tied to a chosen predictive focus.

Small computational examples illustrate the approach and demonstrate the algorithm's data efficiency. These results support the usefulness of concentrating modeling effort on relevant predictions within the examples studied. The stated evidence is specifically at that scale: the contribution combines a new way to frame approximate predictive modeling with an initial implementation and empirical demonstration.
summary.tldr: The paper learns approximate models of partially observable environments by retaining information needed for selected predictions, demonstrating data efficiency in small examples.

title: Approximate Predictive Representations of Partially Observable Systems

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of Rule Ensemble Learning (REL), where the goal is simultaneous discovery of a small set of simple rules and their optimal weights that lead to good generalization. Rules are assumed to be conjunctions of basic propositions concerning the values taken by the input features. From the perspectives of interpretability as well as generalization, it is highly desirable to construct rule ensembles with low training error, having rules that are i) simple, {\em i.e.}, involve few conjunctions and ii) few in number. We propose to explore the (exponentially) large feature space of all possible conjunctions optimally and efficiently by employing the recently introduced Hierarchical Kernel Learning (HKL) framework. The regularizer employed in the HKL formulation can be interpreted as a potential for discouraging selection of rules involving large number of conjunctions -- justifying its suitability for constructing rule ensembles. Simulation results show that the proposed approach improves over state-of-the-art REL algorithms in terms of generalization and indeed learns simple rules. Although this is encouraging, it can be shown that HKL selects a conjunction only if all its subsets are selected, and this is highly undesirable. We propose a novel convex formulation which alleviates this problem and generalizes the HKL framework. The main technical contribution of this paper is an efficient mirror-descent based active set algorithm for solving the new formulation. Empirical evaluations on REL problems illustrate the utility of generalized HKL.

paragraphs: Rule ensemble learning seeks a small collection of simple rules and suitable weights for combining them. Each rule joins basic conditions on input features. The difficulty is that all possible combinations form an exponentially large space, while interpretability and generalization favor selecting relatively few rules with relatively few conditions.

The paper applies Hierarchical Kernel Learning to explore this space efficiently. Its regularizer discourages rules containing many conditions, making the framework suitable for learning simple ensembles. Simulations show improved generalization over state-of-the-art rule ensemble methods and confirm that the approach learns simple rules.

The authors also identify an undesirable restriction: the framework selects a conjunction only when all its subsets are selected. They propose a more general convex formulation that alleviates this restriction. Their main technical contribution is an efficient active-set algorithm based on mirror descent for solving the new problem. Empirical evaluations support the usefulness of this generalized framework for rule ensemble learning.
summary.tldr: A generalized hierarchical-kernel formulation efficiently learns simple rule ensembles while easing an undesirable rule-selection restriction.

title: Efficient Rule Ensemble Learning using Hierarchical Kernels
